10149-home-as-found-sequel-to-homeward-b:
James Fenimore Cooper published this novel in the 1830s as the sequel to Homeward Bound, and this edition dates from 1871. It picks up where the earlier book left off, following Americans home after years abroad. Cooper warns that readers who skip the first book may miss the thread.

The story satirizes American manners, talk, and social climbing, through characters who praise Europe one moment and scorn it the next. Pride, gossip, and new wealth drive much of the comedy and sting. Readers get a sharp, sometimes testy portrait of young America judging itself.
10490-the-golden-legend:
Henry Wadsworth Longfellow wrote this verse drama, opening at night in storm on the spire of Strasburg Cathedral. Lucifer and the powers of the air try to tear down the iron cross, while saints, angels, and bells defy them with holy water and song. The prologue sets a medieval, musical world of faith and struggle.

The legend follows a prince, a maiden, and a pilgrimage through trials, miracles, and grace, in Longfellow's smooth, popular verse. Bells, spires, and painted glass fill the scenes. Readers get a beautiful, old-style poetic drama of medieval faith, still pleasant for reading aloud.
10494-henry-the-second:
Mrs. J. R. Green wrote this biography of Henry II, first of the Plantagenet kings, in chapters that move from his youth to his empire and government. Green, a respected historian, treats Henry as a maker of English law and rule, not merely as a king of wars and quarrels. The book is clear, scholarly, and readable.

Chapters cover the Angevin empire, government of England, first reforms, Constitutions and Assize of Clarendon, strife with the church, conquest of Ireland, and revolt of the baronage. Each stage shows Henry building a stronger state. Readers get a solid, classic life of a great medieval king.
10588-seeing-europe-with-famous-authors-:
Francis W. Halsey selected and edited Seeing Europe with Famous Authors, a ten-volume travel anthology, and this first volume covers Great Britain and Ireland. Passages by famous writers guide the reader from landing at Liverpool, Fishguard, or Plymouth, through the customs house and the train to London, and on into British towns and country.

The book pairs practical travel notes with literary description, so a visitor sees both how a journey was made and how good writers felt about the places. Nelson, Drake, and other historic names appear as the tour moves past harbors and battle sites. Armchair travelers get a rich, old-fashioned tour of Britain, told in the voices of its best-known authors.
10612-supply-and-demand:
Hubert Henderson, an English economist, published Supply and Demand in 1922, with an introduction by John Maynard Keynes. The book sets out to explain how prices are set, how work is divided, and how buyers and sellers react to each other. It was written as a clear guide to economic ideas for readers who were not trained economists.

Chapters take up the division of labor, the laws of supply and demand, the value people place on goods, the cost of making them, and the ups and downs of trade. Henderson uses simple diagrams and everyday cases, such as coal, to show why prices move and why markets sometimes swing. The book still reads as a plain, careful primer on how a market economy works.
10861-paris-under-the-commune-the-sevent:
John Leighton published Paris Under the Commune in 1871, an account of the seventy-three days of the second siege, with illustrations and sketches taken on the spot and portraits from photographs. Leighton writes as a hostile witness: socialism, or the red republic, would tear down the tricolor, melt the Vendome Column, and raise Marat over Napoleon.

The book follows the Commune's rule, its decrees, and its fall, from inside Paris. Its pictures give the volume lasting value as a visual record. Readers get a vivid, partisan history of 1871, from an Englishman who watched the barricades.
11-alice-s-adventures-in-wonderland:
A bored girl follows a waistcoated rabbit down a hole and lands in a world of odd rules. Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland began as a tale told on a river trip. Twelve chapters carry Alice through tears, keys, doors, and talking beasts.

She meets the Caterpillar, the Cheshire Cat, the Mad Hatter, and the Queen of Hearts. Size shifts, riddles, and croquet with flamingos test her logic at every turn. The book ends with a trial over stolen tarts. Its wordplay made it a lasting classic for children and adults alike.
11013-letters-of-a-traveller-or-notes-of:
William Cullen Bryant, American poet and editor, gathered letters written over sixteen years of travel in Europe and America, published in 1850. Bryant warns that the letters are occasional sketches, not a regular tour, and he avoids gossip about distinguished men he met. Most had already appeared in print.

Letters describe first impressions of France, Paris churches and cemeteries, Florence in autumn, Venice, and the Rhine valley, then turn to America: Rock River in Illinois, lynch law, horse thieves. Bryant observes scenery, customs, and institutions with a poet's eye. The book gives a mid-century American's view of two continents, calm, curious, and well written.
11119-personal-memoirs-of-a-residence-of:
Henry R. Schoolcraft published these personal memoirs in 1851, covering a residence of thirty years with the Indian tribes on the American frontiers, from 1812 to 1842. Schoolcraft dedicates the book to Alexander B. Johnson of Utica, recalling their journey to the Genesee country, then called the Garden of the West, which led him to deeper inroads into the wilderness.

Schoolcraft disclaims autobiography or a methodical record of his times, offering instead brief memoranda in diary form, from a position on the frontiers connected with the management of Indian tribes. He returned to New York after many years in the Mississippi Valley, his name already associated with distinguished actors in western history. The memoirs remain a first-hand source on exploration, frontier life, and United States Indian policy in the early nineteenth century.
11138-comic-history-of-england:
Bill Nye wrote this comic history of England, from the Druids to Henry VIII, illustrated by W. W. Goodes and A. M. Richards and published in 1896. Nye promises that dates and facts are correct, but the lights and shades, pictures, and ornamental words adorning characters and events are his own invention. A preface notes with regret that Nye's illness prevented him from writing his own humorous foreword, or carrying the history beyond Henry VIII's marriage to Anne Boleyn.

Chapters cover Caesar's invasion and the discovery of tin, the Roman yokes, the Angles, the Danes, the troublous Middle Ages, and the Danish oligarchy. A popular knight wears a crest adorned with German favours from lady admirers, like a slump at the Bon Marché. Nye's history amuses while keeping its facts straight.
11226-building-a-state-in-apache-land:
Drawn from articles by Charles D. Poston in the Overland Express, this 1894 account explains how Arizona Territory took shape after the United States acquired land from Mexico. Poston starts with California politicians debating a southern railroad route and the treaty obligations that pushed Washington toward a new purchase. He then follows the practical work of organizing a territory on a violent frontier.

Apache resistance, mining interests, and federal politics all shape the story, and Poston writes as a participant rather than a distant observer. The result reads as both memoir and political history, useful for readers who want the Arizona story from someone who helped argue for it. Its plain, argumentative prose keeps the focus on land, law, and survival.
11324-this-is-the-end:
Stella Benson's 1917 book This Is The End opens with an unfinal conclusion. there is no reason in tangible things and no system in the ordinary ways of the world, only unaccountable things to count on. Hands grope, feet stumble, and a policeman might grow wings or the sea wash out the land without surprising the narrator. She introduces Jay, a bus-conductor and idealist, as the most constantly apparent woman in the book, though not its heroine.

Benson's narrator questions everything, answering Be Good and other accepted facts with Why. The book blends fantasy, satire, and wartime London observation in a voice both whimsical and bleak. Readers who enjoy unconventional novels will find its refusal of system its main argument.
11399-the-pirates-of-malabar-and-an-engl:
Colonel John Biddulph's 1907 book, The Pirates of Malabar and an Englishwoman in India Two Hundred Years Ago, joins two narratives of the Indian seas. The piracy chapters trace Portuguese, Dutch, and West Indian rovers, Every's seizure of the Charles the Second, the Madagascar settlements. the capture of the Gunj Suwaie, and Captain Kidd's career from the Adventure to the Quedah Merchant, with danger to English trade at Surat and Bombay throughout.

The Englishwoman's story adds a domestic counterpart to maritime violence. Biddulph, a soldier-historian, writes with archival detail and adventure pacing. The book remains a readable introduction to Indian Ocean piracy and East India Company life at the turn of the eighteenth century.
11489-some-historical-account-of-guinea-:
Anthony Benezet's 1771 Some Historical Account of Guinea, reprinted in London in 1772, describes Guinea's situation, produce, and inhabitants, then inquires into the slave trade's rise, progress, nature, and lamentable effects. Chapters cover the Senegal and Gambia rivers, Ivory, Gold, and Slave Coasts, Benin, Kongo, and Angola. Arabian and Portuguese descents, English traders violently carrying off natives, and slavery under pagans and Turks compared with colonies. Extracts from Granville Sharp and others close the argument.

Benezet, a Philadelphia Quaker, grounds abolition in scripture, Acts on one blood for all nations, and in testimony from travelers and philosophers including Montesquieu. The book is among the earliest systematic American attacks on slavery. For historians, it marks Quaker abolitionism turning to print and evidence.
11490-american-negro-slavery-a-survey-of:
Ulrich Bonnell Phillips surveys American slavery from the first Portuguese seizures on the west coast of Africa to the plantation regime of the American South. Chapters follow the maritime slave trade, the sugar islands, the tobacco colonies, and the rice coast, then the closing of the African trade and the rise of cotton.

Later chapters deal with large plantations, their management and labour, town slaves, free Black people, slave crime, and the force of law. Plantation rules quoted in the book, down to nursing times for mothers, show how closely the system ordered daily life.
11554-the-crimes-of-england:
Gilbert K. Chesterton's 1916 book answers a German professor, whom he calls Professor Whirlwind, and takes up where England is really wrong. Chapters move from the Protestant hero and Frederick the Great to the enigma of Waterloo, the coming of the Janissaries, and German mercenaries in English service.

Later chapters deal with Ireland and Heligoland, the dirty work of empire, and Cobbett, defeated, as the writer sees it, because the English people were defeated. Peterloo, Chesterton argues, was as much a defeat for England as Waterloo was for France. The book is a wartime polemic, sharp and partisan.
11585-the-young-emigrants-madelaine-tube:
Published by Charles Scribner in 1851, this children's volume binds four tales together. The Young Emigrants follows a family at sea, in the New World, and in a new home, with a narrow escape, an intruder, and chapters on striving and thriving.

Madelaine Tube tells of a broken cup, poverty, Christmas gifts, and a journey to the baths at Toeplitz, where an operation restores sight. The Boy and the Book and The Crystal Palace complete the set. All four mix adventure with moral lessons, written for young readers of the 1850s.
11599-withered-leaves-from-memory-s-garl:
Abigail Stanley Hanna's 1857 volume gathers poems and prose pieces. Its title is Withered Leaves from Memory's Garland. An index lists shadows of the past and the old homestead. The old schoolhouse and the graveyard appear there too.

Later pieces include an evening in a village and thoughts in a graveyard. A scene on the Kennebec River follows. One piece tells of a girl drowned in a rapid current. Her withered bouquet was covered in green slime. The book is a New England keepsake of loss, home, and passing years. Later pieces include the fatal feast, lines to a maiden, and verses on the frailty of earthly things.
11703-the-swiss-family-robinson-or-adven:
The Swiss Family Robinson, or Adventures in a Desert Island, follows a family shipwrecked and left to build a life from nothing. Its preface says few books won such deserved popularity, and every young reader chose a favourite son: noble Fritz, studious Ernest, or generous Jack.

The family's progress, the preface says, runs from utter destitution to happiness and abundance, through labour, perseverance, and obedience. An early scene has the father thanking God for lives saved, then telling his wife Elizabeth that their sons are given back a second time. The Baroness de Montolieu supplied the ending the first author left unfinished.
11917-the-story-of-ireland:
Emily Lawless's Story of Ireland, in the Story of the Nations series and published in New York and London in 1896, with additions by Mrs. Arthur Bronson, opens with Holy Island on Lough Derg. Dedicated to the Earl of Dufferin, then Viceroy of India, it surveys Irish history from early times to the modern period.

Lawless, author of Hurrish, follows kings, invaders, and rebels: John marching from Carrickfergus through Downpatrick and Drogheda to Dublin. English soldiers pursuing a nephew of the late Desmond, derisively called the Sugane Earl, or Earl of Straw, in league with Tyrone. The narrative favors vivid episodes and strong personalities over constitutional detail, in the popular-history style of its series.
1193-the-coxon-fund:
Henry James tells of Frank Saltram, a brilliant talker who lives off friends' charity, and of the Coxon Fund, a bequest meant to support genius. The narrator, a young writer, watches Saltram charm, borrow, and fail, while a practical American offers the fund with strings attached.

The novella turns on a question: should genius be kept alive at any cost, and who pays? James writes the dilemma in his fine, ironic prose, with no easy verdict. The tale stands as a sharp study of art, money, and friendship. James leaves the question open, and the tale still provokes debate.
11998-sight-to-the-blind:
Lucy Furman's 1914 story Sight to the Blind, with an introduction by Ida Tarbell and dedicated to Harriet Butler, opens at the Settlement School on Perilous in the Kentucky mountains. One morning in early September, Miss Shippen, the trained nurse, sets off for district-visiting over on Clinch, accompanied by Miss Loring, another worker.

After riding up Perilous Creek, the visitors carry medicine, teaching, and practical help into isolated homes, where blindness and poverty meet. Furman, who knew settlement work from inside, writes about mountain families with respect and humor. The story becomes a portrait of women doing public-health and educational work in a place the wider world had largely forgotten.
12020-a-woman-of-the-world-her-counsel-t:
Ella Wheeler Wilcox's A Woman of the World offers counsel to other people's sons and daughters in the form of letters. It was first published in 1904 and in a fourth impression by April 1910. Addressees include Ray Gilbert, a law student aged twenty-three, Winifred Clayborne at Vassar College, Edna Gordon during her honeymoon, and Gladys Weston facing necessity.

Wilcox, a popular poet and journalist, writes as an experienced woman of the world advising the young on love, marriage, work, and conduct. The letters are direct and moral without being priggish. They capture an era when advice literature spoke personally, one young person at a time, rather than in general rules.
12033-what-s-the-matter-with-ireland:
Ruth Russell's 1920 book What's the Matter with Ireland is dedicated to her mother. It asks its title question through chapters on Sinn Féin and revolution, Irish labor and class revolution, AE's peaceful revolution, the Catholic Church and communism, and what about Belfast. A letter from the elected government of the Republic of Ireland, American delegation, dated January 29, 1920, addresses Miss Ruth Russell of Chicago, Illinois.

Russell, a journalist, reports from a country in the midst of its war of independence, interviewing leaders, workers, and clergy. Her book captures American interest in Ireland at a moment when Irish-Americans, labor, and the Catholic Church all pressed Washington to notice what was happening across the Atlantic.
12111-the-glories-of-ireland:
The Glories of Ireland, edited by Joseph Dunn and P. J. Lennox, professors at the Catholic University of America, appeared in 1914 and is dedicated to the Irish race in every land. Its epigraph from John Boyle O'Reilly declares that Ireland's life has been a symbol, only partly read. That God will flood her yet with sunshine for the woes that drench her heart.

Dunn and Lennox, writing from Washington, D.C., in November of the previous year, gather essays on Irish history, literature, art, and faith. The volume belongs to the Irish cultural revival in America, presenting Ireland's glories not as antiquarian curiosities but as a living heritage for emigrants and their children.
12221-beggars-bush-a-comedy-from-the-wor:
Beggars Bush, a comedy by Beaumont and Fletcher, is set in Flanders, where Wolfort has usurped the earldom and Gerrard, falsely called Clause, rules as king of the beggars. The cast mixes lords, merchants, courtiers, and beggars in a plot of lost rank and hidden birth.

Florez, a rich merchant of Bruges falsely called Goswin, and Bertha, falsely called daughter to a drunken merchant, move through disguises, while Hubert, an honest lord, works to restore right. Beggars sing, hunt, and mourn with bell-horn and funeral tears, and the comedy turns on revelation: who is truly noble, and who merely plays the part. The play shows the partners love of disguise, low company, and sudden reversals of fortune.
12291-the-teacher-moral-influences-emplo:
Jacob Abbott published The Teacher in a new and revised edition in 1873, on moral influences employed in the instruction and government of the young. Abbott, a prolific writer for children and teachers, details a system for organizing and managing a school.

The preface promises a familiar and practical account of school arrangements, with engravings. A mid-book passage treats parental affection as a moral force in every human soul, which teachers may use without interfering with home. Abbott argues for government by influence rather than fear: order through habit, kindness, and clear rules. The book shaped American common-school teaching, and it reads as a humane manual from the age of the one-room school.
12402-the-poets-and-poetry-of-cecil-coun:
George Johnston collected and edited The Poets and Poetry of Cecil County, Maryland, published at Elkton in 1887. Johnston, author of the History of Cecil County, gathered the volume at the desire of teachers and pupils in public schools.

The preface quotes Herbert: a verse may find him whom a sermon flies, and turn delight into sacrifice. Poems celebrate county scenes, with dogwood and myrtle scent, jessamine, and great yellow petals heavy with perfume like the tube rose. Local bards, schoolteachers, and amateurs fill the pages. The book is a charming piece of local literary history, preserving verse that would otherwise vanish with its authors.
12532-the-shades-of-the-wilderness-a-sto:
Joseph A. Altsheler's Civil War novel, seventh in his series, follows Lee's great stand in the Wilderness. Principal characters return from earlier volumes: Harry Kenton, fighting for the South, and his cousin Dick Mason, fighting for the North, with their fathers, commanders and servants around them.

Battles, scouting and camp life carry the story, as cousins meet war from opposite sides. Altsheler writes for young readers in a clear, patriotic style, favouring courage and loyalty over irony. The novel forms one chapter in a long series that runs from Bull Run and Shiloh through Gettysburg and Chickamauga to Appomattox.
12558-snarleyyow-or-the-dog-fiend:
Captain Marryat's Snarleyyow, or The Dog Fiend, is the earliest of three novels in its prefatory note's grouping, here in an 1895 printing. Fifty-five chapters follow a dog fiend, a creature of ill omen aboard ship and ashore, through naval life, smuggling and coastal adventure. Marryat, himself a naval officer, writes from service experience.

The dog, Snarleyyow, becomes a focus for superstition, comedy and menace, as sailors blame him for mishaps and enemies use him for mischief. Marryat mixes sea story, humour and gothic fancy in his robust style. The novel remains a curious, entertaining example of naval romance, where a dog carries as much plot as any human villain.
12569-through-the-mackenzie-basin-a-narr:
Charles Mair's narrative of the Athabasca and Peace River Treaty Expedition of 1899, dedicated to David Laird, leader of the expedition, follows the treaty party through the Mackenzie Basin. Chapter one runs from Edmonton to Lesser Slave Lake, with treaty and half-breed commissions, Athabasca Landing, a gas well, boats, trackers and police volunteers.

Burnt forests, muskegs, tracking difficulties, the old tracker Peokus, river scenery, placer mining and fertile soil fill the account. Later chapters reach Lesser Slave River and Lake, and treaty councils beyond. Mair writes as a participant-observer, vivid on land and people. The book is a key source for Treaty Eight and the Canadian north.
12585-seaward-sussex-the-south-downs-fro:
Edric Holmes's 1920 Seaward Sussex, the South Downs from end to end, walks the downs with one hundred illustrations by Mary M. Vigers and maps by the author. A Tempest verse fronts the book, asking how to tell of downs freedom to lovers of dusty towns who think flowers only embroider gowns.

Holmes thanks M. A. Lower, first serious historian of Sussex, and successors who were good companions of the way, for teaching him things beautiful and precious. Hurstmonceux illustrates the volume. Holmes writes as a walker-historian, fond of villages, churches and chalk hills. The book offers a leisurely, illustrated tramp across Sussex, from end to end.
12689-the-high-school-freshmen-or-dick-c:
H. Irving Hancock's High School Freshmen, or Dick and Co.'s First Year Pranks and Sports, follows Dick Prescott and friends through freshman year at Gridley. Chapters run from the high school sneak and Dick and Co. after the school board's scalps through captain of the hounds, muckers and gentleman, a locker mystery, a suspended freshman and Laura Bentley wide awake.

Tip Scammon talks but not enough, a welcome with a big W, and football boosted follow. An oath of the dub, gridiron play, a fake kick, a find that makes Gridley shiver and a toboggan outing close the year. Hancock writes brisk schoolboy sport and mystery, where team work and fair play win. The book is a lively start to a long Gridley series.
12690-the-high-school-pitcher-or-dick-co:
Hancock's Gridley school story follows Dick Prescott and his friends as they build a baseball nine worth cheering. A new principal, a sly rival named Ripley, and a training camp full of schemes stand in their way. Tryouts, pranks, and a final big game give the plot its shape.

Dick's pitcher's arm matters less, in the end, than fair play: the boys face cheating, bullying, and a crowd ready to back a wrong. Dave Darrin and the rest of Dick and Co. supply loyalty and laughs. Young readers get a spirited tale of school sport, teamwork, and standing up to a sneak.
12762-the-story-of-a-piece-of-coal-what-:
Edward A. Martin published this short popular science book in 1896, tracing one lump of coal from its start to its end uses. He opens with the plants of the coal forests and the rock layers that buried them, then moves through the kinds of coal and carbon found in the earth. Mining, gas making, tar products, and dyes all get their turn in plain chapters.

Later pages weigh the smoke and fog that coal fires caused in British towns, and ask how long home supplies might last. Martin also covers oils, coke, and the bright colours drawn from coal tar, showing how a dull black rock fed light, heat, and trade. Readers come away with a clear map of coal as plant matter, fuel, and raw stuff for a whole new chemical trade.
12815-american-cookery-the-art-of-dressi:
Amelia Simmons published American Cookery at Hartford in 1796, the first cookbook written by an American for American cooks. She gives methods for meats, fish, poultry, vegetables, pastes, pies, puddings, custards, preserves, and cakes, from plain cake to imperial plum. Her preface speaks to young women and to orphans who must earn a living in service.

Recipes use local stuff and plain measures: stuffed legs, corned pork, alamode beef, and roast joints with gravy and ketchup. The book's fame rests on its American voice and its early use of native foods. It remains a landmark for food historians and for cooks curious about the early republic's table.
12971-the-man-in-lonely-land:
The Man in Lonely Land, by Kate Langley Bosher in 1912, is a novel about Winthrop Laine, a man who lives alone with his collie, General. Laine comes home soaked from two weeks of rain, sleet, and snow to find his old dog no better, and the book follows his slow return to company. Dorothea, Claudia, and a circle of kin draw him out.

Tea trays, shopping trips, Christmas calls, and a visit to Virginia carry the plot, while a young girl wonders aloud whether Uncle Winthrop wants Claudia for a sweetheart. The charm lies in its warm domestic comedy and in Laine's change from a solitary man to one who belongs again.
12981-the-thirsty-sword-a-story-of-the-n:
Robert Leighton's Thirsty Sword tells of the Norse invasion of Scotland in 1262 and 1263, opening on a bright June evening in Bute. A girl in grey homespun with a crimson girdle walks a stream bank, longing for Kenric, when a dead capercailzie with an arrow in its breast falls at her feet. A stalwart youth bounds from the trees to claim his shot.

Later a king's court hears grievances, from a maid promised in marriage to a farmer whose watchdog was slain, after which wolves took his sheep and goats. Leighton blends island legend, sea warfare, and young love. The novel offers stirring historical romance for readers who like Norse Scotland.
13109-about-ireland:
E. Lynn Linton's 1890 book on Ireland begins with a frank apology: she writes on a subject she does not half know. Linton had once been an ardent Home Ruler, moved by sentiment and abstract principle, and she now retraces how her own mind changed. The book is thus a personal account of a political conversion, not a cold history.

Linton writes of land agents who never left home without armed guards, and of tenants who might buy their holdings with government loans at four percent. She sets out how rent could turn into an annuity that ended after forty-nine years. Her case rests on order, property, and slow reform, and it shows one English view of Ireland at a moment of fierce debate.
13226-the-common-people-of-ancient-rome-:
Frank Frost Abbott, Kennedy Professor of Latin at Princeton, published The Common People of Ancient Rome in 1911, a companion to his Society and Politics in Ancient Rome. Abbott treats common folk, their language and literature, work and play, and social, political, and economic life. His preface says plain Romans, not emperors, are his subject.

Chapters sample vulgar Latin from the Twelve Tables, with short, blunt laws on summoning a man to court. Later pages quote Augustus, who restored eighty-two temples in his sixth consulship and built theatres, roads, and bridges. Abbott also notes that Romans expected largesse from leaders, military or civil. The book is a clear, scholarly guide to Rome from below.
13372-the-gloved-hand:
Burton E. Stevenson's 1913 detective story, first published in The Popular Magazine as The Mind Master, opens with a falling star, a strange neighbour, and drama in a garden. Sparks fall on white-robed figures, and a tall man in a rich purple robe, dark haired and magnetic, enters the tale with an air of uncanny power.

Miss Vaughan, alone and nervous in a house that needs watching, becomes the focus of help and suspicion. The narrator offers aid, follows clues, and finds her seated in the library, steadier than expected. Stevenson mixes stage-like mystery with detective work, letting a supposed master of minds test how far fear, suggestion, and plain observation can explain strange events.
13425-wit-without-money-a-comedy-the-wor:
Beaumont and Fletcher's comedy Wit Without Money centres on Valentine, a gallant who will not be persuaded to keep his estate. His younger brother Francisco, his uncle Master Lovegood, and companions Fountain, Bellamore, and Hairbrain, all suitors to a widow, crowd the stage with servants, musicians, and the clown Shorthose.

Lady Hartwel, the widow, her sister Isabel, and waiting woman Luce drive the wit war. Valentine mocks annuities, harvests, timber, and coal as food for hinds, and complains of being made a ladder for a woman's wit, flouted and shown to chambermaids like a strange beast. The comedy turns on money spent, pride kept, and love won by sharp talk.
1367-findelkind:
Ouida, the pen name of Louise de la Ramée, tells of Findelkind, a Tyrolean boy who lives under the shadow of the Martinswand, the mountain where Kaiser Max once hung in peril. The boy, found as a child, grows up among shepherds and goats, with a kind heart and a taste for the wild.

The tale is a children's idyll of mountain life, with danger, loyalty, and a happy ending. Ouida writes the Alps with sentiment and color. The story, a companion to A Dog of Flanders, suits young readers who like old-style tales of brave children.
13731-romance-island:
Zona Gale set this 1906 fantasy novel in New York and on a hidden island. A young newspaper man named St. George and his friend Amory take a strange commission. They must find a prince and a kingdom that most people call mere legend. Olivia, a sharp and warm-hearted woman, joins their quest and soon shapes its course.

On the island, old customs, court intrigue, and magic test every traveller. St. George must learn to act with courage rather than clever talk. Gale mixes humour, romance, and fairy-tale wonder without losing sight of character. The ending turns on loyalty and love, not on force. The novel reads as a light fable about growing up and believing in more than the visible world.
13922-the-visionary-pictures-from-nordla:
Jonas Lie wrote The Visionary, or Pictures from Nordland, translated from Norwegian by Jessie Muir in 1894. Lie pictures Nordland and its people through a childhood lived in open air. Chapters visit home, shore, servants' hall, and rocks of the vætte. Confirmation, a Christmas visit, a storm, and Trondenæs follow.

Lie opens by noting people who choose bad weather to go out, often men raised outdoors. His narrator grows suspicious of simple views of people and disease, suspecting every mortal of hidden causes. The book blends memoir, folk tale, and northern scenery. It suits readers of Scandinavian literature. Lie's northern light and sea air pervade every page.
13932-whosoever-shall-offend:
F. Marion Crawford published Whosoever Shall Offend in 1905, a Roman novel of youth, guilt, and protection. Its epigraph warns that offending little ones deserves a millstone and drowning. Illustrations by Horace T. Carpenter, drawn in Rome, picture an Italian voice calling a hero by name and a professor naming the sleeping death.

Crawford follows a mother who wishes her son manly at all points, yet dreams he might stay a glorified young girl. Rome's streets, churches, and society frame the moral drama. The novel blends romance with Catholic feeling. Crawford, author of Saracinesca, writes with his usual polish. It suits readers of Italian historical romance.
13944-after-london-or-wild-england:
Richard Jefferies imagined England after London's fall in this 1885 romance. Part one, The Relapse into Barbarism, describes a great forest, wild animals, men of the woods, invaders, and a lake. Part two, Wild England, follows Sir Felix of the House of Aquila through stockades, canoes, and forest tracks. Thyma Castle, feasts, and superstitions follow.

Legions of mice destroy small garden crops, showing nature reclaiming human order. Jefferies blends natural history with adventure and social satire. His future England feels both strange and familiar. The novel influenced later post-apocalyptic fiction. It remains Jefferies' most famous work of imagination.
14001-the-mississippi-bubble-how-the-sta:
Emerson Hough wrote The Mississippi Bubble in 1902, a novel of John Law of Lauriston and his famous scheme. Law, a returned traveller, moves through Sadler's Wells, points of honour, and diverse employments. Two maids, a resolution, and a woman's grace shape his rise, fall, and rise again. Henry Hutt illustrated the volume.

Hough sets Law's paper money and Mississippi Company in Paris and London, with coureurs des bois in Quebec and Montréal. Du Mesne notes such runners care naught for law and little for king. The novel mixes history with romance and adventure. It explains a financial bubble through a life story. Readers of historical fiction will enjoy its scope.
14012-ice-caves-of-france-and-switzerlan:
The Rev. G. F. Browne, fellow of St. Catharine's College, Cambridge, wrote this 1865 narrative of ice caves in France and Switzerland. Natural ice caves lie fifty to two hundred feet below the surface, unconnected with glaciers. They appear where ice should not exist under ordinary conditions. Little was known of them in England.

Browne describes hunting for a châlet near La Baronne, spreading out to search wood and glade. His party explores glacières with care and wonder. The narrative blends Alpine travel with early speleology. Browne, a member of the Alpine Club, writes plainly and well. The book suits readers of exploration and natural history.
1413-tom-tiddler-s-ground:
This Christmas story opens with a traveller asking a landlord why a patch of ground bears the odd name Tom Tiddler's Ground. The answer leads to a solitary man, Mr Mopes, who scatters halfpence for tramps and lives apart from the world, and the traveller sets out to learn what drove him there.

Through talk with neighbours and a visit to the hermit himself, the tale weighs solitude against company, and charity against pride. It is short, wry, and full of roadside humour. The ending offers a plain moral about the cost of shutting oneself away from other people.
1431-trooper-peter-halket-of-mashonaland:
Olive Schreiner's protest novel follows Peter Halket, a young trooper serving in Rhodesia during the Matabele rising. On patrol he meets a wounded stranger, nurses him, and hears a plain moral challenge to the violence, land theft, and hangings carried out around him in the name of empire.

Halket's slow change of heart drives the book, which closes with a stark frontispiece scene of men hanged from a tree. Written in anger at colonial cruelty, it is short, direct, and unsparing. It stands as an early voice against the harsh rule of chartered companies in Africa.
1442-the-kingdom-of-the-blind:
E. Phillips Oppenheim's spy novel opens in the lounge of the Ritz Hotel, where Lady Anselman counts her guests among actors, diplomats, and men of uncertain trade. Beneath the glitter, a network of spies moves secrets across Europe on the eve of war, and a few watchers try to trace its threads.

Through hotels, embassies, and country houses, the plot turns on coded messages, false friends, and a kingdom of the blind led by the sighted few. Oppenheim's pace is brisk and his world is polished. It is a classic pre-war thriller of espionage dressed as high society.
14465-gods-and-fighting-men-the-story-of:
Lady Gregory arranged and translated these Irish tales into English in 1905, with a preface by W. B. Yeats. The first part tells of the Tuatha de Danaan, the god-like folk who came to Ireland, and the second of Finn and the Fianna.

Battles, enchantments, voyages, and tragic loves unfold in plain, rhythmic prose drawn from old manuscripts and oral lore. Heroes such as Lugh, Finn, and Oisin move through a landscape of hills, seas, and otherworld islands. The book became a cornerstone of the Irish literary revival, giving English readers the myths Yeats and his circle prized.
1464-contributions-to-all-the-year-round:
Charles Dickens's contributions to All the Year Round, the journal he founded in 1859, gather his short pieces from its pages. An announcement from Household Words opens the set, and The Poor Man and His Beer shows Dickens arguing, with humour and anger, against laws that closed the poor man's pleasures.

Other pieces cover London life, social reform, and the journal's own business, all in Dickens's brisk editorial voice. The volume is a record of a working editor as well as a novelist. It will interest readers who want Dickens the journalist, campaigning in short, sharp form.
14653-the-feast-of-st-friend:
Arnold Bennett's 1911 Christmas book, The Feast of St. Friend, argues that Christmas has lost its old excitement and should be remade as a festival of goodwill. Doran published it in New York.

Bennett recalls houses rustling with secrets in November, parcels wrapped and unwrapped, and tension rising to a point, then contrasts that past with a duller present. He defends feasting, the gift of oneself, and universal goodwill at the solstice. The book is a short, humane essay, urging readers to revive Christmas as a feast of friendship. Bennett wrote the book as a Christmas gift to readers.
14667-a-christmas-garland:
Max Beerbohm's 1912 volume collects short pieces first seen in part in The Saturday Review, with other items printed here for the first time. Its charm lies in imitation: Beerbohm borrows the voice, habits and mannerisms of other writers and bends them to his own witty ends.

Christmas supplies the occasion and the title, but the real subject is style itself. Each piece lets a reader hear how a well-known manner sounds when pushed a little further, then enjoy the joke of recognition. Short, polished and lightly mocking, the garland suits readers who like literary parody and a sharp eye for the tics of fashionable prose.
14697-lewis-rand:
Mary Johnston's 1908 Virginia novel Lewis Rand follows a young man on the road to Richmond, through Jefferson's Virginia, Fontenoy, and the politics of two candidates. Houghton Mifflin published it with illustrations by F. C. Yohn.

Rand courts Cary and Jacqueline, visits Monticello, and navigates duels, dinners, and elections in a society reading Swift and Vathek. Johnston inscribes the book to Senator John Tyler Morgan. The novel is a rich historical romance of the early republic, written with Johnston's usual color and care for Virginia manners. Johnston's Virginia novels made her a popular historical novelist.
14742-vanishing-england:
P. H. Ditchfield's Vanishing England, published by Methuen in London in 1910 with illustrations by Fred Roe, pleads for the old buildings and customs disappearing under modern change. Ditchfield was a fellow of the Society of Antiquaries and the Royal Historical Society.

Chapters move through walled towns, streets and lanes, castles, vanishing churches, mansions, prehistoric remains, cathedral cities, old inns, municipal buildings, crosses, and stocks. Ivy unchecked brought down the roof of Chingford church in Essex, and about sixty ruined churches stand in Norfolk alone. Ditchfield urges the National Trust and kindred societies to save what remains.
14879-the-hilltop-boys-on-lost-island:
Cyril Burleigh's 1917 boys' adventure strands the Hilltop Boys on a lost island, beginning with a floating academy and Jack's daring rescue. The unexpected happens, the boys are caught on the island, and exploration, a walk under water and a remarkable find follow.

A last visit to a wreck, a thrilling encounter, voices in the woods, adventures in the woods and a strange light at sea keep the pace high. A man with a white moustache, a messenger sent for help, Ben's strange story and the lair of the fox lead to the way out found. Burleigh writes schoolboy adventure in the classic mode: pluck, friendship and a mystery solved.
14951-a-wanderer-in-holland:
E. V. Lucas wanders Holland with twenty illustrations in colour by Herbert Marshall and thirty-four after old Dutch masters. Sunrise on the Maas, Rotterdam, Gouda, the great church at Dort, Utrecht and the beach at Scheveningen open the journey, with Leyden, the turf market at Haarlem and canals in Amsterdam.

Volendam, cheese market at Alkmaar, harbour tower at Hoorn, market place and weigh house, Dromedaris tower at Enkhuizen, Harlingen, Kampen, Arnheim, Nymwegen and Middelburg follow. Pictures after Vermeer and de Hooch add art history to travel. Lucas writes as a companionable wanderer, noting towns, markets, churches and the Dutch love of water and light.
14971-history-of-holland:
George Edmundson's History of Holland was published by Cambridge University Press. It runs from the Burgundian Netherlands through Habsburg rule to the revolt, William the Silent and the beginnings of the Dutch Republic. Government, the twelve years' truce, Maurice and Oldenbarneveldt follow.

East and West India Companies, letters, science and art follow. The rule of William the Second, the rise of John de Witt, and war with France and England under William the Third complete the survey. Edmundson writes a scholarly national history, clear on politics and trade. The volume remains a solid introduction to a small country whose ships, banks and ideas shaped early modern Europe.
15031-sermons-on-various-important-subje:
Andrew Lee, pastor of the North Church in Lisbon, Connecticut, published these sermons at Worcester in 1803. Each takes a hard Bible text as its starting point, from Paul on the wisdom of God to Abram's horror of great darkness. The sermons run in order, with several subjects spread across two or more discourses.

Lee argues in calm, reasoned prose, defending the truth of Christianity against doubt and decline, and weighing God's fairness to all people. His style is that of a learned New England minister speaking to his own flock. The volume preserves early American preaching at a moment when the young republic was still finding its religious voice.
15168-bowser-the-hound:
Thornton Burgess's 1920 animal tale follows Bowser the Hound, led away by Old Man Coyote and caught in a run of tricks and mishaps. Chapters trace a bad night, a surprise for Blacky the Crow, and Reddy Fox's prying, with Harrison Cady's pictures to match. The book is dedicated to the child's loving playmate, the dog.

Blacky takes pity on Bowser and helps him, while Coyote hints darkly and a night breeze stirs mischief. Burgess writes in his familiar woodland style, giving each creature a voice and a moral. Young animal lovers will enjoy Bowser's trials and his loyal, funny friends.
15259-pearl-of-pearl-island:
John Oxenham's 1908 novel, in six parts from Pearl to Pearl in a Ring, sings its heroine as pearl of the silver sea. Verses open the book, calling her white in sun-flecked and moon-decked water, lapped in smiles and ringed in foam. Smaller pearls close the set, like jewels in a casket.

The story follows Pearl through love, loss, and island life, in Oxenham's romantic, lyrical style. The dedication goes to his wife, a sign of the book's tender feeling. Readers who enjoy Edwardian romance with a poetic glow will find Pearl of Pearl Island warm, musical, and gently idealistic.
15277-the-open-secret-of-ireland:
T. M. Kettle's 1912 book, with an introduction by John Redmond, calls Home Rule for Ireland an open secret. Chapters move from humility and colored versus plain history to the obviousness of Home Rule, the ravages of unionism, the hallucination of Ulster, and the mechanics of rule after it comes. Loyalty gets an epilogue.

Kettle argues that Ireland, rejected in 1886 and 1893, blocks the way again, and needs a new remedy never yet found. His prose is witty, learned, and partisan. Readers of Irish history will find the book a sharp, eloquent case from inside the Home Rule movement.
15301-narratives-of-shipwrecks-of-the-ro:
Compiled by William O. S. Gilly from Admiralty documents, this 1850 volume narrates Royal Navy shipwrecks between 1793 and 1849. A preface by William Stephen Gilly fronts the set, with wrecks of the Boyne, Amphion, Tribune, Resistance, Proserpine, and many more. A full list closes the book.

Each narrative shows discipline, danger, and loss at sea, drawn from official papers rather than romance. Gilly chose the most interesting cases to illustrate naval life and fate. Sea history readers will find the volume gripping, grim, and rich in firsthand detail. The stories honor sailors who faced storms with courage and discipline.
15367-the-magic-speech-flower-or-little-:
Melvin Hix's 1912 children's book, The Magic Speech Flower, tells of Little Luke and his animal friends, with pictures throughout. Hix, a New York school principal and author of Once Upon a Time Stories, aimed his retellings at first and second grade pupils. Longmans published the book in New York, London, Bombay, and Calcutta.

Luke's adventures with beasts who speak, thanks to a magic flower, teach kindness, courage, and wonder in simple prose. The stories suit reading aloud to young children. Families will find the book gentle, fanciful, and firmly in the school-story tradition of its day.
15413-the-book-of-three-hundred-anecdote:
Burns and Oates published this new selection of three hundred anecdotes, historical, literary, and humorous, in London and New York. An index runs from Abernethy and actors to affection, artists, and benevolence, letting a reader dip in anywhere. Each item is short, often a paragraph or two, and each turns on one sharp point.

Inside, a doctor cures a gloomy clothier with a trick letter, a sea captain scorns physicians yet yields to a surgeon on a cruise, and kings, bishops, actors, and beggars trade wit. The set suits browsing: no plot to follow, only a run of true-seeming tales about famous and obscure folk. As a Victorian commonplace book, it shows what readers once kept for table talk and moral example.
15782-scenes-in-switzerland:
A travel sketch book issued by the American Tract Society in New York in 1868. Short pieces take the reader through Swiss towns, lakes, and mountains, with a moral and religious tone. The Tract Society aimed at family reading, wholesome and instructive. Each scene pairs a place with a story or a lesson.

Gretchen opens the book, followed by A Night in the Cathedral and The Glaciers of Savoy. The Bride of the Aar, A Sabbath in Lausanne, and The Guide of Montanvert follow, before Mont Blanc and the road from Berne to Basle. The prose stays simple and earnest. The book charms as a Victorian tour: wonders of nature read as signs of a higher order.
15795-the-rover-boys-in-camp-or-the-riva:
A boys' school story by Arthur M. Winfield, issued in 1904 as part of the Rover Boys series. The Rover brothers return to Putnam Hall, a military academy, and then march out to camp. Winfield, writing for the Stratemeyer stable, keeps the tone clean, loyal, and full of fun. Rivalry, sport, and pranks drive each chapter.

At home, at school, and on the boat to Putnam Hall, the boys meet old friends and old enemies. Election of officers, a fight at the boathouse, and hazers at work fill the camp chapters. A storm on Pine Island and a tug of war test pluck and teamwork. The book charms as a period school tale, where fair play matters and brothers stand together.
15799-walter-harland:
A novel of memory by H. S. Caswell, author of Clara Boscom, issued in 1874. The narrator, alone on a quiet afternoon in the Indian summer of Eastern Canada, lets his thoughts wander to the past. Caswell writes in the reflective manner of an older age, where mood carries the tale. Early Canadiana Online preserved the page images for this edition.

Walter Harland's story unfolds through recollection: youth, friendship, love, and loss, seen through the haze of years. The Canadian setting gives the memories colour, from still afternoons to far-off scenes. Caswell keeps the prose gentle and the morals plain. The book appeals to readers who like a slow, tender backward glance at a life.
15884-young-folks-library-volume-xi-of-2:
Volume eleven of the Young Folks' Library, twenty volumes richly illustrated, issued by Hall and Locke in Boston in 1902. Thomas Bailey Aldrich edited in chief, with President William Jewett Tucker, Hamilton Wright Mabie, Henry Van Dyke, and Nathan Haskell Dole. The series gathers the choicest literature of all lands for young readers. This volume treats wonders of earth, sea, and sky.

Folk-lore, fairy tales, fables, and legends share the series with natural history and animal stories. Sea tales, brave deeds, explorations, and school and college life follow, with biography, history, patriotic eloquence, and poetry. The volume gives children the marvels of nature in short, vivid pieces. It shows Edwardian home education at its best: varied, moral, and full of wonder.
15920-outward-bound-or-young-america-afl:
A story of travel and adventure by William T. Adams, writing as Oliver Optic, issued by Lee and Shepard in Boston in 1869. Adams dedicates the volume to George Webster Terrill. The book opens the Young America Abroad library, sending schoolboys afloat for learning and adventure. Optic, a beloved boys' writer, mixes seamanship with geography.

Young America sails, with boys learning ropes, sails, and foreign ports under firm masters. Discipline, fun, and danger share the voyage. Each port brings a lesson in history or manners. The book delights as a school-ship tale: boys becoming men at sea, with the world as their classroom.
15948-the-hollow-land:
A fantasy romance by William Morris, opening with a verse from the Nibelungen Lied on heroes, joy, and woe. Morris, poet and craftsman, tells of a land sought long and lost. An old narrator asks if readers know the Hollow Land, where he first saw his love. His memory fails, and he must wait and think to tell how it happened.

Trumpet-blasts sing over desolate moors in his ears, with clashing horse-hoofs and a world of chivalry. The Hollow Land holds love, quest, and a past that will not fade. Morris writes in dreamlike prose, rich with medieval colour. The tale charms as an early fantasy: a place half-remembered, and a love that draws the seeker back.
15955-a-short-history-of-scotland:
A short history of Scotland by Andrew Lang, in the 1911 William Blackwood and Sons edition. Lang opens with a magic mirror: Scotland as Agricola found it in 81 AD, when Romans crossed the border. Hills and mountains alone look familiar, while rivers overflow, forests cover the plains, and huts of clay and wattle cluster round a chief's stockaded house. The style is vivid and swift.

Lang carries the story from Romans through kings, wars, and reformations to modern days. Battles, clans, and parliaments pass in brisk chapters. His tone stays lively and partisan, fond of Scotland and its heroes. The book still works as a first history: short, readable, and full of the country's rough colour.
16174-the-gun-brand:
James B. Hendryx's 1917 Northern novel opens with Chloe Elliston perched on a burlap-covered bale of freight, watching scows load in the far North. Contents promise Vermilion showing his hand, Pierre Lapierre, Brute MacNair, and a master mind. A shot in the night, Snare Lake, and the Yellow Knife country follow. Whiskey runners, a frame-up, and the Louchoux girl lead at last to the wolf-cry, the battle, and the gun-brand itself.

Hendryx writes rough, outdoor adventure in which traders, police, and outlaws clash over fur, liquor, and pride. Chloe's watchful presence gives the wild country a human center. Readers who like Canadian Northwest yarns will find a fast, colorful tale of the trail.
16348-dreamland:
Julie M. Lippmann gathers eight dream tales for children in this 1914 volume. The Waking Soul opens with Larry, a lazy boy lying under the trees wishing the heat away while schoolchildren pass him by. Betty's By-and-By, The White Angel, Marjorie's Miracle, and Nina's Christmas Gifts follow, each mixing a child's wish with a gentle wonder.

The stories are soft and fanciful, meant for reading aloud. Lippmann keeps the language simple and the morals kind. Children who like tales where dreams slip into real life will enjoy the set, and the book shows the warm, homely style of American children's fiction before the First World War.
16437-the-children-of-france-a-book-of-s:
Ruth Royce tells fourteen stories of French boys and girls who acted with courage during the Great War, issued in 1918 while the war still raged. Remi the Brave, the heroine of Fort Montere, a child dispatch bearer, and Marie the Courageous lead the tales. Some outwit Prussian troops, some carry news, some give their lives.

Royce notes that she heard the tales from men who saw the fighting, though she cannot vouch for each one herself. The stories are short, plain, and aimed at young readers. Together they form a wartime book of praise for youth, meant to stir pride and pity in equal measure.
16604-poison-island:
Arthur Thomas Quiller-Couch, writing as Q, spins a treasure-island adventure in this novel. The hero first meets Captain Coffin, enters Copenhagen Academy, fights in the street, and glimpses a chart. A crime in the summer-house, a bloodstain on the stile, and Captain Branscome's confession lead to the chart of Mortallone and a voyage to the island itself.

Q writes with gusto, mixing school story, mystery, and sea adventure. Women in a graveyard, a man in black, and a master of the island thicken the plot. Readers of classic adventure will find a brisk, old-fashioned yarn with a strong Cornish flavor.
17016-division-of-words-rules-for-the-di:
Frederick W. Hamilton wrote this manual on rules for dividing words at the ends of lines. He served as educational director of the United Typothetae of America. The book adds remarks on spelling, syllabication, and pronunciation. The committee on education issued it as typographic technical series part six, number thirty-five. A transcriber's note warns that some examples seem not to follow the guideline, as if the guideline itself were at times mistaken.

Hamilton gives printers and apprentices plain rules for breaking words, marking stressed syllables and diacritics with care. The book is a practical shop manual, not a theory of language. Readers of printing history and typography will find a useful, exact guide to how books were once set, line by line, with rules that still inform good typesetting.
17071-folk-lore-and-legends-scotland:
An 1889 London volume gathers Scottish folk tales and lore shaped by moors, lochs, hills, and rough coasts. Its prefatory note links the harsh, grand land to the tales that grew there. Fairies, brownies, bogles, mermen, ghosts, and wise folk fill the pages, and the old stories carry the fears and humor of the people who told them.

Thomas the Rhymer, Michael Scott, Saint Columba, and the seal-catcher stand beside lesser known local figures in tales of deals, haunts, and strange meetings. Some pieces read like short legends, others like notes on folk belief. Together they give a vivid first door into Scottish story lore, with the wild land always close behind the tale.
17108-the-house-of-the-misty-star-a-roma:
Frances Little's 1915 romance, told by Jane Gray, takes root in old Japan. Jane keeps house, meets Kishimoto, and welcomes Zura Wingate, a young woman caught between two worlds. Gardens, shrines, festivals, and calls on neighbors give the tale its daily texture, while a detective named Kobu and a visitor from America stir its later chapters.

Hope and love run through the book, but so do duty, shame, and the cost of old customs. Jane learns to listen before she judges, and Zura's path tests what kindness can mend. The novel offers a gentle, vivid look at Japan through foreign eyes of its time, with a warm close that rewards its slow build.
17152-rosa-s-quest-or-the-way-to-the-bea:
Anna Potter Wright's 1904 children's tale follows Rosa, a poor girl who serves a sharp-tongued mistress while her mother coughs and fades. Rosa asks how much the fare is to a better place, and her quest for the beautiful land becomes a search for faith, hope, and a home beyond sorrow. Esther's doubts and Mrs. Gray's hard house frame the early chapters.

The book, printed by the Moody Press, teaches its lesson in story form: small kindness, prayer, and trust lead Rosa on. Its dialect speech and short chapters suit young readers. Today it reads as a gentle period tale of a child facing loss with courage and a steady, seeking heart.
17299-fifty-years-of-railway-life-in-eng:
Joseph Tatlow's 1920 memoir covers fifty years of railway life in England, Scotland, and Ireland. Tatlow, manager of the Midland Great Western Railway of Ireland, recalls boyhood, the Midland Railway and King Hudson, Victorian manners, early office life, and the Caledonian line in Glasgow. Acts of Parliament, rates and fares, brakes and blocks, and light railways fill the working chapters.

Later parts add Belfast lines, Ballinasloe Fair, a parcel post contest, congress trips to Spain, Paris, and Constantinople, and King Edward's change of chair. Tatlow writes with a manager's eye and a friend's warmth. Railway fans will find a rich, firsthand life of the age of steam, told by a man who ran it.
1740-the-flying-u-s-last-stand:
B. M. Bower returns to the Flying U ranch, where the Happy Family of cowboys face a new kind of trouble. Settlers, a colony, and the law all press on the open range they once rode free. Andy Green takes a hand in the fight, the Kid learns about horses and about men, and a lost child and a burnt shack raise the stakes.

The novel's fight is over water, fences, and lawful improvements. Bower keeps it comic as well as tense, with the cowboys turning nesters, buying cattle, and lying to ladies for the cause. It is a late-range western about the end of an era, told by a writer who knew ranch work and loved the crew she wrote about.
17415-money-island:
Andrew J. Howell Jr. published this pair of tales in Wilmington, North Carolina, in 1908, with the Commercial Printing Company. The first, Money Island, tells of buried treasure on a little island among the marshes in Greenville Sound, not far from Wilmington. The story was told by Jonathan Landstone many years before, and written down by him so that it would be told correctly when published.

A second tale, The Conquest of Jamesby, follows at page fifty-one. Landstone's narrator recalls boyhood visits to a grandfather in Charleston, a fine old man fond of stories of colonial days, whose father had been a pirate. Readers get a coastal Carolina treasure tale, homely, local, and fond of its marshy ground.
17453-up-in-ardmuirland:
Michael Barrett, a Benedictine priest, published this book of Ardmuirland sketches in New York, Cincinnati, and Chicago in 1912 with Benziger Brothers. Chapters run from personal memories and Archie, through golden dreams, Dominie Dick, and Bildy, to smugglers, phenomena, and spring's return. A rustic pastor, a sprig of shamrock, and Penny close the set.

Barrett writes of forest, meadow, hill, and the steel-blue rim of ocean lying silent in afternoon shadow and sunshine. Readers get a priest's affectionate portrait of a Scottish coastal countryside and its people. The book suits readers of Scottish local writing and of gentle, reflective sketches.
1751-twilight-land:
Between day and night lies Twilight Land, where a stool of fortune, the talisman of Solomon, and a fiddler's ill luck all take their turns. Its tales turn on a stool of fortune, Solomon's talisman, a fiddler's ill luck, empty bottles, and a piece of good luck, with Pyle's own illustrations in the original shaping the mood.

The stories draw on old folk material and retell it in Pyle's clear, old-fashioned prose, with morals that favor wit and kindness over greed. Readers who like the Arabian Nights manner — strange gifts, foolish bargains, and a twist that sets things right — will find the book a gentle companion. It is made for reading aloud.
17678-the-apology-of-the-church-of-engla:
John Jewel, Bishop of Salisbury, wrote this apology of the Church of England. It was published in 1888 by Cassell and Company in London, Paris, New York, and Melbourne. Jewel wrote the apology in Latin, to be read throughout Europe as the answer of the Reformed Church of England. It answered those who said the Reformation had set up a new church, at the beginning of Queen Elizabeth's reign.

His argument was that the English reformers were going back to the old church, not inventing a new one. Readers get a founding text of Anglican self-defence, in a handy modern edition. The book suits readers of Reformation history and of Anglican thought.
18131-the-rescue-of-the-princess-winsome:
Annie Fellows Johnston wrote The Rescue of the Princess Winsome as a fairy play for old and young, printed in Boston in 1908 by L. C. Page, with music by Albion Fellows Bacon. Johnston, author of the Little Colonel books, here gives children a play to act, not just to read.

The songs were first set with lyrics under the music, and this text puts them in lyric form for ease of use. A princess, a rescue, and fairy folk drive the short play, with tunes to sing along the way. It is a sweet, old children's play, made for school stages, parlors, and holiday fun.
18184-animal-carvings-from-mounds-of-the:
Henry W. Henshaw wrote this Smithsonian Bureau of Ethnology paper on animal carvings from the mounds of the Mississippi Valley. Henshaw studies stone and shell figures found in the mounds, asking which animals the mound builders knew and how well they carved them. His contents list the manatee, the toucan, and the paroquet, with notes on errors of identification.

The paper also weighs skill in sculpture, the totemic origin of the figures, animal mounds, and the so-called elephant and alligator mounds. Human sculptures and a comparison of Indian and mound-builder art close the study. Readers get a close look at old American art: what the carvings show, what they get wrong, and what they prove about trade, belief, and craft.
18299-the-norwegian-account-of-haco-s-ex:
Rev. James Johnstone translated this old Norse account of King Haco's expedition against Scotland in 1263. The text comes from the Flatey and Frisian manuscripts in Icelandic, and Johnstone printed it for himself in 1782; this edition dates from Edinburgh in 1882. Notes accompany the literal rendering.

The fragment tells how a Norwegian king sailed against the Scots, with anecdotes of the lords of the Hebrides who stood between the two powers. It is a primary source in translation, not a modern history. Readers meet the campaign in the voice of its own age, with kings, fleets, and island chiefs, and can weigh a medieval account against later histories of the same war.
18383-anecdotes-of-painters-engravers-sc:
S. Spooner, author of A Biographical History of the Fine Arts, compiled this third volume of anecdotes of painters, engravers, sculptors, and architects, with curiosities of art. The New York edition, copyrighted in 1853 and re-entered in 1880, gathers short tales and facts for readers who love art but lack a library of lives. Each entry is brief, and the whole reads like a commonplace book.

This volume opens with Egyptian art: ancient Thebes, the temples of Carnac and Luxor, the statues of Memnon, Heliopolis, Memphis, Lake Moeris, the colossal sphinx, and the labyrinth. It moves to catacombs, pyramids, obelisks, and the removal of an obelisk from Thebes to Paris. Readers get art history as anecdote: wonders, craftsmen, and the moving of great stones, told in short, memorable pieces.
18396-the-modern-scottish-minstrel-volum:
Charles Rogers, a fellow of the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland, compiled this first volume of The Modern Scottish Minstrel, or the songs of Scotland of the past half century. Adam and Charles Black published it at Edinburgh, with memoirs of the poets and their songs. A portrait of Sir Walter Scott fronts the volume, and the old house of Gask, birthplace of Lady Nairn, appears as a plate.

Contents open with John Skinner, whose songs include Tullochgorum, John o' Badenyon, and The Ewie wi' the Crookit Horn. William Cameron, Mrs. John Hunter, and Alexander, Duke of Gordon, follow, with songs such as The Flowers of the Forest and The Indian Death Song. Readers get Scottish song with its makers: brief lives, then the verses that kept their names alive in parlors and at gatherings.
18601-an-account-of-some-of-the-principa:
Joshua Coffin gathered this 1860 account for the American Anti-Slavery Society, just after John Brown's raid on Virginia stirred fresh debate. It collects reports of slave revolts and plots in the United States and elsewhere over the prior two centuries. The longest section covers the revolution in St. Domingo from 1790 to 1802.

Coffin frames the facts as a moral case: holding people in bondage invites danger, while prompt freedom brings safety. Short notes, Bible verses, and comments on recent events run through the text. Readers today get a clear view of how abolitionists used past revolts to argue their cause.
18614-at-the-back-of-the-north-wind:
George MacDonald wrote this children's classic, here simplified by Elizabeth Lewis and published at Philadelphia and London in 1914 with color pictures by Maria L. Kirk. Its hero is Diamond, a coachman's son who sleeps in a hay loft over the coach house, named for a favorite horse. He makes friends with North Wind, a great lady of wind and weather.

Chapters follow Diamond's trips with North Wind, a ship sunk by storm, the land at the back of the wind, his father's lost job, cab driving, and hard times for his family. Lewis keeps MacDonald's wonder in short, simple chapters. The book suits young readers meeting the tale for the first time.
18619-the-modern-scottish-minstrel-volum:
Charles Rogers compiled this second volume of his Modern Scottish Minstrel at Edinburgh in 1856. It gathers songs of Scotland from the prior half century, with short memoirs of the poets who wrote them. A long opening essay also defends Gaelic verse against doubts raised by the Ossian dispute, and sketches modern Gaelic bards in English verse.

Rogers argues that old Highland lays were kept with care by reciters who prized them as relics of their forebears. The volume thus mixes song texts, life notes, and literary debate. Readers get both a song book and a mid-Victorian view of Scotland's poetic past.
18636-the-story-of-newfoundland:
Lord Birkenhead, Lord High Chancellor of Great Britain, wrote this short history of Newfoundland, issued in a new, enlarged London edition in 1920. It opens with the island's land and people, noting its place as the nearest American coast to Ireland and a landing point for ocean cables. Maps of the island and its place beside western Europe help the reader follow the tale.

Later chapters trace discovery, early settlement, the hard fight for a living, the English colonial system, self-rule, and modern growth, with the Reid contract and the French shore question closing the account. Birkenhead writes in a brisk, confident style. The book serves as a compact guide to the island's past.
18764-life-in-morocco-and-glimpses-beyon:
Budgett Meakin, author of The Moors, The Land of the Moors, and The Moorish Empire, published Life in Morocco and Glimpses Beyond with Chatto and Windus in 1905, with twenty-four illustrations. The front matter of this copy is given over to his earlier Morocco books, listing their chapters on Moorish dress, food, courts, saints, and trade.

The companion volumes range from Tangier and Fez to Marrákesh, with histories of the empire from its foundation to its present rule. Life in Morocco belongs to that same shelf of Morocco writing, though its own chapters lie beyond the excerpt in this copy. Readers should expect the same ground, towns, customs, and people, seen through travel rather than history.
18824-fairies-and-folk-of-ireland:
William Henry Frost wrote this 1900 book of Irish fairy lore for Scribner's, with pictures by Sydney Richmond Burleigh. Frost explains that the long tale running through the book is his own, shaped to fit the laws of fairy folk as Irish lore reveals them.

Shorter tales set between its chapters are genuine Irish folk tales, retold in his own way, sometimes cut short and sometimes filled out, but seldom changed in substance. Chapters tell of O'Donoghue, the big poor people, the little good people, little Kathleen and little Terence, and an old king who comes back. The book gives young readers a full shelf of Irish wonder in one volume.
18845-seeing-europe-with-famous-authors-:
Francis W. Halsey selected and edited this volume in 1914, the seventh of ten in Seeing Europe with Famous Authors, covering Italy, Sicily, and Greece in its first part. Halsey, known for historical anthologies, gathered passages by well-known writers and added his own introductions. The book is illustrated and was issued by Funk and Wagnalls in New York and London.

The selections guide a reader through Rome, Naples, Genoa, and the road to Greece, mixing practical travel notes with literary description. Steamers, rail journeys, and the cost and time of routes all get attention. Readers get a literary travel companion from the age before mass tourism, useful both for its chosen passages and for its picture of how Americans toured Europe.
19004-the-customs-of-old-england:
F. J. Snell wrote this survey of old English customs, first published in 1911 and issued in cheap form by Methuen in London in 1919. The book gathers customs of the year, the home, and the countryside, drawing on history, folklore, and literature. A short selection only, the volume promises, yet its range runs wide across English life.

Snell explains the origins and meanings of practices that survived into modern times, from seasonal feasts to local usages. He writes for general readers rather than specialists, with a storyteller's ease. Readers get an enjoyable guide to the England of fairs, holidays, and household rites, useful for anyone curious about how everyday life once marked the year.
19033-alice-s-adventures-in-wonderland:
Sam'l Gabriel Sons and Company published this edition of Alice's Adventures in Wonderland in New York in 1916, in the Storyland series. It presents Lewis Carroll's classic in a popular illustrated form for children. The story opens as Alice, tired of sitting by her sister on the bank, follows a White Rabbit with pink eyes down the rabbit-hole.

From there come the pool of tears, the caterpillar, the Duchess, the Cheshire Cat, the Mad Tea-Party, and the Queen's croquet-ground, in Carroll's familiar sequence. This edition's pictures, including Alice in the Duchess's room, suit young readers. Readers get the Wonderland tale in a handsome early twentieth-century children's edition, good for reading aloud or for a first meeting with Alice.
19061-seeing-europe-with-famous-authors-:
Francis W. Halsey edited this eighth volume of Seeing Europe with Famous Authors, covering Italy, Sicily, and Greece in part two. Published in 1914, it gathers travel writing by noted authors, with introductions and pictures, and arranges it by famous cities and sights. The Parthenon fronts the book.

Taine writes on Pisa's two faces, one sleepy and one glorious, while other pieces linger in cathedrals where light falls like a forest through stained glass. Each excerpt lets a known writer guide the reader. Readers get a literary grand tour, rich in place, art, and old-world colour.
19071-the-way-of-the-wind:
Zoe Anderson Norris wrote this 1911 novel about Celia, a young wife who follows her husband Seth to a rough prairie home. The wind rules the place, slamming shutters, moaning at night, and testing her nerve from the first cart ride in. Seth loves the land and its wild weather.

Celia must learn housekeeping, neighbours, and loneliness on open ground far from town comforts. Her fear of the wind slowly gives way to a sterner kind of love for the life she chose. Readers get a prairie tale of marriage, grit, and the slow work of making a home in a hard place.
19160-disturbed-ireland:
Bernard H. Becker, special commissioner of the Daily News, wrote these letters from Ireland during the winter of 1880 to 1881. He travelled town to town with route maps, reporting unrest, land strife, and daily life in a disturbed land. The book appeared in London in 1881.

At Claremorris he finds busy shops, talkative commercial men, peat fires, and a maid of all work hauling turf up and down stairs. Small scenes like these sit beside graver reports of fear and faction. Readers get a vivid, first-hand view of Ireland in the Land War years, sharp on detail and local voice.
19205-the-vikings-of-helgeland:
Henrik Ibsen wrote this prose drama, The Vikings of Helgeland, in 1858, here translated by William Archer as volume three of his prose dramas. Set about 933 in the time of Erik Blood-axe, at Gunnar's house on Helgeland in north Norway, it follows Ornulf, Sigurd the Strong, Gunnar Headman, Dagny, and Hiordis. Pronunciation notes guide English readers.

Hiordis enters in black with armed house carls, spear in hand, seeking Kare her foeman, while Gunnar yields peace for a slaying and Dagny greets her coldly. Honour, love, and revenge drive the action. Readers get an early Ibsen saga drama of Norse pride and fate.
1930-penguin-island:
Anatole France's Penguin Island is a satirical history of France disguised as the history of penguins. Saint Maël, sailing the ocean of ice, baptizes a flock of penguins by mistake. An assembly in Paradise must decide what to do with birds who are now, by baptism, human.

The books that follow trace the penguins through monks driven from Brittany, King Brian's wooden monastery, and the whole pageant of French history, from the Middle Ages to modern politics. France writes with irony and elegance, and the novel's joke is serious: a nation's history, retold with birds, looks no less absurd and no less grand.
19385-the-modern-scottish-minstrel-volum:
Charles Rogers edited this third volume of a six-volume set on the songs of Scotland from the past half century, published in Edinburgh in the mid eighteen hundreds. Each poet gets a memoir, with songs in Scots and, in places, English verse versions of Gaelic bards.

Songs of home, loss, and love dominate, from a motherless child left alone to verses that find heaven in love at home. The volume preserves both the words and the lives behind them, and it is a key source for the song culture of Victorian Scotland.
19525-the-modern-scottish-minstrel-volum:
Charles Rogers edited this fourth volume of his Modern Scottish Minstrel, published in Edinburgh in the late eighteen fifties. Like its sisters, it pairs memoirs of poets with their songs, in Scots and in English versions of Gaelic verse.

One song praises Mary Shearer, fairest of her kind, while its singer bids farewell to Glenlin, Dunoon, and Loch Striven to wander the wide world. The volume keeps alive the voices of Victorian Scotland's song makers, from love lyrics to songs of parting. Henry Scott Riddell opens the book with songs of the wild glen, Scotia's thistle, and the land of gallant hearts.
19601-frank-and-andy-afloat-or-the-cave-:
Vance Barnum wrote this boys' adventure of Frank and Andy afloat, published in Wisconsin in the early nineteen twenties. A whale strike, a wrecked motor boat, a boy's rescue, and a rival claim lead to Cliff Island, a cave, a rising tide, and a storm.

At a dock office the boys ask after a partly burned motor craft, and hear instead of a tall dark man and a sailboat captain. Barnum's sea tale keeps its young heroes moving from wreck to rescue, with a cave climax that tests nerve and friendship.
19761-a-girl-in-ten-thousand:
A Girl in Ten Thousand is a story for girls by L. T. Meade, a prolific writer for young readers. Its heroine is dark-eyed and sweet-faced, though her words can sound hard. She might be any age between seventeen and twenty. Meade's girls usually face school, work, or family trials. One in ten thousand is the praise her worth must earn.

Meade wrote hundreds of books for girls in her lifetime. Her stories mixed school life with moral tests and romance. Readers followed heroines who worked, studied, and held their ground. This novel fits that popular pattern. It shows what Victorian and Edwardian girls were offered as models. The charm is period charm, preserved whole.
19799-the-rural-motor-express-to-conserv:
The Rural Motor Express was a wartime plan to move farm goods by truck. Its stated aims were to conserve foodstuffs and labor and help win the war. The argument runs on efficiency: highways must be used to the maximum. Motor trucks can run where no fixed rail lines exist. They can also relieve railroads of short-haul loads. Trucks would act as feeder lines in thinly served districts.

Food rotted when rail cars ran short in wartime. A truck route from farm to town saved both crop and car space. Federal and state groups pushed the express idea in 1918. This pamphlet is their sales pitch and manual. It marks the moment trucks joined national transport planning.
19806-everyman-s-land:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson wrote Everyman's Land as a postwar travel romance. Its speaker confesses to wanting hatred and misunderstanding. He disguised himself as a Leprechaun and sulked, he admits. It did not work with the one person who understood him. She taught him people are much the same all over the world. The voice is whimsical, wounded, and confessional at once.

The Williamsons wrote bestselling travel novels between the wars. Everyman's Land crosses Europe's battle-scarred lands. A fairy-tale mask lets the narrator say hard things lightly. The lesson he learns is the book's thesis. Travel here heals a man the war left bitter. It is a gentle, strange period piece.
19822-with-the-british-army-in-the-holy-:
Henry Charles Woods wrote With the British Army in the Holy Land about the Palestine campaign. He opens with the land's long war history. Palestine was the cock-pit of the known world before Belgium held that name. Egyptians, Assyrians, Israelites, Canaanites, Greeks, and Romans fought there. Saracens and Crusaders followed on the same high road. The British Army of 1917 marched into that deep past.

Allenby's campaign took Jerusalem and broke Ottoman rule in Palestine. Campaign histories appeared while memory was fresh. Woods writes for readers who followed the war in newspapers. Sacred geography and modern logistics fill the same chapters. The book is a primary record of that campaign. It also shows Britain framing conquest as history.
19928-sunset-pass-or-running-the-gauntle:
