Sunset Pass promises a run through the gauntlet of Apache land. A captain in its pages thinks first of the children. Renegades from the reservation are out in great numbers, he says. They are supposed to be down in the Tonto Basin. Yet their moccasin tracks have shown up nearby. Charles Seltzer wrote such Arizona westerns with a working cowboy's knowledge. Fear rides every mile of this one.

The Tonto Basin was real Apache country, steep and ambush-ready. Seltzer's novels pit settlers and soldiers against that terrain. Tracks in dust carry more dread than gunfire here. Sunset Pass belongs to his early, lean westerns. It shows the genre before Hollywood standardized it. Local detail is its claim on readers.
19966-the-statesmen-snowbound:
The Statesmen Snowbound is a comic tale of congressmen trapped by weather. Its narrator pleads the sacrifices congressmen make to serve the nation. They give up home life, business interests, and personal comforts, he says. Yet unthinking persons begrudge them a little pleasure. Snow gives the statesmen that pleasure by force. Robert Grant, a Boston judge and novelist, wrote the satire. Washington marooned makes his whole joke.

Grant first published the tale in the 1880s, and it stayed famous. Snowbound politicians must amuse themselves without constituents or press. Their stranded leisure exposes pomposity and boredom alike. The piece is gentle Thackeray-style satire, American style. It also preserves Gilded Age political manners. Few Washington comedies have lasted as well.
20043-the-angel-children-or-stories-from:
The Angel Children, or Stories from Cloud-Land, tells tales for young readers about child life and loss. One girl, Genevieve, has a large playroom full of fine toys. Other children think she must be perfectly happy with so much. Yet she would trade it all for a little brother of her own.

Genevieve longs to walk in the garden with a brother and watch over him. Her mother watches her in just that caring way. The tales blend home life, faith, and gentle moral lessons. They show what children's books of the era taught about love and want.
20057-pocket-island-a-story-of-country-l:
Charles Clark Munn published Pocket Island in 1901, a story of country life in New England. The sample turns to the Maine coast and the rum trade. Rum was cheap in Nova Scotia and dear in Maine. That gap made smuggling liquor a risky but rich trade.

Munn knew Maine life well and set much of his work there. Inside, coast folk, traders, and law men move around hidden cargo. The tale mixes local color with crime and cash. Readers get a sharp look at a coast where work and smuggling often sat side by side.
20068-sarah-s-school-friend:
May Baldwin wrote Sarah's School Friend, a girls' school story set in a London home. Mrs. Clay speaks in a strong cockney voice, with dropped h sounds. She scolds Sarah, a girl of sixteen, for sharp talk at home. Sarah has called her mother a humbug and slighted her father.

That clash opens a tale of school, family, and a young girl's pride. Baldwin wrote many such books for girls of her day. Inside, friendship tests Sarah's temper and her sense of right. Readers get period speech, home friction, and the pull of a school friend's sway.
20226-snow-bound:
Snow-Bound gathers writing shaped by winter, storm, and the fireside. Its opening verse comes from Emerson on the arrival of snow. Announced by all the trumpets of the sky, the snow arrives. It seems nowhere to alight as it drives over the fields.

The whited air hides hills, woods, river, and heaven from sight. Sled and traveler stop, and housemates sit by the radiant fire. Such scenes made snowbound tales a loved winter form in New England. Readers get poems and prose that turn deep winter into warm company.
2026-the-coming-conquest-of-england:
August Niemann imagines a future war in which rival powers strike at Britain, translated here by J. H. Freese. Councils of state, officers' messes, spies, and stolen documents carry the plot from India and the Pamirs to London and Scotland. Niemann wrote invasion fiction at a time when Britain feared attack by sea and by land.

Battles at sea and on land, a landing in Scotland, and courtroom drama follow as the invasion unfolds. As an early example of invasion fiction, the novel shows the fears of an age when empires watched each other across maps and borders. The novel's spies and stolen papers reflect real anxieties about empires, alliances, and secret plans.
20288-edward-the-second:
Christopher Marlowe wrote Edward the Second, a history play of a weak king's fall. Edward asks why the Lord of Coventry hurries so fast past him. The bishop replies that he goes to mark the old king's funeral. But wicked Gaveston has returned, the bishop protests in alarm.

Edward vows that Gaveston shall live to be revenged on the priest. Gaveston was the king's favorite, and his exile had been forced by barons. Marlowe turns their bond into a tragedy of power, pride, and revolt. Readers get one of the great early English history plays in verse.
20311-the-bobbsey-twins-on-blueberry-isl:
Laura Lee Hope published The Bobbsey Twins on Blueberry Island in 1917. Bert sits beside his sister Flossie in a boat on Lake Metoka. He says he is hungry yet, despite having eaten not long before. He wants some of Dinah's pie, but he also wants to stay out longer.

That small choice sets the twins' holiday mood of fun and appetite. Blueberry Island gives the four Bobbsey children a camp to explore. The series blends twins, lakes, and gentle mysteries for young readers. Readers get sunny days, boat rides, and pie worth rowing home for.
20467-handbook-of-the-trees-of-new-engla:
Lorin L. Dame's Handbook of the Trees of New England is a field guide to the region's native and planted trees. It covers New England, with notes on ranges across the United States and Canada. Keys and descriptions help readers name a tree in any season.

Dame warns that near the limit of a species, size and habit change a great deal. In trees this change is often very noticeable. He also notes there is no fixed, absolute line between trees and shrubs. Such cautions make the handbook a careful tool, built for people who would test every name outdoors.
20522-the-story-of-the-mind:
The Story of the Mind is a popular survey of psychology, the science of how minds work. Its author thanks the magazines that first printed parts of it. Passages came from the Popular Science Monthly, the Century Magazine, and the Inland Educator.

The Macmillan Company and the owners of copyright also gave their leave. That list shows how the book was built: short, clear chapters first tested on magazine readers. It covers memory, feeling, instinct, and thought for people with no training. Books like this one carried the young science of psychology into ordinary homes.
20588-the-wonder-island-boys-exploring-t:
Roger T. Finlay's The Wonder Island Boys: Exploring the Island, published in 1914, continues his series about boys cast away on a strange island. The boys explore with a friendly professor's help, and every chapter teaches real skills along with the adventure. Their finds raise as many questions as they settle.

The contents promise an arrow found in the skull of an animal, and notes on different kinds of arrows. There is a light across the river, the test of firing a gun, and the disappearance of the light. The boys also learn the qualifications in scouting. Curiosity drives every chapter.
20625-young-americans-abroad-vacation-in:
Young Americans Abroad records a vacation in Europe by a party of American youths, told in letters home. The travels run through England, France, Switzerland, and Italy. Letter writing was the natural form for travel books aimed at young readers of the time.

I have just arrived at this place, one letter begins, and have found my companions on hand. All are ready for the start of the long-hoped-for voyage. The writer regrets the duties that keep their friend at home, and says all feel sorry for the absence. The letters mix sights, history, and boyish fun.
2064-a-journey-to-the-western-islands-of:
Samuel Johnson travelled to the Hebrides with James Boswell in the autumn of 1773, and this account, published in 1775, records what he found. From Edinburgh northward, he visits islands, towns, and lairds, noting land, language, and custom. Johnson travelled at sixty-four, an age when such a rough journey took real courage.

Johnson judges the old clan world with a sharp eye, praising hospitality while doubting romance about the past. The book remains a landmark of travel writing, pairing Johnson's strong prose with a Scotland on the edge of change. Boswell's own journal of the same trip lets readers compare the master's account with his friend's.
20712-trail-s-end:
G. W. Ogden's Trail's End is a Western novel of the Kansas plains after the cattle years. Its opening paints the prairie as a graveyard of hopes. Bones lie everywhere: a waste of bones, a sepulcher that does not hide its bones but spreads them to bleach under the stern sun.

They are bones of deserted houses, the skeletons of men's hopes, crumbling on sterile wastes. Into that emptied country Ogden brings his riders and ranchers, men and women chasing a second chance. Ogden knew Kansas newspaper life, and his West is drier and harder than the dime novel kind.
2080-the-flower-of-the-mind:
Alice Meynell chooses the best English poems for this 1898 anthology, ranging from Chaucer to Wordsworth and judging by quality alone rather than by subject or period. The book was reissued in a limited run of 250 copies. Meynell, a poet and critic, chose poems she loved, not those a school syllabus demanded.

Meynell's introduction defends a general anthology made by personal taste, and her selections reward slow reading. For lovers of verse, the volume works as a compact library of English poetry at its finest. The limited reissue of 250 copies shows the book was prized as a beautiful object as well as a text.
20885-the-promised-land:
A little girl's world once split in two: Polotzk, where she lived, and a strange land called Russia. Mary Antin opens The Promised Land with that child's sharp map. Russia was where one's father went on business, far and dim.

Antin tells how her Jewish family left Polotzk for Boston and a new life. School, English, and hard work remake her across the book's famed arc. Her memoir became a classic tale of the immigrant's road in America. Few books state the hope and cost of that change with her clarity, pride, and eye for telling detail.
20897-a-short-history-of-england:
Britain is less an island than a maze of peninsulas, says G. K. Chesterton. Sea in the fields and fields in the sea strike the eye at every turn. A Short History of England opens with that edgy, bright paradox.

Chesterton retells England's tale as a story of the common folk. Romans, Normans, kings, and revolts pass in his brisk, witty prose. He skips dry lists to chase the spirit of each age. First issued in wartime 1917, the book still charms readers who want history with a pulse, told by a master of the telling phrase.
21003-bell-s-cathedrals-the-cathedral-ch:
Thanks to the Rev. Perkins and the Photochrom Company open W. D. Sweeting's Ely Cathedral guide. Their photos ground the plates that walk readers through the great church. Loans of rare, out-of-print books aided his history of the monastery and see.

Bell's Cathedrals paired sound text with fine photos for church lovers. Ely's nave, lantern, and lady chapel star in Sweeting's calm account. He sorts tangled building tales into clear, dated order. The book served as pocket guide and home study alike, a trusted mate for one of England's grandest churches.
21069-for-treasure-bound:
A November gale at Weymouth opens Harry Collingwood's treasure novel, told by a young hero who shares the author's pen name. His father never came back from a voyage and is presumed lost at sea. Hints point to a treasure island somewhere in the Pacific.

A beautiful, fast cutter is built for the search, and Collingwood writes the shipyard scenes with a working shipwright's eye. The party sails for the Pacific and meets adventures on the way. A charming young woman joins the voyage, and the hero falls in love. Treasure, family loss, and sea travel drive the tale.
21085-the-wreck-of-the-nancy-bell-or-cas:
John Conroy Hutcheson's Nancy Bell sails from Britain for New Zealand in good order, then meets a storm that leaves her rudderless and mastless. Among the passengers travels a former Royal Navy commander in disguise. He offers the captain advice, which is brushed aside as a landsman's talk.

A mutiny breaks out before the ship is wrecked off Kerguelen Island in the far southern ocean. The survivors land, build shelter, and face a hard winter there. Hutcheson gives his Jamaican, Irish, American, and Norwegian characters their own speech. The castaways must also deal with the mutineers who landed apart from them.
21132-frank-oldfield-lost-and-found:
Langhurst, a mining village in south Lancashire, opens the Reverend T. P. Wilson's temperance novel, published in London in 1872. A collier with his Davy lamp meets Alice, a woman whose looks have been scorched away by drink, searching for her boy Sammul. Drink and the pit rule the village's hard life.

Wilson wrote for the Band of Hope movement, which taught children never to start drinking. Frank Oldfield's story of being lost and found plays out among colliers, drinkers, and those trying to save them. The novel won wide circulation as a prize temperance tale, mixing dialect speech with a clear moral purpose.
21198-anecdotes-of-painters-engravers-sc:
S. Spooner was a doctor who also wrote a biographical history of the fine arts. He packed this second volume of anecdotes with lives and curiosities of art. It opens with Titian: his manners, works, imitators, and his dealings with Emperor Charles V and Philip II. A sketch of Horace Vernet follows.

Later pieces range over the Colosseum, the remains of Nineveh, a palace dug up at Nimroud, and the ruins of Pompeii and Herculaneum. The origin of the arch, ancient fresco and mosaic, and the Portland Vase all get entries. Published in New York, the volume serves as a lively miscellany for art lovers.
21245-three-boys-in-the-wild-north-land:
Mr Ross welcomes three sunburnt boys to Sagasta-weekee, his house full of sunshine on the Nelson River, in Egerton Ryerson Young's tale. Frank, Alec, and Sam have sailed by the Prince Arthur to York Factory on Hudson Bay. Ross, a retired Hudson's Bay Company officer, hosts them in his hunting lodge.

The boys spend a season of adventures in the wild north land. They meet Inuit travellers and learn the country from a man whose father also served the Company. Young had worked as a missionary in the region and wrote from experience. Hunting, travel, and winter coming on give the three visitors their education in the North.
21246-winter-adventures-of-three-boys-in:
A November storm rages outside while Frank, Alec, and Sam sit at breakfast in a cosy northern home in Egerton R. Young's sequel. The three boys came from Britain the previous summer by Hudson's Bay Company ship and stayed on as guests of Mr Ross. Now winter, their first in the great lone land, is the adventure.

Dog teams, whips, and the dog keeper Kinesasis start the season's lessons. Ross had spent his career in the fur trade on friendly terms with the Indigenous peoples around him, and his household keeps that closeness. Snow travel, hunting, and the long dark shape a winter the boys will not forget.
21284-six-years-in-the-prisons-of-englan:
An unnamed merchant tells how he began business in a northern city in 1856. He paid his creditors in full after a failed partnership, and still ended in prison. Frank Henderson edited the account, first printed in Temple Bar Magazine and reissued in London in 1869. The author writes for a kind brother who cheered his darkest hours.

Chapters follow his feelings on entering prison, his trial and sentence, three months in a Scottish prison, and removal to a Yorkshire one. Fellow prisoners fill the pages: an old jail bird, a soldier, an innocent convict, and a cracksman planning murder and escape. Victorian prison life is shown from a cell.
21321-before-the-dawn-a-story-of-the-fal:
Joseph A. Altsheler set this 1903 novel in Richmond as the Confederacy falls. It opens on a raw, gusty morning. A thin, brown-faced officer with a stiff left arm and a bullet-holed uniform boards a train for the capital. Chapters move through the Mosaic Club, the Secretary's manoeuvres, and a woman in brown pursued through the city.

Robert and Lucia carry the love story through the pall of winter, while the chapters on feeding the hungry show a starving capital. Altsheler knew the Civil War deeply and wrote many novels of it. The fall of Richmond ends an era for his characters, in flight, fire, and change of flags.
21357-nic-revel-a-white-slave-s-adventur:
Nic Revel grows up on a small Devon estate where poachers keep raiding the family's salmon pool. In George Manville Fenn's tale, a big fight at the pool ends with Royal Navy men supporting the Revels. Wounded in the dark, Nic is mistaken for a poacher and press-ganged with the men he fought.

Carried to America still half conscious, he is sold by the ship to a slave dealer. The dealer sells him on to a settler far up a river in alligator land. Hard work and poor food follow for Nic and a poacher turned friend. Their long effort to escape and reach Devon again drives the tale's second half.
21391-great-african-travellers-from-mung:
Finding the sources of great rivers drove the men in W. H. G. Kingston's Great African Travellers. The book runs from Mungo Park to Livingstone and Stanley, the best known names in African travel. At the start of their age, the coasts were mapped, but the deep interior was not.

Kingston tells how each traveller set out from a coastal base and won leave to pass inland. Some African rulers gave a warm welcome, and others did not. The Nile and its twin branches drew many of the boldest trips. The book gives a clear, joined account of a whole age of bold travel.
21393-hendricks-the-hunter-or-the-border:
Hendricks earns his living by the gun in W. H. G. Kingston's tale of Zululand, Hendricks the Hunter. He hunts game and trades skins and other goods along the border farms. The book opens among the steep ranges and deep valleys of South Africa.

One long hunting trip carries the action, told with Kingston's usual care for place. Wild beasts, snakes, and thirst are constant threats on the trail. The Zulu people he meets are drawn with warmth when they prove friends. A heavy wagon, built of stink wood, hauls the loads. The tale mixes trade, travel, and danger in equal parts.
21416-randy-of-the-river-or-the-adventur:
Randy Thompson works his way up from the river bank in Horatio Alger's Randy of the River, published in 1906. Randy is a patient fisher who waits at the hole while other boys wander off. That same steady grit marks all his dealings in the tale.

As a young deckhand on a river boat, Randy meets greed, blame, and unfair charges. In one key scene he tells Mr Polk that a loss was not his fault, and he will not stand for it. Alger's hero holds to honest work and a clear name. The tale rewards him in the usual Alger way, by steady rise.
21458-charley-laurel-a-story-of-adventur:
Charley Laurel passes into a sailor's hands as a small child in W. H. G. Kingston's Charley Laurel. At a West Indian place just attacked by the British, his nurse is fatally wounded. Seaman Dick Driver takes the boy and raises him aboard ship.

Their luck runs wild: cast away on a raft, picked up by pirates, saved by a privateer. On a South Pacific island, captors hold the two apart. Charley's trick frees Dick, and a British ship takes them off. In England a shipowner's family takes to the boy and sends him to school.
21489-the-secret-of-the-island:
W. H. G. Kingston translated Jules Verne's The Secret of the Island from the French. The tale follows a party cast away on a Pacific island after a balloon trip. Kingston also gave English readers a version of The Swiss Family Robinson.

Pirates and escaped convicts from Australia trouble the settlers' hard-won home. At odd times, unseen help saves them, as if some power watched over the island. That power proves to be Captain Nemo, hidden in a vast cave with his wealth. The book stands as a sequel to Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea.
21579-snarleyyow-or-the-dog-fiend:
Snarleyyow, the dog fiend, survives every attempt on his life in Captain Marryat's novel of 1837. Frost coats the spars and small iron guns of his ship at dawn. All hands but his owner treat the ugly beast with spite, and he returns the favour.

Marryat sets the tale when a Dutch-born king sat on the English throne. His Dutch courtiers and officials fill the court, and the cutter runs often to the Netherlands. Side plots breed in those crossings, among a crew of hopeless, unkind folk. The dog outlasts them all, as nasty at the end as at the start.
21591-the-harbours-of-england:
John Ruskin writes on Turner's ports in The Harbours of England, given here from his complete works. Turner and the engraver Lupton began the Ports of England as a serial in 1826. Only three numbers appeared before the plan stalled for want of time.

Ruskin's text, first issued in full in 1856, treats Dover, Ramsgate, Plymouth, and Portsmouth. Margate, Falmouth, Sidmouth, Whitby, Deal, and Scarborough follow in short, rich chapters. Collectors paid eleven or twelve guineas for proof sets of the plates. The editor laments that Ruskin's readers have passed the book by, and this edition makes the case anew.
21721-the-coral-island:
Ralph Rover tells his own story in Ballantyne's most famous book, a tale of boys cast away on a South Sea island. Ralph was born at sea, the son and grandson of captains, and roving runs in his blood. He ships out as a boy, hungry for adventure in foreign lands, and a wreck gives him more than he asked for.

On the island, Ralph and his companions must find food, build shelter, and face dangers from sea and land. Ballantyne never saw the Pacific, yet his coral shores and lagoons convinced generations of readers. The book shaped nearly every island adventure written after it, and boys read it eagerly for a century.
21729-dusty-diamonds-cut-and-polished-a-:
London street children stand at the center of this Ballantyne novel, first published in 1884. Two homeless boys near Whitechapel, in the East End, are taken off the streets by rescuers. They are trained up and sent to Canada, to live with a farmer's family there. Their story runs beside a grimmer one.

The mother of one boy struggles with drink, too many children, and a violent, thieving husband. Her eldest daughter holds the family together while the father sits in jail. Ballantyne drew the title from his theme: rough lives hold worth that care can polish. The tale gives a close look at street life in the London of his day.
21732-fort-desolation-red-indians-and-fu:
Jack Robinson is the plain, quiet hero of this Ballantyne tale of a lonely fur-trade fort in Rupert's Land. To strangers he looks like the most commonplace of men, sandy-haired and unnoticed. In truth a deep stream of romance runs in him, flashing out only in rare moments. Solitude does not suit him, yet his work gives him plenty of it.

Ballantyne sets the story among the traders and native peoples of the far northern wilderness. He knew that world from his own Hudson's Bay years in Canada. Trade, travel, and the long winters of an outpost shape the tale. Jack's calm grit holds it together from first page to last.
21826-my-pet-recipes-tried-and-true-cont:
Favorite dishes of a church circle fill My Pet Recipes, a Canadian cookbook gathered by the ladies and friends of St. Andrew's Church in Quebec. Each recipe comes as a pet of its giver, tried and true in her own kitchen. The pages carry the marks of their time and place. Furs by Holt, Renfrew are advertised at the front, and grocers promise the freshest goods in Quebec.

Community cookbooks like this one preserved home cooking that no chef ever wrote down. Soups, cakes, and preserves pass from neighbor to neighbor in print. The ads around the recipes are part of the record too, showing the shops those cooks relied upon. For food historians, such books are gold: plain, practical, and close to real tables.
21948-little-busybodies-the-life-of-cric:
Insects get biographies in Little Busybodies, a nature book for children aged eight to fourteen. Jeannette Marks and Julia Moody of Mount Holyoke College published it in 1909. The life of crickets, ants, bees, beetles, and their kin is told as story-led science. A journey to Rangeley Village frames the lessons. Chapters march with the little army of grasshoppers, listen to cricket fiddlers, and ask how Katy did with the katydids.

Dragonflies go fishing, and may-flies live their brief day in the telling. The book belongs to a Harper series covering crabs, shells, fish, birds, and flowers in the same plan. Pictures name the cast, from cicada killer to mole cricket. It teaches close watching as a form of fun.
22108-the-untroubled-mind:
Herbert J. Hall, a doctor who treated nervous patients, wrote The Untroubled Mind about worry and restless living. Hall warns that peace will not arrive in a flash of revelation. Change comes slowly, by returning again and again to honest work. He refuses to belittle that struggle; he wants it fought at a better level.

His counsel joins medical sense to a quiet faith in purposeful occupation. Ordered work, outdoor life, and simple interests steady the mind in his practice. The book grew from Hall's work with invalids who had lost their trades. It is an early, humane entry in the literature of mental health, still readable for its calm good sense.
22142-the-modern-scottish-minstrel-volum:
Charles Rogers, a Scottish minister and antiquary, edited The Modern Scottish Minstrel. Volume V continues his gathering of Scotland's songs with lives of the song-makers. The series aimed to carry Scottish song from Burns's age into Rogers's own century. Each song comes with notes on its author and its air.

This volume's opening matter praises bodies that relieved poor men of genius and learning. Such societies kept Scotland's literary spirit alive, Rogers believed. Portraits of the poets face their songs. The Minstrel volumes are quarries for anyone studying Scottish song: words, tunes, and biographies together. Volume V holds the later letters of the alphabet of poets.
22201-the-butterfly-s-funeral-a-sequel-t:
The Butterfly's Funeral continues the insect world made famous by The Butterfly's Ball. That tiny verse fable, written for the Roscoe children, had charmed Georgian England. In this sequel the butterfly is dead and must be buried in state. The corpse is embalmed at sunset and enclosed in a case spun by the silkworm herself.

The hornet helps lay the coffin on a bier of myrtle and jasmine. Beetles, bees, and all the ball's bright company form the funeral train. The poem teaches children nature's names through pageantry and grief. Such miniature books, printed for the nursery trade, were the picture books of their day, and this sequel kept a beloved trifle alive.
22210-in-the-forbidden-land:
A. Henry Savage Landor travelled in Tibet when Tibet was closed to foreigners, and In the Forbidden Land tells how. Landor was captured, tortured, and expelled by Tibetan officials in 1897. His two-volume account caused a sensation on its release. Reviewers quoted in the book praise its vivid verbal pictures and the author's own drawings and photographs.

Landor describes passes, monasteries, and the men who hunted him across the plateau. He presents himself as artist and explorer in one, emphasising the letterpress with his pencil. Some contemporaries doubted details; the adventure's core was never in question. The book remains a classic of forbidden-frontier travel writing.
22229-the-modern-scottish-minstrel-volum:
Volume VI closes Charles Rogers's Modern Scottish Minstrel, his great gathering of Scotland's songs. Rogers pairs each song with the life of its maker. This volume's frontispiece shows Paisley, birthplace of Tannahill, Alexander Wilson, and John Wilson. Weaver poets and Paisley shawls stand behind many of these songs.

Rogers opens with a reflection on poetry as the first language of nations. The lyric muse, he writes, chose lands of mountain and flood, and left them when liberty died. The songs that follow, with their notes, prove his devotion to that idea. Six volumes strong, the Minstrel remains a working library of Scottish song and song-makers.
22342-supermind:
Supermind is a science fiction story preserved from Project Gutenberg, again featuring Malone. He agrees peacefully with whatever the Director of the FBI says. He eyes that powerful man with due wariness.

After all, Malone argues, the news is nothing new. The country has always been going to hell in a handbasket. One way or another, he says, decline is the old story. That shrug sets the tale's tone of dry humor under pressure. A supermind, by the title, stands behind the trouble. Readers get a wry period story where vast powers and federal men meet one unflappable talker.
22377-rollo-in-switzerland:
Rollo in Switzerland sends a young American traveler through the Alps. Rollo was the hero of a famous series of travel books for children. His last day in Paris opens this volume's journey.

In Paris, Rollo learned the passport system by actual experience. That lesson in paperwork readied him for crossing into Switzerland. The series taught geography through a boy's questions and mishaps. Adults in the books explain countries, customs, and rules as they go. Young readers toured Europe without leaving home. This Swiss volume offers mountains and manners together. It shows how nineteenth-century families taught travel, order, and curiosity in one small package.
22581-the-child-voice-in-singing-treated:
Francis E. Howard wrote The Child Voice in Singing, a teaching treatise published in 1895. Howard treats the child's singing voice from both a bodily and a practical angle, with special care for girl and boy choirs. His audience is the large body of vocal music teachers in public schools.

Howard argues that the core of all vocal teaching must be brought home to school instructors in a convincing way. He holds that teachers accept a new idea only when its truth is proved to them plainly. The book therefore mixes body science with classroom argument. It remains a useful window on how singing was taught, and how reformers tried to change school music from inside.
22590-wind:
Wind is a science fiction story with a Dutch flavor, set partly around Earth's seas and partly on Venus. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Its dialogue name-checks the IJsselmeer and the old Zuider Zee, and its sailors speak like men used to rough water and tall claims.

In the sample, a captain named Heemskerk teases young Jan about returning punctually, broom at the masthead and all, the old sailor's sign of a swept, victorious sea. Jan answers that brooms are scarce on Venus. The blend of sea lore and space travel marks the tale's playful spirit. It offers readers a short, salty mix of nautical tradition and planetary adventure.
22756-the-enchanted-island:
The Enchanted Island is a children's fantasy issued by E. P. Dutton and Company in 1919. The catalog record credits the publisher. Its world is an archipelago of four big islands, each a separate kingdom that has nothing to do with the others, ripe ground for a young traveler's adventures.

The largest island is called the Island of Sunne because it is the nicest and has the finest weather. It never rains there in the daytime, but only at night, which, the narrator admits, is very convenient. That confiding voice, half guide-book and half fairy tale, carries the story from kingdom to kingdom. The book belongs to the shelf of gentle wonder tales written between the wars, when enchanted islands still dotted children's maps.
22765-lynton-and-lynmouth-a-pageant-of-c:
Lynton and Lynmouth: A Pageant of Cliff and Moorland is a topographical book about the twin villages of north Devon and their wild coast where Exmoor meets the sea. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Pageant is the right word: the book parades the district's history, legends, and scenery in order.

Up and down the length of England, the text reflects, lie traces of far-off peoples. They run from Land's End to the Northumbrian dales. Their very names are faint guesses kept only in local speech. Around Lynton those traces run through cliff, combe, and moor. The Valley of Rocks, the East Lyn river, and smugglers' tales all take their turn. Such books served walkers in the great age of British hiking, and they keep the local lore that guidebooks now shorten.
22972-rollo-in-holland:
Jacob Abbott explains Dutch dikes in Rollo in Holland. The dikes are so immense, and so covered by houses, trees, mills, and even villages, that a traveler first seeing them can hardly believe they are dikes at all. Some run several hundred feet wide, with a broad public road on top and a canal beside it.

Rollo's Holland tour follows the Abbott formula, questions from the boy, patient answers from his elders, and a whole country turned into lessons. Windmills, canals, and tidy towns supply the sights. The series taught American children geography by pretending to travel with them. Its Holland remains a fair picture of what educated tourists admired there, order, industry, and land won from the sea.
23090-yr-ynys-unyg-or-the-lonely-island:
A Welsh title crowns Yr Ynys Unyg, or The Lonely Island. Its narrator settles business briskly. The action took place close enough to home, she says, that a stranger would have little difficulty recognizing the heroes and heroines mentioned. As the narrative begins very abruptly, she will first give some personal account of the parties concerned.

An island, a household cut off from the world, and a woman's retrospective voice give this old tale its shape. The book descends from an eighteenth-century Welsh novel tradition, part romance, part conduct tale. Solitude tests its people's tempers, faith, and affections in turn. Readers meet a rare survival, Welsh fiction in English dress, preserved here under its bilingual title for anyone tracing the novel's spread beyond London.
23390-the-true-life-of-betty-ireland-wit:
Printed in London and reprinted in Dublin in seventeen fifty three, this satire tells the life of Betty Ireland as if she were a girl, with a sister named Blanch of Britain. Betty, a younger daughter by a second marriage, is left to run wild in the woods, clad in skins and fed on acorns.

A famous hunter takes her in and gives her to his son to raise. Her birth, schooling, and adventures follow in mock heroic style. The joke is political: Betty stands for Ireland, Blanch for Britain, and each curious particular points at real rule, trade, and pride. Readers who know the history will catch the satire, while others can enjoy the tale as a brisk, odd fable of a wild girl tamed by fortune.
23467-fairy-s-album-with-rhymes-of-fairy:
Cassell and Company printed this Fairy's Album in eighteen eighty four, with rhymes of fairyland and pictures on nearly every page. Fairy herself, bright as spring and loving every living thing, opens the book, prattling for hours to brooks, trees, flowers, birds, and butterflies.

The contents add the old woman who lived in a shoe, fairy's friends, peace and war, and fairy's dream, each in easy verse for small readers. The rhymes stay sweet and simple, made for reading aloud and for pointing at pictures. Children who love fairies will enjoy the album as a whole, a gentle, old fashioned picture book where kindness rules and every creature loves Fairy in return.
23653-how-it-all-came-round:
Mrs. L. T. Meade, a prolific writer of girls' stories, opened this novel on a rich young woman named Charlotte, seated by the fire with a book while two men talk nearby. One is her handsome father, whose fine face carries lines of long-felt anxiety; the other is a shrewd, commonplace-looking younger man whose blank face may hide more than it shows.

From that quiet room the story unwinds questions of fortune, family, and character: who Charlotte truly is, what her father fears, and how old choices return to shape the present. Meade's title promises what the plot delivers — events that circle back until debts, secrets, and affections settle where they belong.
23681-cupid-s-almanac-and-guide-to-heart:
John Cecil Clay and Oliver Herford compiled this humorous almanac for lovers in 1908, published by Houghton Mifflin and dedicated to lovers and lovers of lovers. It borrows the shape of a farmer's almanac — weather, tides, planets' motions, sun and moon risings, length of days, fairs, courts, and holidays — and turns every entry toward love.

The proposal plant, Heartis throbolae, must not be confused with the wild popper weed, Paterfamilias furiosis, which chokes it off and prevents its blooming. Tides keep coming in as usual along the coast, the Gulf Stream shifts its flow, and rains fall where Cupid wills. It is a light, illustrated joke book for Valentine's season, best read aloud.
23692-south-africa-and-the-transvaal-war:
Louis Creswicke published the first volume of his history of the South African war in Edinburgh in 1900, with numerous illustrations and maps. His stated aim was an unvarnished tale of the circumstances that brought about the crisis in South Africa. Those circumstances stretched back nearly half a century, and he drew on the best authorities of the day.

The volume runs from the foundation of Cape Colony to the Boer ultimatum of October 9, 1899. It covers the growth of the Transvaal, the Orange Free State, Zulu disturbances, the disaster at Isandlwana, and the march toward Ulundi. Written while the war was still being fought, it gives readers the British view of how Briton and Boer reached the breaking point.
23874-no-man-s-land:
H. C. McNeile, writing as Sapper, published No Man's Land in 1917 and dedicated it to the infantryman. It came suddenly when it did come, the narrator says, though everyone knew war was coming. Clive Draycott, home on leave from Egypt, stares foolishly at his recall telegram in his club, then crosses next day to Boulogne.

Four parts structure the book: The Way to the Land, The Land, Seed Time, and Harvest. Chapters bring a day of peace, over the top, the man-trap, my lady of the jasmine, morphia, and the song of the bayonet. McNeile, who also wrote Men, Women, and Guns, gives the Western Front in stories that are grim, tender, and darkly funny by turns.
24159-customs-and-fashions-in-old-new-en:
Alice Morse Earle wrote this study of old New England life, published by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1894. Its fifteen chapters move from child life, courtship and marriage customs, and domestic service to home interiors and table plenishings. Later chapters cover larder supplies, colonial drinks, travel by tavern and turnpike, holidays, sports, books, dress, doctors, and funeral customs.

Earle opens with the Puritan baby, who faced a Spartan struggle in ill-heated houses, scorched by the fireplace on one side and chilled four feet away from it. The book gathers homely detail into a full picture of colonial days. Readers get a rich, readable guide to how New Englanders lived, worked, and buried their dead.
24200-american-men-of-mind:
Burton E. Stevenson wrote this survey of American minds, published by Doubleday, Page and Company in 1913, as a companion to his Men of Action. That book sketched discoverers, pioneers, presidents, statesmen, soldiers, and sailors. This one turns to writers of prose and verse, painters, sculptors, figures of the stage, scientists and educators, philanthropists and reformers, men of affairs, and inventors.

Each chapter ends with a summary, and portraits face the text, from Longfellow, Hawthorne, and Emerson to Greeley, Stuart, Booth, Agassiz, Eliot, Girard, Beecher, Wanamaker, and Morse. Stevenson aims to give the essential facts of American culture through its makers. Readers get a broad, readable gallery of the nation's thinkers and artists.
24235-mary-ware-s-promised-land:
Annie Fellows Johnston wrote this girls' book as part of her Little Colonel series. Volumes sold at a dollar and fifty cents each, or eighteen dollars for twelve volumes boxed as a set. The series follows the Little Colonel through a house party, holidays, a hero, and boarding school. Later books add Arizona, a Christmas vacation, maid of honor, and a knight come riding, with Mary Ware as the Little Colonel's chum.

Mary Ware's own books include Mary Ware in Texas and Mary Ware's Promised Land, the volume of the title. Johnston writes warm, old-style stories of girls, homes, and growing up, with pictures throughout. Readers get a cheerful entry in a beloved series, following Mary Ware toward the promised land of the title.
2453-beyond:
John Galsworthy's Beyond follows a woman whose love for a married man tests the boundaries of Edwardian morality. The novel traces Gyp's passion, her marriage of convenience, and her later choices, with Galsworthy's sympathy for women trapped by social rules. The story moves between London, the country, and the Continent.

Galsworthy's quiet, reflective style suits a novel about feeling and consequence. Its heroine's independence was bold for its time. Readers of Galsworthy's social novels will find a thoughtful, moving work. Galsworthy later won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1932. Galsworthy's heroine was daring for Edwardian readers.
24577-the-hindered-hand:
Sutton E. Griggs wrote this novel, subtitled The Reign of the Repressionist, first published at Nashville in 1905 and reprinted in a third revised edition. Its epigraph quotes the Psalm: princes shall come out of Egypt, and Ethiopia shall soon stretch out her hands unto God. Griggs dedicated it to his father, a man of peace, and his mother, tender and serene.

The novel answers the racism of its age with a story of Black life, dignity, and resistance under repression. Griggs, a Black minister and novelist, wrote to uplift and to argue. His book remains a landmark of early African American fiction, powerful, earnest, and historically important.
24757-the-atonement-and-the-modern-mind:
James Denney, a professor at the United Free Church College in Glasgow, published this work of theology in 1903. It asks how the Christian doctrine of the atonement, the death of Christ for sin, can be stated honestly to a modern mind. Denney treats the subject as the center of the faith, shaping how believers think of God, man, and history.

Chapters take up sin and God's reaction to it, then Christ and man in the atonement. Denney argues against soft views that turn God into mere indulgent kindness, holding that a moral relation must rest on law as well as love. The book suits readers who want a serious, plainly argued statement of classic doctrine.
2498-addresses-by-henry-drummond:
Henry Drummond, the Scottish evangelist and naturalist, collects addresses on faith, science, and the Christian life in this volume. The addresses include his famous meditation on love, applying the language of evolution to spiritual growth with warmth and clarity. Drummond's voice is earnest, accessible, and hopeful.

The book's popularity in its day reflected a hunger for faith reconciled with science. Modern readers will find its optimism dated but its sincerity appealing. It serves as a record of Victorian religious thought. Drummond's address on love became one of the best-selling pamphlets of its age.
25032-a-yacht-voyage-round-england:
W. H. G. Kingston's Yacht Voyage Round England follows a boy and his brother, sent home early from boarding school by illness among the pupils, on a lengthened summer holiday afloat. Their father, a retired naval captain with a beautiful new yacht, proposes a cruise round England, taking in southern Scotland and the Caledonian Canal. The boys keep journals, and Kingston turns those notes into story and commentary on the places passed.

The voyage opens at dinner on the day of their arrival home, as the boys discuss the weeks ahead and their father asks whether they might cruise with him that summer. They prick up their ears, promise to work their passage, pull and haul, and never tire. Later the yacht must run back to Falmouth for repairs after a brush with the Dolphin near the Stags. The book is a boy's summer in full sail.
25068-the-book-of-sports-containing-out-:
William Martin's Book of Sports, in its second London edition of 1852, is a how-to guide to outdoor play for boys and girls. Published by Darton and Company, it gathers games, exercises, and crafts that children could learn without a teacher standing over them.

Marble games and cold-weather games come first, then gymnastics, cricket laws, swimming, gardening, and carpentry. Each section explains the rules or steps in plain order. The volume reads as a Victorian handbook for active leisure, and as a record of games many children still know.
25174-rollo-in-scotland:
Jacob Abbott's Rollo in Scotland, published in Boston in 1864, is one volume of the popular Rollo's Tour in Europe series. It follows the boy Rollo, his uncle George, and his friend Waldron on a tour meant to teach as much as to amuse.

The party lands at Glasgow, sails down the Clyde, and enters the Highlands for the Trossachs, Stirling, and Loch Leven. Edinburgh brings Holyrood Palace, Queen Mary's rooms, and the castle. Abbott mixes travel facts with small adventures, including a fishing plan that goes wrong, in the instructive style young readers loved.
25186-the-border-watch-a-story-of-the-gr:
Joseph A. Altsheler's Border Watch, published in 1941, is a frontier tale subtitled A Story of the Great Chief's Last Stand. It belongs with Altsheler's long shelf of American adventure novels, from the Young Trailers to the Texan and Civil War series.

A young frontiersman named Henry shows his woodcraft by imitating a wolf's cry so well that a real wolf answers and a British lieutenant pays him a shilling for the feat. Scouts, warriors, and forest rivers fill the story as a great chief's resistance nears its end. Altsheler writes with his usual pace and love of the border country.
2529-the-analysis-of-mind:
Bertrand Russell published this philosophy book in 1921, in the Muirhead Library of Philosophy, and it grew from his lectures on what the mind is. Russell asks whether we need a soul or self standing behind thoughts, or whether thoughts, feelings, and memories can be explained on their own.

He works through sensation, images, memory, belief, desire, and emotion, arguing that mind is a pattern of events rather than a hidden thing. The prose is clear and bold, with examples from daily life and from science. The book still rewards readers who want a sharp, modern account of how minds work without mystery.
25307-drolls-from-shadowland:
J. H. Pearce's Drolls from Shadowland, published in New York in 1893, is a book of Cornish fantasy tales. Pearce, known for novels of Cornish life, writes drolls in which ordinary people meet strange bargains, witches, and wonders.

Stories include a miner who coins his blood into gold. Another man learns the language of birds, only to find they talk of food and nests. A third desires to be a tree. An unchristened child, a man who met hate, and a haunted house complete the set. The tales mix mining life, dialect, and eerie humor.
25545-children-s-literature-a-textbook-o:
Charles Madison Curry and Erle Elsworth Clippinger edit this textbook of sources for teachers and teacher-training classes. Both men were professors of literature at Indiana State Normal School. Rand McNally published the book in 1920, with a 1926 edition.

Introductions, notes, and bibliographies frame each section. Mother Goose jingles and nursery rhymes open the book, from Baa Baa Black Sheep and Hickory Dickory Dock to Humpty Dumpty and Hey Diddle Diddle. An epigraph from C. B. Tinker praises peasants and nurses as unsurpassed narrators, guardians of legend from the childhood of nations.
2557-old-mother-west-wind:
Thornton W. Burgess wrote these animal tales for his young son, and dedicated them to his mother and the boy whose love of stories inspired them. Old Mother West Wind herself blows through the Green Forest, where Peter Rabbit, Reddy Fox, Jimmy Skunk, and Grandfather Frog live their small, busy lives.

Each chapter answers a child's question, such as why Jimmy Skunk wears stripes or why Grandfather Frog has no tail. Burgess teaches woodland facts through jokes, mishaps, and chases, never lecturing. The book remains a gentle first guide to wild neighbors, told in a voice made for bedtime.
25787-on-the-edge-of-the-arctic-or-an-ae:
Ashton Lamar writes this Aeroplane Boys tale, On the Edge of the Arctic, or An Aeroplane in Snowland, published in Chicago by Reilly and Britton in 1913 with pictures by Norman P. Hall. The airship Gitchie Manitou, ready for its first flight in the far north, fronts the book.

Chapters introduce an airship and Count Zept, a curious stranger learning the Gitchie Manitou's object, and Colonel Howell making a novel proposal. Howell discovers an old friend in Jack Zept, and northern flying, snow, and adventure carry a boys' aviation story to the Arctic edge.
2595-ramsey-milholland:
Booth Tarkington wrote this novel for the memory of Billy Miller, a boy patriot who died in 1918, and it follows Ramsey Milholland from small town boyhood into the world. The opening marches home with soldiers, cheers, and ladies turning out to welcome Johnnie, setting a tone of youth and war.

Ramsey grows through school, friendship, first love, and the pull of duty, in Tarkington's warm, plain American prose. The book is a coming of age story shadowed by the Great War, and a portrait of a decent boy learning what manhood asks. It charms as a small, humane tale of growing up.
26006-a-girl-s-ride-in-iceland:
Mrs. Alec Tweedie rides Iceland in this travel book, second edition printed by Horace Cox in 1894. Tweedie, author of a winter jaunt to Norway, calls the book her maiden effort, and notes it sparked a fierce row over whether women should ride astride. Picture papers took sides for and against, families quarreled, and bitter words flew over a simple and harmless matter.

The ride itself takes in high barren places among huge boulders, where a botanist gathered plants and lost more from a pony's back. His list runs from sea plantain and meadow buttercup to eyebright, lady's mantle, alpine fleabane, sorrel, forget me not, and saxifrage. With pictures and a map, the book gives a lively Victorian woman's view of Iceland's lore and light.
26007-from-paris-to-new-york-by-land:
Harry de Windt travels from Paris to New York by land in this book from Nelson, crossing Europe, Asia, and America without a sea voyage. Part one runs by Trans Siberian Railway, the Paris of Siberia, the great Lena post road, the city of the Yakute, and darkest Siberia. Through Verkhoyansk and an Arctic inferno it reaches the lower Kolyma and a cruel coast. Among the Tchuktchis, the journey reaches Bering Straits.

Part two crosses to Cape Prince of Wales, an Arctic city, a river of gold, Dawson, and the upper Yukon. Then by White Pass Railway and the Franco American railway it runs through Skagway to New York. Appendices list distances, post stations, reindeer stations, and settlements. One ruined chapel town, Bassarika, lost all its people to smallpox and want save a priest. The book is a bold overland epic.
26026-the-surrender-of-santiago-an-accou:
Frank Norris writes an eyewitness account of the surrender of Santiago to General Shafter on July 17, 1898, printed by Paul Elder in 1917 for Red Cross funds. Norris spent two days at Second Brigade headquarters in the Hacienda San Pablo, a six room villa where even tarantulas shaken from blankets seemed no terror beside a real roof. The army lay in a great crescent to the sea, resting on arms through a twenty four hour truce.

The surrender scene felt larger than life, Norris writes, like Appomattox, Mexico, and Yorktown at once. General Toral rode forward on a little white bronco, both generals uncovered, and shook hands with Shafter as the world watched. Toral, sun reddened and gray mustached, looked well, and the moment seemed a play viewed from the saddle. The account is vivid war reporting.
26036-the-sylvan-cabin-a-centenary-ode-o:
Edward Smyth Jones honors Lincoln in a centenary ode in The Sylvan Cabin and Other Verse, printed by Sherman, French in 1911 with an introduction by William Stanley Braithwaite. Dedicated to Justice Arthur P. Stone of Cambridge. The book holds the title ode, life in a dream, the morning star, songs of thanks, and a bouquet. An ode to the soldiers' and sailors' monument and verses to a faded flower and dainty Dora follow.

Later poems include the bachelor's song, floating with the gale, Lula Johnson's song, a tribute to Dunbar, an ode to Ethiopia, the mayor's ring, and behind the bars. One singer hopes, when sods lie on his breast and his soul seeks rest, to wing home to glory on Lula Johnson's song. Jones writes of Lincoln, race, and faith in warm, plain verse.
26150-the-proverbs-of-scotland:
Alexander Hislop's Proverbs of Scotland, here in a new edition revised and supplemented at Edinburgh in 1868, gathers Scots sayings with notes that explain them and a glossary of hard words. Its preface traces earlier collectors, from Archbishop Beaton near the Reformation to David Fergusson's 940 proverbs and James Kelly's near 3000, printed in London in 1721.

The sayings run in Scots dialect, each with plain sense notes and, at times, an English parallel. Readers meet thrift, caution, pride, and neighbourly wisdom in short, sharp lines. The book preserves a folk voice that might else fade, and it still serves as a guide to how Scots folk summed up life in a sentence.
26320-the-merry-go-round:
Carl Van Vechten's Merry-Go-Round, issued by Alfred A. Knopf in 1918, gathers essays on music, taste, and the theatre. Contents list In Defence of Bad Taste, Music and Supermusic, a long piece on Edgar Saltus, and The New Art of the Singer. Other essays treat Au Bal Musette, music and cooking, and two young American playwrights.

Music and cooking links national food with national sound, from Hungarian goulash and rhapsodies to Russian kascha, bortsch, and vodka behind Boris Godunow and Petrouchka. Theatre notes cover The Land of Joy, Mimi Aguglia, a new Isadora, and Margaret Anglin in As You Like It. Many pieces first ran in The Smart Set, Vanity Fair, and other journals.
26388-a-humorous-history-of-england:
C. Harrison's threepenny booklet, published in 1920 with forty-eight illustrations, tells the essentials of English history in light, amusing rhyme. Kings and crises pass in short stanzas, each pairing a date with a jest. James I arrives as a double-barrelled king, learned, hostile to tobacco and witches, and sure of divine right, while Puritans who will not comply face his threats.

The Pilgrim Fathers follow in 1620, sailing in the Mayflower to escape persecution and unfurl freedom's flag in an uncharted world. Harrison keeps the verse brisk and the jokes broad, aiming at readers who want the shape of the story without the weight of a textbook. The booklet's charm lies in its speed, its pictures, and its cheerful irreverence.
26437-the-rubaiyat-of-a-huffy-husband:
Mary B. Little's 1908 comic poem, written in quatrains after Omar Khayyam, gives voice to a husband undone by his wife's new fad. On Christmas Day a well-meaning friend presents his wife with the Rubaiyat, and once the holidays settle, she revels in its ancient lore. Earlier fads, vases, fans, and spoons, never touched the comfort of the home, but Omar proves different.

Each evening the husband returns to find his spouse deep in the book, scarcely rousing, or else grinding out quatrains of her own and demanding that he listen. He fumes that, had he known his fate, the volume would have vanished into a locked drawer. The joke turns on a real literary craze, told with mock solemnity in Omar's own stanza form.
26445-songs-from-the-southland:
Selected by S. F. Price and published by D. Lothrop in 1890, this anthology gathers verse from the American South. George D. Prentice's The Closing Year opens the collection at midnight, with the bell tolling the departed year and moonlight lying like a pale shroud on stream and wood. Spring, Summer, Autumn, and Winter stand as spirits above the cloud, breathing a dirge over the dead year.

Later poems turn to the sea and the harbor, with sails lowered, anchors uncovered, and lights glimmering at last after a tempest voyage. Memory and tears run through the book, as poets mourn hopes and joys that have passed to nothingness. The volume preserves a regional voice of its time, tender, musical, and fond of twilight scenes.
26491-the-sand-hills-of-jutland:
Hans Christian Andersen's Sand-Hills of Jutland, translated by Mrs. Bushby and published in London in 1860, gathers Danish tales around its title story. The title tale begins far from Jutland, in sunny Spain, where pomegranates bloom among laurels, children parade with lights and banners, and a young married couple enjoy health, humor, riches, and rank. The sea forms the highway between Spain and the Danish dunes.

Other tales include The Mud-King's Daughter, The Girl Who Trod Upon Bread, The Old Oak Tree's Last Dream, and The Wind Relates the Story of Waldemar Daae and His Daughters. Shorter pieces, such as The Pen and the Inkstand and The Quickest Runners, mix fancy with moral point. Andersen dedicates the volume to Baron Charles Joachim Hambro.
26539-the-rover-boys-at-big-horn-ranch-o:
Arthur M. Winfield, the pen name of Edward Stratemeyer, published this Rover Boys book with Grosset and Dunlap in 1922, in the second Rover Boys series. It opens at Colby Hall in snow, with Fred and Andy Rover, their cousin Jack, and fellow cadets in a snowball contest. School rivalries, a sneak, and a shooting contest fill the first half, ending with good-bye to school.

The boys then head west to Big Horn Ranch, where the subtitle's double round-up awaits. In the saddle, they meet a cattle stampede, a mountain lion, and a cave, with a confession and a capture to close the tale. It is a clean, fast serial adventure, moving from schoolboy pranks to ranch work without pausing for breath.
26552-fruits-of-queensland:
Albert H. Benson, late instructor in fruit culture for the Queensland Government and then director of agriculture at Hobart, published this guide at Brisbane in 1914. He writes for home-seekers weighing Queensland against the United States and Canada, arguing that it offers room, work, and no intensely cold winter. Congested towns, he says, drive surplus workers to seek new land.

Chapters cover climate and soils for tropical, semi-tropical, and deciduous fruit, then take fruits one by one. Banana, pineapple, mango, mangosteen, papaw, citrus, persimmon, loquat, grape, apple, and cherry each get culture notes, with a list of fruits and vegetables grown in Queensland to close. It is a practical settler's handbook, not a cookbook.
26635-the-rose-garden-husband:
Margaret Widdemer published this novel with Grosset and Dunlap in 1915, with illustrations by Walter Biggs, in memory of Howard Taylor Widdemer. Its heroine is Phyllis Narcissa Braithwaite, whom children call the Liberry Teacher, though her payroll title is Assistant for the Children's Department, Greenway Branch. At twenty-five she earns fifty dollars a month, after starting at eighteen on thirty.

Phyllis hides her romantic name, which belongs to a New England parsonage garden of pink roses and girl-dreams, not to a smutty city library. An illustration caption gives the book's joke and promise: she married principally for a rose-garden, and that is lovely. Widdemer follows a working girl's wit, weariness, and wish for a garden of her own.
26755-cornwall-s-wonderland:
Mabel Quiller-Couch published this children's retelling of Cornish legends in 1914, hoping to save romances and legends of old Cornwall that were rapidly being forgotten. Her preface recalls skipping long, involved paragraphs written in dialect often beyond even a Cornish child to translate. She presents a few tales in simpler form, to suit Cornish children and children everywhere.

Contents run from Corineus fighting the chief of the giants and the giant of St. Michael's Mount through the fairies on the Gump and the fairy ointment. Barker and the buccas, Lutey and the mermaid, and cruel Coppinger the Dane follow. Madge Figgy the wrecker and Sir Tristram and La Belle Iseult close the book. The opening tale sends Brutus and Corineus with a Trojan army against giants, until only the great Gogmagog, too injured to run, is left bellowing with rage and fear.
26781-letters-on-the-nicobar-islands-the:
The Reverend John Gottfried Haensel, the only surviving missionary of the Nicobar mission, addressed these letters to the Reverend C. I. Latrobe, published at London in 1812 and dedicated to William Wilberforce. Haensel, formerly of St. Thomas in the West Indies, resided seven years on Nancauwery, after eighteen years in the East and seventeen in the West Indies, thirty-eight years in the Brethren's missions.

Latrobe, who translated the letters, says Haensel wrote them from recollection at his request, without aiming at a complete history. They describe the islands' natural productions and the manners, customs, and superstitions of the natives, with an account of the Church of the United Brethren's attempt to convert them, undertaken in 1758. A green serpent with a frog-like mouth and red eyes, whose bite killed a woman within half an hour, shows the dangers Haensel recorded.
26880-the-bronze-age-in-ireland:
George Coffey, keeper of Irish antiquities in the National Museum and professor at the Royal Hibernian Academy, published this survey with Hodges, Figgis of Dublin and Simpkin, Marshall of London in 1913. Eleven plates and eighty-five illustrations carry the argument through twelve chapters, from the chronology of the Irish Bronze Age and a transitional copper period to bronze-age pottery and ornamentation. Coffey traces Irish halberds to a probable Spanish origin.

The chapters follow the metalwork in order. They cover flat copper celts and their moulds, the evolution of the bronze celt, and spear-heads from knife-dagger and rapier. They cover Irish gold lunulae, daggers and rapiers, gold gorgets and sun-disks, leaf-shaped swords and shields, torcs, trumpets, sickles, and disk-headed pins. A closing list gathers the well-authenticated Irish finds, and the ornamentation at Newgrange gets a chapter of its own.
2713-maiwa-s-revenge-or-the-war-of-the-l:
H. Rider Haggard tells this African tale in eight chapters, from Gobo's strike through a morning's sport, two rounds of fighting, and Maiwa's message. The plan of campaign, the attack, and Maiwa avenged close a swift, violent story.

Haggard's preface owns that the incident of the Thing that bites is no invention, but drawn from life. Maiwa, wronged and relentless, drives the plot with a warrior's logic. The novella offers Haggard's adventure at its most concentrated, with revenge as both justice and doom. Haggard keeps the tale short, fierce, and unsparing.
2716-sir-dominick-ferrand:
Henry James wrote this tale of a writer offered a manuscript with strings attached. Mr. Locket's curt note says there are several objections, but he will take it if the writer will alter it, and a postscript adds terms without wasting words.

The manuscript proves to be the letters of Sir Dominick Ferrand, and publishing them means weighing truth, reputation, and money. James writes with his fine irony about authorship and the market for scandal. The tale bites as a study of what a writer owes the dead, and what the living will pay.
27226-an-essay-on-the-antient-and-modern:
Henry Brooke's An Essay on the Ancient and Modern State of Ireland, printed at Dublin and reprinted at London in 1760 under George II, defends his native country. Dedicated to Matthew McNamara of Limerick, it answers sprightly young gentlemen back from continental rambles who affected contempt for Ireland.

Brooke gives a particular account of the great and glorious St. Patrick, adds the farmer's case of the Roman Catholics of Ireland, and recalls a wise, free, and truly parliamentary constitution. Military prowess against Romans and French, and a long run as a free state, anchor his plea for a fairer idea of the kingdom.
27337-from-the-car-behind:
Eleanor M. Ingram's From the Car Behind, second edition of 1912 from Lippincott with illustrations in color by James Montgomery Flagg, follows a motor tour to its end of the road. Ingram, author of The Flying Mercury and The Game or the Candle, dedicates the book to her dear and gracious mother.

Chapters run through Val de Rosas, The Strength of Ten, and The White Road of Honor, with the frontispiece showing people bursting over the course and overwhelming the victors. By an open door, a man clasps his hands behind his head with leisurely grace, while Rupert warns of a wet course, in Ingram's bright motoring romance.
27572-dickens-land:
J. A. Nicklin described this Dickens-Land, pictured by E. W. Haslehust, in Blackie's Beautiful England series, published in London, Glasgow, and Bombay in 1911. Companion volumes cover Oxford, the English Lakes, Canterbury, Shakespeare-Land, the Thames, and Windsor Castle.

Illustrations show Chalk, the house where Dickens spent his honeymoon, Gadshill Place from the gardens, Rochester from Strood, and Restoration House. Cobham Park, Cooling Church, Aylesford, and the Leather Bottle at Cobham follow. Nicklin notes that a literary shrine is often a hero's home of adoption, not his birthplace. The book guides readers through Dickens country.
27612-christmas-eve-at-swamp-s-end:
Norman Duncan, author of The Measure of a Man and Doctor Luke of the Labrador, published this Christmas story with Fleming H. Revell, copyrighted 1911 to 1915. An illustration bears the words: make of this child, a man.

The tale opens in the far, big, white Northwest, long after noon, with Christmas Eve splendidly impending. Duncan thanks God for unspoiled childish faith and the joys of children everywhere, as Christmas Eve comes fairly within view in the thickening eastern shadows. Bedtime races round the world, nine o'clock leaping from one longitude to the next, while night chases the children of the world to sleep with her soft, wide broom of dusk.
27669-the-johnstown-horror-or-valley-of-:
James Herbert Walker wrote this fully illustrated account of the Johnstown horror, or valley of death, published by H. J. Smith and Company of Philadelphia, with a Chicago address. Walker dedicates it to those who survived the Johnstown calamity and its neighboring villages.

The book promises a complete and thrilling account of the awful floods and their appalling ruin. It gives graphic descriptions of the terrible rush of waters and the destruction of houses, factories, churches, and towns, with heartrending scenes of agony and separation. Thrilling tales of heroic deeds and narrow escapes follow, with the sufferings of survivors, and the millions of dollars sent for relief from every city and state.
27687-steam-turbines-a-book-of-instructi:
Hubert E. Collins compiled and wrote this book of instruction for the adjustment and operation of the principal types of steam turbines. McGraw-Hill published it in New York and London, first edition, second impression, copyrighted in 1909.

Chapters treat the Curtis steam turbine in practice and the setting of its valves, the Allis-Chalmers turbine, and the Westinghouse-Parsons turbine. Proper methods of testing a steam turbine follow. The book is a practical manual for engineers working with this class of prime movers, giving adjustment and operation in clear order. A transcriber's note keeps the authors' spellings aline, gage, and hight.
27701-the-greatest-highway-in-the-world-:
The Greatest Highway in the World gives historical, industrial, and descriptive information on the towns, cities, and country passed through between New York and Chicago via the New York Central Lines. The lines asked the Encyclopaedia Britannica's editors to prepare this illustrated booklet.

Its foreword hopes the booklet will be a pleasant fellow-traveller on a journey over the lines. The information, it says, will deepen a traveller's sense of the history and industry of the places the lines serve. The lines enter twelve states. Train schedules note times from noon to midnight in dark-face type, rendered here with letters for morning and afternoon.
27780-treasure-island:
Robert Louis Stevenson's Treasure Island appears here in an illustrated children's edition, with color plates by Milo Winter and a foreword from Random House's 1986 edition. The story itself follows young Jim Hawkins from the Admiral Benbow inn.

After a dead guest's sea-chest yields a treasure map, Jim sails with a crew that includes the treacherous Long John Silver toward buried pirate gold. Still the best-known pirate adventure in English, it mixes mutiny, maps, and moral choice with a pace that has held young readers for generations. The contents run from the Old Buccaneer at the Admiral Benbow through the Black Spot and the sea-chest.
27881-in-cha-teau-land:
Anne Hollingsworth Wharton published In Château Land in 1911 with J. B. Lippincott Company of Philadelphia and London, with twenty-five illustrations. The book tours the châteaux of the Loire and beyond, from an embarrassment of châteaux to an island château, an afternoon at Coppet, and a château fête.

Chapters visit Langeais, Azay-le-Rideau, Amboise with its two queens, Blois, Chinon, Fontevrault, Angers, and Orleans with its Maid. Wharton writes as a cultivated traveler, joining history, architecture, and anecdote for readers planning their own French journeys. The frontispiece shows Loches with the gate of the Cordeliers, and later plates show Isola Bella and the staircase at St. Gatien.
27952-the-enchanted-castle-a-book-of-fai:
Hartwell James edited The Enchanted Castle, a book of fairy tales from Flowerland, published in Philadelphia by Henry Altemus Company in 1906 with forty illustrations by John R. Neill. The volume belongs to Altemus's fairy-tale series, priced at fifty cents, beside books of East Indian, Persian, and Chinese tales.

Contents include the title story, The Fair Maids of February, The Loveless Youth, The Wind Flower, The Fate of Hyacinthus, and The Flower Fairies. The tales give flowers voices and adventures, and the book is a charming example of early twentieth-century gift-book fantasy for children.
28197-the-trial-of-reuben-crandall-m-d-c:
The Trial of Reuben Crandall, M.D., Washington, 1836, reports a landmark case on slavery and free speech. Crandall stood charged with publishing and circulating seditious and incendiary papers in the District of Columbia, with intent to excite servile insurrection. A member of the bar compiled the report from court and counsel statements.

The trial lasted ten days before the whole court, the first case of its kind ever tried, with every point of law fully argued. The notice stresses the rights of slaveholders to guard against outside influence, and the danger to northern visitors carrying such papers. The volume gives a primary record of law and slavery before the Civil War.
28209-famous-women-george-sand:
Bertha Thomas wrote George Sand in 1883 for the Famous Women series, published in Boston by Roberts Brothers. Sand, the French novelist who wrote under a man's name, lived a life of singular variety, from early years and married life to a literary debut, Italian travel, and the novel Lelia. Thomas draws on Sand's memoirs and her large published letters.

Thomas admits the record is incomplete, with no full biography yet, and avoids gossip about the living. She aims for a fair outline of Sand's character and the forces that shaped her work. The short life suits readers new to Sand, offering a clear path into a great writer.
28237-a-vanished-hand:
Sarah Doudney's A Vanished Hand is a Victorian novel of a young woman's silent battle. Elsie Kilner fights a strife no one sees, in a small back room in London on a March afternoon. There is no broken weapon, no stain, only a clear view of sky above walls and roofs. Doudney opens with Whittier's lines on grasping and resigning.

Chapters follow Elsie through counsel, church, picnics, and an island visit, as a vanished hand, a roll of paper, and old friends shape her choice. The novel treats conscience, love, and duty with quiet feeling. Readers of Victorian domestic fiction will find it tender and earnest.
28333-messengers-of-evil-being-a-further:
Pierre Souvestre and Marcel Allain wrote Messengers of Evil in 1917 as a further account of Fantomas, the master criminal. Brentano's published the New York edition, following Fantomas and The Exploits of Juve. The novel opens on Monday, April 4, as the evening paper La Capitale reports a drama on Montmartre. Baroness de Vibray was found dead in painter Jacques Dollon's studio, the painter drugged beside her.

Chapters follow Juve through pearls, diamonds, finger prints, a prison van, and an execution, as Fantomas slips from trap to trap. Souvestre and Allain keep the pace breathless and the crimes bold. Readers of early crime fiction get a classic Fantomas chase.
28387-hurricane-island:
H. B. Marriott Watson's Hurricane Island, copyrighted in 1904 and published in 1905, is a sea adventure told by an East End London doctor. The narrator, worn down by club cases and knife wounds among alien sailors, finds his life changed when he is drawn into the world of ships and foreign ports.

Chapters carry him aboard the Sea Queen, into the Three Tuns inn, and into company with Mademoiselle Trebizond. A rising aboard ship, the capture of the bridge, a flag of truce, fog, tragedy, and an escape follow, ending on the island itself. Watson writes a brisk tale of villains, courage, and survival at sea.
28489-the-belove-d-vagabond:
William J. Locke's The Belovéd Vagabond, copyrighted in 1905 and issued by John Lane, is told by a London gutter urchin. The boy was sold to the musician Paragot for half-a-crown, and he recounts his benefactor's life as master, friend, and creator in one. Paragot presides over a club that meets above an attic in Tavistock Street, Covent Garden.

The tale follows Paragot through his talk, his music, and his odd circle of followers. It shows how a street boy gains a home of sorts, and how a gifted wanderer shapes the people around him. Readers meet a London of lodging rooms, clubs, and chance meetings, told with warmth and humor.
28551-the-trail-of-the-goldseekers-a-rec:
Hamlin Garland's The Trail of the Goldseekers, published by the Macmillan Company in 1899, records travel in prose and verse. Chapters follow outfitting, the stage road, camp at Quesnelle, the Blackwater Divide, and swimming the Nechaco. First crossings of the Bulkley, Hazelton midway on the trail, and the great Stikine Divide carry the party north.

Poems punctuate the march, from Anticipation and The Cow-boy to The Gaunt Gray Wolf, Siwash Graves, and The Long Trail. The goldseekers' camp at Glenora, great news at Wrangell, and the rush to Atlin Lake close the journey. Readers get a gold-rush trail told by a writer who walked it.
28573-le-morvan-a-district-of-france-its:
Henri de Crignelle's Le Morvan, translated from French by Captain Jesse and published by Saunders and Otley of London in 1851, sketches a district of France. Crignelle, a former officer of dragoons, grew up among noble forests and extensive vineyards, hunting partridges and hares in dewy stubbles. Wild cats, boars, and wolves filled the shady woods of his youth.

A friend, hearing his tales of sport unlike England's, urged him to scribble them down for restless English readers. Crignelle demurred, fearing comparison with Gordon Cumming's African lions and elephants, yet yielded. Legends, antiquities, and rural sketches join the hunting tales. Readers get a French countryside, near at hand and strange.
2865-otto-of-the-silver-hand:
Howard Pyle wrote Otto of the Silver Hand as a medieval adventure for young readers, set in a Germany of robber barons, monasteries, and warring castles. Otto, son of Baron Conrad, grows up between the Dragon's House and St. Michaelsburg, and the chapters follow the baron going forth to shear and coming home shorn. One-eyed Hans brings terror to the kitchen, and a ride for life tests the boy's courage.

Pyle's own illustrations match his plain, vivid storytelling, and the castle scenes give the book its lasting appeal. Otto wanders dark passages below the hall and finds stone knights and ladies waiting in gray light. The novel still works as an introduction to the Middle Ages, with honor and cruelty shown side by side.
28711-operas-every-child-should-know-des:
Dolores Bacon wrote this 1911 guide that retells famous operas for children, with descriptions of both story and music. Its chapters cover The Bohemian Girl, Fidelio, The Damnation of Faust, Carmen, Robin Hood, and Martha. Hansel and Gretel, Cavalleria Rusticana, The Prophet, The Magic Flute, and Pinafore follow, with three Verdi operas and Wagner's Ring, Mastersingers, and Lohengrin closing the book. Each chapter tells the plot in plain words and points out what to listen for.

Bacon wrote for families who wanted children to enjoy opera before ever seeing one staged. Her retellings keep the drama while leaving out what young listeners would not follow. The book still works as a first introduction to opera, giving a child the story, the characters, and the famous moments of each work in a single short chapter.
2891-howards-end:
E. M. Forster's Howards End opens with Helen Schlegel's letters to her sister Margaret, written from the old red-brick house itself. Helen describes a small, delightful place with a hall that serves as a room, stairs rising through a tunnel, and nine windows facing the front garden. The house, more than any single character, anchors the novel's world.

The story follows the Schlegels, the businesslike Wilcoxes, and Leonard Bast, a clerk at the Porphyrion Fire Insurance Company, as their lives cross over class, money, and culture. Forster's famous injunction to connect runs through failed meetings, misunderstandings, and a final claim on the house. The novel remains a key portrait of Edwardian England and the ties that hold or break it.
28925-lover-or-friend:
Rosa Nouchette Carey wrote this novel, Lover or Friend, first published in 1890 and reprinted many times to 1915 by Macmillan in London. The chapters open with the Blake family discussed, Audrey introducing herself, and the Blake family at home, then bring Michael, a new master, and the gray cottage. Later chapters follow Kester's hero, Mat, and Priscilla Baxter, with a girl after the author's own heart.

Carey, author of Nellie's Memories, Wee Wifie, and Not Like Other Girls, writes domestic romance for a wide readership. Her novels, sold in a popular edition at three shillings and sixpence, filled family shelves for decades. Readers get a period love story of family, friendship, and the question of its title, told in Carey's warm, readable style.
28934-the-surrender-of-napoleon-being-th:
