Rear-Admiral Sir Frederick Lewis Maitland wrote this narrative of Napoleon's surrender and his stay aboard HMS Bellerophon, from May 24 to August 8, 1815. A new edition of 1904, edited by William Kirk Dickson with a memoir of the author, draws on papers that passed from Lady Maitland to her nephew and then to Maitland's family. Sir Walter Scott called the manuscript a great and interesting national document.

Maitland, captain of the Bellerophon, records Napoleon's words and conduct as an eyewitness, and defends the good faith of the British government toward him. The book matters as both history and vindication, written by the officer who received the fallen emperor. Readers get the surrender at close range, in a sailor's manly and explicit account.
28957-the-acts-of-the-general-assemblies:
This volume prints the Acts of the General Assemblies of the Church of Scotland from 1638 to 1649, first printed in 1682. It adds an index of unprinted acts and the acts of 1690, printed in 1691. The Glasgow Assembly of November 1638 opens the book, condemning six late pretended assemblies, from Linlithgow in 1606 to Perth in 1618, and annulling their proceedings.

Later acts condemn the service book, the book of canons, and the high commission, and depose and excommunicate bishops, including the pretended archbishops of St. Andrews and Glasgow. The volume records the Kirk's revolt against episcopacy in its own legal language. Scholars of Scottish religion get a primary source for the Covenanting years, in the acts as the assemblies themselves framed them.
28981-adventures-in-the-rifle-brigade-in:
Captain J. Kincaid wrote this 1830 memoir, Adventures in the Rifle Brigade, in the Peninsula, France, and the Netherlands, from 1809 to 1815, published by T. and W. Boone in London. Kincaid dedicates it to Major-General Sir Andrew Barnard, colonel of the first battalion and its leader through a long and brilliant period. His advertisement says he drew chiefly on reminiscences of military life, aiming to convey the impression events made on him at the time.

Kincaid admits errors of date or trifling circumstance may have crept in through want of memory, not wilful misleading. He quotes Othello on his rude speech and his life in the tented field, promising a round unvarnished tale. Readers get a soldier's Peninsular War memoir, plain, vivid, and close to the fighting it describes.
29059-the-world-beyond:
Ray Cummings published this science fiction novella in Amazing Stories in July 1942. On his twenty-first birthday, Lee Anthony sits beside a dying old woman who raised him, while a party goes on downstairs. Then grim, black-clad strangers arrive out of nowhere, seize three Earth people and haul them off to a strange world.

On that world, the story promises, a man can become a giant at will, and the captives must learn its rules or perish. Cummings mixes a birthday-night opening with a tale of abduction and survival in an alien place. Readers get a brisk pulp adventure about ordinary people thrown into a world where size, strength, and safety all work differently.
29178-literary-tours-in-the-highlands-an:
D. T. Holmes published this travel book in Paisley in 1909, dedicated to James Coats, whose mandate sent the author roaming through heather, broom, and peat country. Holmes toured the Highlands and Islands of Scotland as a literary traveler, visiting village libraries, literary societies, and Gaelic books, and noting the happiness and geniality of the natives.

Chapters cover music, speeches, and literature, church and education, a trip to Shetland, commercial travelers and their anecdotes, and legends and literary notabilia. Winter sailing, a crofting village, and the horrors of the Minch add travel color. Readers get a bookish tour of the north, affectionate toward its people and its reading habits.
2946-howards-end:
In this edition of Howards End, E. M. Forster again begins with Helen Schlegel writing to her sister Margaret from the house that gives the novel its name. Helen finds the place old, little, and altogether delightful in red brick, with three bedrooms in a row above a hall that counts as a room. Nine windows look up from the front garden, and the house already feels too small for its visitors.

Margaret and Helen, with their brother Tibby, argue over art, money, and the Wilcox family, whose practical world collides with Schlegel idealism. A lost umbrella, street lamps, and trees in a morning account show Forster's way of letting small talk carry large themes. The novel asks who should inherit England, and answers through a house, a family, and a child.
29658-italy-the-magic-land:
Lilian Whiting, author of The Florence of Landor and The World Beautiful, wrote Italy: The Magic Land, printed in 1907 by Little, Brown, and Company of Boston, with pictures from photographs. Its verse epigraph recalls dropping into the magic land under many a yellow star. Whiting aims only at fragmentary impressions of various places, making no attempt at Florence beyond mere allusion.

Chapters treat modern art in Rome, social life, and the magic of Italian scenes, with Taormina's temple among its pictures. The book is dedicated to Ella, whose form rests in the Roman cemetery where Keats and Shelley haunt the air. Readers of travel writing will find a fond, impressionistic Italy from a devoted American visitor.
29729-victor-s-triumph-sequel-to-a-beaut:
Mrs. E. D. E. N. Southworth, author of Tried for Her Life and The Lost Heiress, wrote Victor's Triumph as a sequel to A Beautiful Fiend, printed in New York by Hurst and Company. Its heroine sighs that even under the most propitious circumstances, if she is permitted to stay where she is, she shall be buried alive. The sequel follows Victor through trials that test love, fortune, and will.

Southworth writes the popular melodrama of her day: strong heroines, dark plots, and triumphs earned through suffering. The book stands in a long uniform series of her novels. Readers of Victorian sensational fiction will find a full-blooded sequel that rewards those who know the first tale.
29747-aztec-land:
Maturin M. Ballou published Aztec Land in Boston and New York in 1890, with Houghton, Mifflin and Company. Ballou was a seasoned travel writer, with books on Alaska, Cuba, Australasia, and a round-the-world trip already to his name. For Mexico he went first to Raymond and Whitcomb in Boston, the experienced organizers of travel, to plan the trip in the best manner.

His motto comes from N. P. Willis: the dust is old upon my sandal-shoon, and still I am a pilgrim. The book gives Mexico as a traveller of 1890 saw it, from the road, the town, and the old Aztec ground. It is a plain, observant travel book, written for readers who wanted Mexico described by a man who had actually walked it.
29866-hidden-hand:
Mrs. E. D. E. N. Southworth, author of The Curse of Clifton, wrote Hidden Hand, published in New York by Hurst and Company. Hurricane Hall, a large old mansion of dark-red sandstone, stands in one of the loneliest and wildest mountain regions of Virginia. Three sides of the estate are ringed by steep gray rocks, spiked with dark evergreens, in horseshoe form called the Devil's Hoof.

Thirty chapters follow a nocturnal visit, masks, a quest, and Capitola. A discovery, the metamorphosis of a newsboy, Herbert Greyson, and Marah Rocke lead to a room with a trap-door. Storms at Hurricane Hall, the doctor's daughter, and the outlaw's rendezvous follow, with Gabriel LeNoir and the smuggler and Capitola. The book is a full-blooded sensation novel of mystery, storms, and hidden kin.
29886-pioneers-of-the-pacific-coast-a-ch:
Agnes C. Laut wrote this chronicle of sea rovers and fur hunters, printed in Toronto in 1915. A frontispiece by C. W. Jefferys shows the descent of the Fraser River in 1808. Eight chapters carry the tale from the voyage of the Golden Hind and Vitus Bering on the Pacific to the outlaw hunters and Cook and Vancouver. Maps by Bartholomew mark the routes of explorers on the coast.

Alexander Mackenzie's overland trek from Canada, the Fraser descent, and Thompson and the Astorians follow. Portraits of Cook, Vancouver, and Simon Fraser, with views of Nootka Sound, fill the plates. The passing of the fur lords closes the chronicle. Laut writes with color and pace, in a short history meant for general readers and young students.
30016-medical-investigation-in-seventeen:
This volume holds two papers read at a Clark Library seminar on October 14, 1967, printed by the William Andrews Clark Memorial Library at the University of California, Los Angeles, in 1968. Charles W. Bodemer, of the Division of Biomedical History at the University of Washington's School of Medicine, writes on embryological thought in seventeenth-century England. Lester S. King, senior editor of the Journal of the American Medical Association, writes on Robert Boyle as an amateur physician.

Bodemer weighs the embryological ideas of Sir Kenelm Digby, Nathaniel Highmore, William Harvey, and Sir Thomas Browne, a remarkable group of inquiring Englishmen. King deals with the medical side of Boyle's writings, whose collection is one of the chief glories of the Clark Library. The foreword calls it a happy marriage of subject matter and library wealth, with a small audience at the talk and a wider one for the printed papers.
30096-the-camera-fiend:
E. W. Hornung wrote The Camera Fiend, printed in London in 1911 by T. Fisher Unwin. Twenty-two chapters carry the school story, opening with a conscientious ass. Pocket Upton comes down late and panting, despite his daily exemption from first school, and a postcard on his plate takes away his remaining breath. An obvious way out of his difficulty troubles him almost as much as the thought of weeping over it in open hall, since it is hardly an honest way.

The nicest fellows in his house have called Pocket a conscientious ass, and he goes straight to his house-master, found marking proses with a blue pencil, briar pipe in hand. Please, sir, Mr. Coverley cannot have me, sir, he says: Coverley has chicken-pox. The boy produces the intimation in a few strokes of an honored, laconic pen.
3014-the-old-northwest-a-chronicle-of-th:
Frederic Austin Ogg wrote The Old Northwest, volume nineteen of the Chronicles of America series, published by Yale University Press in 1919. Chapters follow Pontiac's conspiracy, a lair of wild beasts, the Revolution, and the conquest completed. Wayne the scourge of the Indians, the great migration, pioneer days and ways, Tecumseh, and the War of 1812 follow. The Ohio Valley and beyond form the stage.

Ogg describes a scheme of government adapted to liberty-loving yet law-abiding frontier populations, flexible enough to grow from settlements into territories and states. Geography and inheritance foreordained an expanding, colonizing nation, he argues. The book gives a compact history of the Midwest's founding, from Native resistance to statehood.
30262-frederic-lord-leighton-an-illustra:
Ernest Rhys records the life and work of Frederic, Lord Leighton, late president of the Royal Academy of Arts, in an illustrated volume from George Bell and Sons. The third edition, revised and issued in crown octavo in 1900, reprints the second edition of 1898 with a few alterations and corrections. A new chapter on Lord Leighton's house in 1900, by S. Pepys Cockerell, joins the set, and Winding the Skein fronts the book by permission of the Fine Art Society.

Earlier editions appeared in 1895 and 1898, and the publishers note warm help from owners and admirers of Leighton's work. By gracious consent of the Queen, the Cimabue from Buckingham Palace appears among the reproductions. Rhys gives a picture-led life of a Victorian master, suited to readers who want Leighton's art and career in one handsome, compact volume.
30329-black-eyes-and-the-daily-grind:
Milton Lesser's tale centers on Black Eyes, a small Venusian household pet whose dislike of New York forces the city itself to adapt. A picture caption gives the joke at once: when Black Eyes needed a nap, everybody slept. The human story opens on Venus. A big-game hunter loves the flat crack of his old-fashioned recoil rifle and the slap against his shoulder, the only such relic on the planet, making sport more interesting.

His wife Lindy, young, pretty, and strong, notes that nothing has been seen for a while, though yesterday game fell one after another as fast as he could fire. Today anything bigger than a mouse hides in a hole, and early Venusian hunters knew days like this, when an area full of big lizards and cats emptied overnight. Lesser turns a pet's nap into a New York problem with comic ease.
3040-the-boss-and-the-machine-a-chronicl:
Samuel Orth wrote The Boss and the Machine, a chronicle of politicians and party organization, for the Chronicles of America series. Chapters trace the rise of the party and the machine, the tide of materialism, and the politician and the city. Tammany Hall, lesser oligarchies, legislative omnipotence, the national hierarchy, and the awakening toward reform follow. Orth opens by calling the party an essential instrument of democracy.

The narrative follows William Tweed, chairmaker by trade and vulgar good fellow by nature, whose ring lurked behind a popular president amid war, reconstruction, and impeachment. Exposures and confessions soon amazed everyone, and Tweed's name became synonymous with bossdom. The book remains a readable introduction to machine politics and its reformers.
30405-the-clean-and-wholesome-land:
Ralph Sholto tells The Clean and Wholesome Land, a short tale whose tagline states the bargain of its utopia. The story imagines a world where every human problem is resolved under a flawless regime, and doubters pay with their lives. While Professor Cargill lectures from the rostrum, Neal Pardeau prowls the auditorium. This is the place to find those who whisper, plot, and scheme, feeling safe in a pure, hard core of patriotism.

Their safety rests on Cargill's post as Director of Education in the New State, matched by Pardeau's as Director of Public Security. Cargill's lectures come before a commanded audience, with attendance mandatory. Cargill's voice booms that on this anniversary of the New State, they look with pride on a clean and wholesome land. Complete fruition awaits the individual who effaces himself and loves the state fanatically, while enemies stand broken and subjugated.
30440-byways-of-ghost-land:
Elliott O'Donnell surveys ghost lore and occult belief in twelve chapters published in London in 1911, drawing on cases, tales, and folk custom rather than a single haunting. He opens with the mind and its hidden powers, then moves through shadows, obsession, possession, and what he calls occult hooligans.

Later chapters treat sylvan horrors, complex hauntings, vampires, werewolves, fox-women, death warnings, family ghosts, superstitions, and fortunes, closing with spirits of sea and rivers, Buddhas, and boggle chairs. O'Donnell writes as a collector and believer, sorting strange reports into kinds and asking what they reveal about fear, fate, and the unseen.
30529-a-stake-in-the-land:
Peter A. Speek writes A Stake in the Land, published in New York and London in 1921 by Harper and Brothers, in the Americanization Studies series directed by Allen T. Burns. Speek, in charge of the Slavic section of the Library of Congress, studies immigrants and land.

An illustration contrasts long, hard months of work separating a rough shanty from white clapboards and an automobile. Contents open with need of a land policy, strength of home ties, immigrants' love of land, and need for land regulation. Learning of land opportunities follows, through friends, agents, and ads. Speek argues for fair land access as a path to American belonging.
30548-the-shores-of-the-adriatic-the-aus:
F. Hamilton Jackson writes The Shores of the Adriatic, the Austrian side, covering the Kustenlande, Istria, and Dalmatia, published in London in 1908. Jackson, vice president of the Institute of Decorative Designers and a Cantor lecturer, illustrates the book fully with plans, his own drawings, and photographs taken specially for the work.

A frontispiece shows Herzegovinian women at a baker's shop in Ragusa, setting the tone for a travel book rich in place and custom. Lists of illustrations and plans precede chapters on coast towns, islands, and inland routes. Jackson blends history, art, and travel notes into a guide for readers who want the Adriatic's Austrian shore in detail.
30550-finn-the-wolfhound:
A. J. Dawson writes Finn the Wolfhound, illustrated by R. H. Buxton, in a 1909 reprint of the first edition published in 1908 by Grant Richards of London. The book is dedicated to the mistress of the kennels and to the memory of Tynagh, mother of wolfhound heroes. It follows Finn from his mother and foster mother through first steps and youth beside the downs.

Later chapters add the ordeal of the ring, revelations, Finn walking alone, the heart of Tara, a transition stage, and a sea change. A frontispiece shows a man with his back to a withered ironbark tree. Dawson tells a dog's life as a hero's tale, with loyalty, hardship, and the wild Irish landscape at its heart.
30618-wings-of-the-wind:
Credo Harris writes Wings of the Wind, copyrighted in 1920 by Small, Maynard of Boston, and dedicated to S. Thruston Ballard, with whom the author shared many a pleasant camp fire. Harris, author of Toby, Sunlight Patch, and Where the Souls of Men Are Calling, opens with a toast to adventure and romance.

Later chapters add the mysterious monsieur, the girl in the cafe, Nirvana, a toast to the very end, and a voice from the water. A bomb and a discovery, the chase beginning, a shot from the dark, a silent enemy, and a strange find follow. Harris blends romance, mystery, and outdoor adventure in a brisk early twentieth-century novel.
30733-the-fate-of-felix-brand:
Florence Finch Kelly writes The Fate of Felix Brand, illustrated by Edwin John Prittie and copyrighted in 1913 by the John C. Winston Company of Philadelphia. Kelly, author of With Hoops of Steel, The Delafield Affair, and Rhoda of the Underground, opens with Felix Brand having a mysterious experience.

Later chapters add a phrase like ottar of roses out of an otter, the mask of his countenance, Billikins frightened, and Mrs. Brand's dream son. Who is Hugh Gordon, Felix reading a letter, days of stress, and battling with the invisible follow, with Hugh winning Henrietta's confidence. An illustration shows Mildred Annister making apprehensive inquiry about him. Kelly writes a western mystery of identity and fate.
30877-the-painter-in-oil-a-complete-trea:
Daniel Burleigh Parkhurst wrote this complete treatise on painting pictures in oil colors, published in Boston by Lothrop, Lee and Shepard in 1898. Parkhurst had studied under William Sartain, Bouguereau and Tony-Fleury, and Aimée Morot, belonged to the New York Water Color Club, and once lectured on art at Dickinson College. He also wrote Sketching from Nature, and he inscribes this book to A. M. P.

Three parts cover materials first, with canvases, easels, brushes, paints, vehicles, varnishes, palettes, and studios, then general principles such as mental attitude, tradition, individuality, and originality. A technical part follows, on drawing, values, perspective, and light and shade. It is a thorough manual for students who want to paint in oil with craft and care.
3122-england:
Warner starts from a puzzle: England weighs far more in modern history than its size would suggest. Great Britain with Ireland is only a little larger than Italy. England and Wales together are less than half Italy's size. England alone is about the size of North Carolina.

Franklin, writing in 1763, called it a stepping stone in a brook, barely enough ground to keep one's shoes dry. Much of that ground stays wet or waterlogged for much of the year. The essay asks how so cramped and damp an island came to matter so much to the wider world.
31234-a-history-of-the-english-church-in:
H. T. Purchas, vicar of Glenmark and canon of Christchurch Cathedral, published this history in Christchurch, Melbourne, and London in 1914. Dedicated to William Leonard Williams, sometime Bishop of Waiapu, in memory of services by himself and others of his name to the New Zealand church, the book opens with a portrait. It shows the Reverend Samuel Marsden.

Purchas, already known for Bishop Harper and the Canterbury Settlement, writes for church readers who wanted a connected story of their church's growth in a new land. The volume traces missions, dioceses, and settlements as the English church took root in New Zealand.
3131-how-spring-came-in-new-england:
Warner calls New England the battle-ground of the seasons. To conquer it is only to begin the fight, he jokes, and when fully subdued it offers no weather at all. The region is less a country than a camp, invaded by turns from the frozen north and the wilting tropics. Icicles hang on its northern heights while mosquitoes fringe its seacoasts.

For a third of the year the contest never quite ends. Spring arrives not as a gentle guest but as a hard-won truce between legions of frost and sirens of heat. The essay delights in that warfare of climate. It explains why New Englanders talk weather as other people talk politics: weather there is an event, not a background.
31396-jack-winters-baseball-team-or-the-:
Mark Overton's 1919 boys' book, published by M. A. Donohue in Chicago and New York, follows Jack Winters' baseball team, the rivals of the diamond, in twenty chapters. It opens with Toby and Steve worrying that something is on Jack's mind just as Chester faces the terrible Harmony nine the day after tomorrow. Chester had beaten them in the first great game.

Later chapters bring a weak link in the chain, a last practice game, Chester awakened, a tie in the ninth inning, Fred put to the test, and a game called by darkness. They go on to a growing puzzle, a warning, one trouble after another, and a cramp seizing Joel. A night alarm, a fire, a startling disclosure, Fred renewing his pledge, Hendrix again in the box, the lucky seventh, and a great victory round out the tale. Clean and brisk, the book is classic schoolboy sports fiction.
31421-through-apache-land:
Lieutenant R. H. Jayne's Through Apache Land, published by the Mershon Company of New York with copyright in 1893, is a boys' adventure of the American Southwest. Jayne, author of Lost in the Wilderness, In the Pecos Country, and The Cave in the Mountain, opens with moonlight on the Rio Gila. He follows Tom Hardynge through a ruse, pursuit by Apaches, an alarming message, and scenes among the Apaches, in Devil's Pass, and with Lone Wolf.

An illustration shows a warrior caught off guard as Tom grasps him by the throat. The story moves from scout to cavalry escort, with narrow escapes and frontier fighting. Written for young readers, it reflects the dime-novel West of its day. Modern readers will note its period attitudes toward Native peoples while following a fast, incident-packed adventure.
3144-froude-s-history-of-england:
Kingsley reviews a history of England by James Anthony Froude in this essay, also drawn from his 1890 collection. He begins with a comic history that had lately caricatured the nation's past. In that book the English appear for centuries as a mob of fools and knaves, led by arch-fools and arch-knaves in each generation. Thoughtful readers met it with contempt and anger.

Against that jeering tone Kingsley sets Froude's graver work. The essay judges how a historian should treat great events and great men, neither flattering them nor turning them into farce. It gives readers a Victorian critic's test for popular history: truth kept whole, without spite and without hero worship.
31553-university-education-in-ireland:
Samuel Haughton's University Education in Ireland was published in London by Williams and Norgate and in Dublin by McGlashan and Gill in 1868, at one shilling. It is a short work by a fellow of Trinity College, Dublin. Haughton, a reverend, doctor of medicine, and fellow of the Royal Society, writes on the state of university education in Ireland at a moment of reform and debate. Printed at the University Press in Dublin by M. H. Gill, the pamphlet speaks from inside the Irish university world.

Its subject is the shape of higher education: who should teach, who should learn, and how Irish universities should be organized. Haughton argues as an academic and a churchman, with Trinity College as his model and his concern. Readers of Irish educational history will find a compact, partisan statement from the 1860s, when the university question was a national question.
3159-the-hermit-of-far-end:
Margaret Pedler published this romance in 1920. A prologue opens in a little room high under the roof of Wallater's Buildings, where glowing logs burn quietly in the grate. The distant roar of London traffic reaches the room dulled to a gentle monotone, filtered through a honeycomb of narrow side streets. Stillness rules the scene, and the hermit of the title stands at its center.

Pedler, a popular writer of romantic fiction, builds her story on solitude and return. Far End promises refuge from the city's noise, and the plot tests what refuge costs. Readers who like early twentieth-century romance will find the book's pleasures familiar: a withdrawn hero, a persistent heroine, and feeling worked out at a distance from the crowd.
31594-the-song-of-lancaster-kentucky-to-:
Eugenia Dunlap Potts's The Song of Lancaster, Kentucky, addressed to the statesmen, soldiers, and citizens of Garrard County, was written in May 1874. It was printed at Cambridge by the Riverside Press in 1876. Potts explains in her note that she borrowed Longfellow's celebrated Hiawatha versification, peculiar in style. She searched the records at hand for her story's facts, and warns that gaps will come from how meager the surviving evidence is.

The poem tells Lancaster's little history in Hiawatha's trochaic measure, turning local annals into verse. Potts hopes that events dear to hearts now at rest may live on in the present generation's memory. Readers of local history in verse will find a sincere, old-fashioned chronicle, where a Kentucky town's past is sung rather than merely recorded.
31672-the-triads-of-ireland:
Kuno Meyer's Triads of Ireland appeared as volume thirteen of the Royal Irish Academy's Todd Lecture Series. It was published at Dublin by Hodges, Figgis, and Company and at London by Williams and Norgate in 1906. It presents the old Irish triads, short sayings grouped in threes, with their text and translation on pages 1 to 35.

Glosses and notes follow on pages 36 to 43, with an index of places and an index of names to close the volume. Meyer's book gives scholars the triads in Irish and in English together, with the notes needed to read them. These compact sayings pack counsel, observation, and lore into three short strokes.
31708-the-pond:
Carl Ewald's The Pond, translated from the Danish by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos and illustrated by Warwick Reynolds, was published at London by Thornton Butterworth in 1922. It belongs to the Royal Road Library of Carl Ewald books, in the same translation. The book tells stories of life in and around a pond, in twelve chapters.

Ewald's pond is a small world of its own, with its creatures, its seasons, and its quiet dramas, told for young readers and for any reader who likes nature close at hand. Reynolds's pictures carry the pond's inhabitants, and de Mattos's translation keeps Ewald's plain, observant prose.
31721-elizabeth-gilbert-and-her-work-for:
Frances Martin's 1887 biography tells the life of Elizabeth Gilbert and her work for the blind. The little girl called Bessie was born on August 7, 1826, the second daughter of Ashhurst Turner Gilbert, principal of Brasenose College, Oxford, and later Bishop of Chichester. She grew up in a large family.

Twenty-three chapters follow her childhood, her time in the dark, a palace garden, a sense of loss, and her growing work. That work includes blind children of the poor and the removal of stumbling blocks. Readers get a Victorian life of a woman whose personal experience of blindness became a public mission.
31747-sound-mind:
John Haslam's 1819 book Sound Mind, or Contributions to the Natural History and Physiology of the Human Intellect, was written by a physician who had already published several works on insanity. Haslam, formerly president of the Royal Medical, Natural History, and Chemical Societies of Edinburgh, dedicates the volume to Sir James Mackintosh.

His preface argues that to describe mental derangement, one must first fix the standard of intellect in its healthy state. He set out to think for himself amid conflicting systems of metaphysics. Readers get an early nineteenth-century study of the sound mind, philosophical in aim but grounded in a doctor's clinical experience.
31888-some-conditions-of-child-life-in-e:
The Reverend Benjamin Waugh's 1889 paper Some Conditions of Child Life in England was read at the Baptist Union meeting at Birmingham on October 10, 1889. It comes from his work as honorary director of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children. Waugh asks whether we should not expect some conditions of child life to be sad.

He lists vagrant habits, gambling, extravagant self-indulgence, idleness, unmarried parentage, unfaithfulness in married parents, and habitual drunkenness as forces that disturb and sometimes destroy the natural parental instinct. Readers get a pioneering child-welfare document, plain and urgent, from the early years of organized protection for children.
31889-the-great-mississippi-flood-of-187:
Mayor Wiltz of New Orleans issued this 1874 circular on the Great Mississippi Flood, its extent, duration, and effects. It went to city and town mayors across the republic, and to philanthropists, for seventy thousand Louisiana sufferers alone. Dated May 30, 1874, it recalls a dispatch sent on May 25 to thirty-four large cities.

That dispatch, by request of the Relief Committee and leading citizens, called for aid in cash and provisions. It noted that in thirty-five days contributions had totaled under one hundred and eighty thousand dollars, while daily rations went to about forty-five thousand people. Readers get a mayor's urgent appeal from a drowned city, a document of disaster relief in the nineteenth century.
32-herland:
Three male explorers stumble on a hidden land run entirely by women. Charlotte Perkins Gilman's Herland, told by one of the visitors, imagines a society that has raised children without men for generations. The narrator writes from memory, his notes lost.

The visitors test the land's schools, gardens, cities, and mother-centered faith. Their assumptions crack as the women answer with calm logic and order. Romance grows, but so does debate about freedom and sex roles. The novel stands as a sharp early work of feminist utopian fiction. Later feminist writers returned to Gilman's island as a model for imagining fairer societies.
32055-the-hand:
Jerry Sohl's short story, printed in Imagination in January 1955, begins in an ordinary kitchen on a November morning. Alice McNearby is washing breakfast dishes and watching the sky when she spies her dog, Dobie, sneaking toward the house. She knows at once that he has killed something. During the past month, Dobie has killed two rabbits, a pheasant, a cat, and a field mouse. Alice fears he will next take a chicken or a suckling pig.

Her husband Mac has threatened to take a gun to Dobie, and the dog seems to know it, often growling at him. The story's turn comes when Dobie brings Alice the hand of the title, a find far worse than any rabbit or pheasant. Readers get a short, unsettling tale that starts with a farm dog's hunting habit and grows, through one grim delivery, into something much stranger and darker.
32114-command:
William McFee's novel, published by Doubleday, Page and Company at Garden City in 1922, is a seafaring tale of command. McFee inscribed it to commanders under whom he had served. They combined firmness with tact, sympathy, and appreciation, without fuss or self-advertisement, yet won the respect of their lieutenants despite a seafaring life's trials.

A prefatory note warns readers not to hunt for real people in the book. The tale is an original invention, McFee states, not founded on fact, and its characters are not portraits of actual persons. Its incidents and topography are imaginary as well. The opening chapter introduces a girl of the upper-middle classes, a type McFee notes as newly common. Readers get a novel about what command asks of a man, and what it costs those around him.
32158-rural-wealth-and-welfare-economic-:
George T. Fairchild's Rural Wealth and Welfare, published in New York and London by Macmillan in 1900 as part of the Rural Science Series edited by L. H. Bailey, applies economic principles to farm life. Its first part, Productive Industries, analyses aims, forces, means, and methods. Its chapters cover aims of industry, forces in production, labour and capital defined and classified, and personal attainments.

Later chapters cover combination of forces for individual efficiency and methods of association. They continue through exchange with its advantages and limits, value as the basis of exchange, banks and banking, and deferred settlement and credit expansion. A second part treats distribution of wealth for welfare, opening with general principles of fair distribution and wages. Readers get a turn-of-the-century farm economics textbook, systematic and practical in tone.
32160-chain-of-command:
Stephen Arr's short story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in May 1954, follows a man who must work through channels to reach the top. The cover line says George climbed by proper steps from lowly obscurity to high command. The story opens where Clara tells George with fury that the least he could do is ask him whether he is a mouse or a worm.

George has gone out and moved it every night, he protests, but every morning he puts it back. Clara says she can never have a moment's peace while that trap stays outside their front door, worrying about the children. George hesitates. He fears They might not be happy to find out about them. Clara retorts that their being there is Their own fault. Readers get a science-fiction comedy, where a household quarrel opens onto neighbours and a chain of command.
32165-venerable-philippine-duchesne-a-br:
G. E. M.'s brief sketch of Venerable Philippine Duchesne was published in New York by the America Press in 1914. It tells the life and work of the foundress of the Society of the Sacred Heart in America. The book carries the Church's marks of approval: nihil obstat from two censors and the imprimatur of John Cardinal Farley, Archbishop of New York. A frontispiece shows Mother Philippine Duchesne.

A prefatory note explains the book's careful language. Under the decrees of Urban VIII and other popes, terms such as holy and saintly are used in their ordinary, untechnical sense. They do not anticipate the Church's authoritative decision. The preface recalls the heroic figures of American Catholic history, for whom sowing the faith required anguish of soul and weariness of body. Readers get a short, reverent life of a pioneer religious founder.
322-st-ives-being-the-adventures-of-a-fr:
Robert Louis Stevenson dictated St. Ives to his stepdaughter Mrs. Strong between January 1893 and October 1894. The tale, in its 1898 Heinemann second edition, follows a French prisoner in England during the Napoleonic wars. Stevenson laid it aside six weeks before his death.

Thirty chapters bring the tale within sight of its end, and Mrs. Strong knew the intended remainder in outline. A completion by another hand follows for readers who dislike unfinished stories. The adventure mixes escape, romance, and prison life. St. Ives shows Stevenson's late storytelling power. Stevenson's unfinished tale still grips readers of adventure fiction.
32209-assignment-s-end:
Roger Dee's short story, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in December 1954, follows a man whose gift torments him. Philip Alcorn emerges, for the hundredth time in a week, from a frightening hallucination that plagues him, when Kitty Murchinsom enters his office. It is almost three in the afternoon, she says, and her face takes on the placid look everyone wears, unwittingly but inevitably, the instant they come near Alcorn.

Kitty's cool blonde loveliness, set against the bleak polar plain of Alcorn's waking dream, shows how much more she is than fiancee or secretary alone. She is a reassuring beacon amid uncertainty for him. The story's sidenote theme is that Alcorn's wild talent brings peace to everybody near him, while he alone is exempt. Readers get a story of a peacemaker who cannot find peace himself.
32299-women-of-england:
Bartlett Burleigh James's history, copyrighted in 1907 and 1908, traces women's lives in England from prehistoric Britain through the nineteenth century. In fifteen chapters it moves from ancient and Anglo-Saxon women through the Anglo-Normans and the Middle Ages, then to women of the manors, the monasteries, and the industrial classes. Later chapters cover the Tudor, Commonwealth, and Restoration periods, with a closing chapter on Scotland and Ireland.

James looks at work, worship, household rule, and social rank, asking how each age shaped what women could do and be. The book treats queens and commoners side by side, setting court life next to farm, workshop, and convent. It offers a broad survey for readers who want English social history told through women's experience rather than through kings and battles alone.
324-a-knight-of-the-cumberland:
A narrator leads his small sister and a city girl called the Blight up a Cumberland gap. John Fox Jr.'s Knight of the Cumberland opens at high noon on a crisp October day, with a gray horse and two mules. The party climbs where few women but mountaineers have trod.

Contents follow the blight in the hills, a wild dog's trail, and a tournament at last. Fox writes mountain folk with local color and romance. The knight of the title proves his worth in a closing passage. The book shows Fox's Kentucky mountains at their most vivid.
32411-queen-of-the-flaming-diamond:
Leroy Yerxa's tale, printed in Amazing Stories in January 1943, opens at the crowded Owl Limb Night Club, where owner George Lardner steps up to announce the midnight attraction. Among the guests are Jim Drake, unsteady after drink, and his right-hand man, Puffy Adams, who tries to steer him out before the show. Puffy, broad-backed and plain-spoken, lifts Drake to his feet while Drake protests that he wants to see the dance.

The attraction is the biggest diamond in the world, displayed in a night club for reasons that puzzle the onlookers. Yerxa's opening question drives the story: why is the stone here when a whole race depends on it for existence? From a smoky club floor, the tale moves toward that race, its jewel, and the danger of taking what others cannot live without.
32415-the-nursery-rhymes-of-england:
James Orchard Halliwell's collection, in a fifth edition published in London and New York in 1886, gathers the nursery rhymes of England with illustrations by W. B. Scott. Halliwell notes that earlier editions were warmly received, and he argues that children had not deserted rhymes chanted ages earlier by mothers of the North. In his view, old nonsense rhymes still held meaning and romance that no modern verses could fully replace.

The book presents traditional rhymes as the light reading of the infant scholar, a first step beyond the alphabet into story, rhythm, and fancy. Parents, teachers, and collectors will find familiar verses preserved in an early scholarly collection, with notes on their old roots. It remains a useful source for the history of children's verse in England.
32434-all-in-the-mind:
Gene L. Henderson's tale, printed in If Worlds of Science Fiction in April 1954, follows Mel Carlson. He wakes floating in deep, intense dark, with a sharp pain when he tries to open his eyes. Bits of memory return: a small lab hidden in an old mine tunnel in the mountains, an hour's drive from the city, and an argument with his partner Neil. Neil insisted they had gone as far as possible with animal brains and must now work with a human one.

Mel objected that papers learning of animal-brain work would cause uproar, and that using a hospital patient's brain after death would close the lab tighter than a drum. Henderson's sidenote asks when life begins, noting books that say forty, radio shows that say eighty, and views that call it mental or physical. Mel's strange case gives that question a chilling, personal form.
32566-the-triumph-of-hilary-blachland:
Bertram Mitford's Triumph of Hilary Blachland opens at a camp on the Matya'mhlope, where Christian Sybrandt points out a towering pile of rocks across a valley: Umzilikazi's grave. His companion, Blachland, wants a closer look, but Sybrandt laughs, warning that holy ground is guarded day and night by armed majara, and no white man has ever seen it close. Blachland persists, drawn by the grave of a remorseless, all-destroying war-leader who founded a martial nation.

Sybrandt insists Blachland will never get there, and if he did, would never get away, yet the mystery and peril appeal to Blachland's adventurous side. From that campfire challenge, Mitford builds a South African adventure of chiefs, warriors, and a white man's ambition. The novel mixes travel, history, and romance in the manner of Victorian frontier fiction.
3274-the-complete-works-of-artemus-ward-:
Part four of Artemus Ward's complete works follows the humorist to California and back. On the steamer opens the journey, with the isthmus, Mexico, and California itself following. Washoe, Mr Pepper, and Horace Greeley's ride to Placerville keep the tour moving, with Reese River and Great Salt Lake City beyond.

Mountain fever, a piece spoken, and the ball fill the later pages, with Phelps's almanac and hurrah for the road. Very much married and the revelation of Joseph Smith close the set. Ward reports the mining West in his misspelled voice: booster, showman, and skeptic at once, amused by every town that promised him a fortune.
32775-the-ties-that-bind:
Walter Miller Jr. tells of Earth's children and the starmen who come home, in this story from IF Worlds of Science Fiction of May 1954, illustrated by Kelly Freas. Earth is green and quiet. Nature has survived man, and man has survived himself.

Then sleek ships rise in the west at twilight, gleaming slivers crossing the sky like geese. No vessel from space has crossed Earth's skies for countless generations, and the children have no word for ships. Ancient mechanisms wake beneath the ground as the fleet lands in waves. Analyst Meikl must choose between leaving with the starmen and staying with Letha, a girl of Earth.
32863-cottage-economy-to-which-is-added-:
William Cobbett teaches a labouring family to live well on little, in a New York volume from John Doyle dated 1833. Numbered paragraphs, with an index, cover brewing beer, making bread, and keeping cows, pigs, bees, ewes, goats, poultry, and rabbits. Further instructions treat hats and bonnets from English grass and grain, and ice-houses built after the Virginian manner.

Cobbett insists that economy means management, and nothing more, not parsimony or stinginess. A liberal disposition, he argues, is perfectly consistent with economy, while misers merely disguise their propensity under its name. The added Poor Man's Friend defends the rights of those who do the work and fight the battles. Practical detail fills the book, from milk for puppies against distemper to straw walls held by posts and stakes, and rafters pitched at forty-five degrees.
3288-the-sky-pilot-in-no-man-s-land:
Ralph Connor sends his sky pilot to the Great War in this sequel. Only a missionary opens the chapters, with the Red Pine Trail and a question of conscience. Rejected, then called by the war drum, the hero joins the men of the north, through barricades and bayonets. A question of nerve, submarines, bullpups, and other things carry him toward France.

The new message, a man of God, and intensive training follow, as the missionary becomes a chaplain of the trenches. Connor, himself a wartime chaplain, writes of faith under fire without flinching. A preacher learning that the gospel he carried to the hills must now hold in no man's land: Connor's wartime test.
32908-the-ruined-cities-of-zululand:
A tale of ruined cities in Zululand, based on a document from the author's brother, a longtime resident of the Zulu frontier, opens far from Africa. The first chapter finds Her Majesty's 150th Regiment garrisoning Bellary Fort in India in 1856, roasting on a bare sugar-loaf hill. Officers and men endure three years in what the narrator calls a baker's oven.

The preface insists the tale is not mere fiction: the brother's paper, with a map of Zulu Land, went to the Emperor of the French and was graciously acknowledged. The country the daring men traverse remains unexplored. The ruins of the Fort of Sofala lie buried in sand on the Indian Ocean beach, where Arabs still search for smelted lumps of gold. Mysterious slabs, encrusted with ages of dirt, still stand on the mountain land of Gorongoza.
33060-a-living-from-the-land:
William B. Duryee's Living from the Land, published by McGraw-Hill in 1934, guides city people who want to make a living in the country. Duryee, secretary of agriculture for New Jersey, opens with turning from the city to the country, getting established there, and financing and protecting the investment. He then takes up the attributes of a house in the country. A frontispiece shows country homes backed by intensive types of agriculture serving modern human needs.

The book speaks to Depression-era readers weighing a move to the land. It balances hope with hard figures: what land costs, what it can earn, and what a family must learn. Duryee writes plainly, from state agricultural work, not from romance. As a guide it is practical and sober, and as history it captures a moment when farming looked, to many city dwellers, like a safer way to live.
33198-the-borghesi-astronomical-clock-in:
This Smithsonian paper studies the Borghesi astronomical clock in the Museum of History and Technology, a complex work designed by Father Francesco Borghesi and built by the clockmaker Bartolomeo. It appears as Paper 35 in the museum's Contributions series, drawn from Bulletin 240, and it sets out the clock's design, mechanism, and place in the history of timekeeping. The text pairs close description with notes on how the instrument shows the heavens.

The paper suits readers who like machines and museums, giving both the story of the clock's makers and the detail of its gears and dials. Its front matter, notes, and index entries from the wider bulletin are kept, so the study stands alone. For lovers of old instruments, it is a careful, well-illustrated guide to a rare and clever device.
3321-children-of-the-whirlwind:
Leroy Scott opens this novel on an uninspiring bit of street. Narrow and paved with cobble, it is hot and noisy in summer, and reeking with unwholesome mud through the drizzling, snow-slimed months of winter. On a May afternoon it looks anything but a starting place for drama. Scott answers that objection at once: the great dramas of life often avoid splendid estates and trappings.

Conventional romance dresses its heroes in fine houses, but Scott's children of the whirlwind begin on a poor street, where life presses hard. The novel follows them through the city's storms, literal and moral, toward whatever shelter they can find. Readers who like social fiction with a pulse will find the book's argument in its setting: drama lives where people struggle, not where they pose.
33224-principles-of-geology-or-the-moder:
Sir Charles Lyell's Principles of Geology, or The Modern Changes of the Earth and Its Inhabitants Considered as Illustrative of Geology, is one of the founding books of modern geology. It is in a new and entirely revised edition with illustrations. A frontispiece shows the Temple of Serapis at Puzzuoli in 1836, a site whose rising and sinking columns proved the ground itself moves. Lyell, vice-president of the Geological Society of London and author of a manual of elementary geology, argues that present causes explain past changes.

The book's method, uniformitarianism, treats slow, everyday forces, erosion, volcanoes, earthquakes, and sediment, as the keys to earth's long history, rather than sudden catastrophes. Lyell's clear prose and careful examples persuaded a generation, including Darwin, to think in deep time. As a classic of science, it remains essential reading for anyone who wants to understand how geology became a modern discipline.
33225-the-memoirs-of-count-carlo-gozzi-v:
Count Carlo Gozzi's memoirs, translated into English by John Addington Symonds, continue the Venetian playwright's own story in this second volume. The edition, printed in a limited run of five hundred and twenty copies for England and two hundred and sixty for America, pairs Gozzi's life with essays. Those essays cover Italian impromptu comedy, his dramatic fables, and his place in the theatre.

Gozzi writes with wit and candor about stage rivals, masks, and the plays that made his name. Symonds's translation keeps the flavor of an eighteenth-century voice while adding scholarly notes. For readers of theatre history, the volume is a rich source on commedia dell'arte, Venetian life, and one dramatist's fight to keep his art alive.
33228-a-master-hand:
Richard Dallas's story of a crime, published in 1903, opens twenty years after the events it recounts. A man, convinced by the papers that all think him guilty, speaks the book's key line: it is no use, for all believe his guilt. From that bleak start, Dallas unwinds a tale of evidence, suspicion, and a master hand behind a crime that has haunted its actors for two decades.

The novel blends mystery with courtroom tension, as old facts are weighed anew and new clues shift the blame. Its pace is steady, its mood somber, and its close aims to set right what time and rumor got wrong. For readers who enjoy a slow-burn crime story with a Victorian flavor, A Master Hand offers a thoughtful, well-built puzzle.
33298-spies-of-the-kaiser-plotting-the-d:
William Le Queux's book warns that German spies are plotting the downfall of England, in chapters that read like secret reports. It tells how the plans of Rosyth were stolen, how a silent submarine and new aeroplanes, armor plates, and dreadnoughts were kept secret, and how Germans were preparing for invasion. Le Queux, author of The Invasion of 1910, writes with the urgency of a man sounding an alarm.

The volume belongs to the pre-war spy scare, when invasion tales filled British papers and books. Its tales mix fact, rumor, and invention, all aimed at waking England to peril at its back door. For modern readers, it is a vivid period piece: part thriller, part propaganda, and a window on the fears that shaped Britain before 1914.
33341-secret-power-or-the-secret-of-succ:
D. L. Moody's Secret Power, copyrighted in 1881, seeks the secret of success in Christian life and work. Moody opens by weighing two one-sided kinds of faith: eager but uninformed, and informed but cold. He argues that with an open Bible no one need lack knowledge of God's will. His book aims to help readers find the source of true power for service.

The work is short, plain, and earnest, written for ordinary believers who want their faith to bear fruit. Its chapters press the need for the Spirit's power in preaching, prayer, and daily life. For readers of evangelical classics, Secret Power remains a direct, searching call to a life that is both zealous and wise.
33352-little-oskaloo-or-the-white-whirlw:
T. C. Harbaugh's Little Oskaloo, or the White Whirlwind, is a five-cent nickel library tale, complete in one number, of frontier adventure. Its hero, a young backwoodsman, moves through a world of rivers, hatchets buried in trees, and foes like Wolf Cap, who comes up from the river to rejoin his band. Harbaugh writes in the brisk, thrilling style of the dime novel.

The tale's appeal lies in its pace and its wild setting, where a boy's courage is tested by chase and fight. Its short, cheap form marks it as popular reading of its day, made to be read fast and passed on. For fans of frontier pulp, Little Oskaloo offers a lively, old-fashioned whirlwind of adventure.
3338-sir-humphrey-gilbert-s-voyage-to-ne:
Edward Hayes tells the story of Sir Humphrey Gilbert's voyage to Newfoundland in this account, included in Voyages and Travels: Ancient and Modern. The 1910 Collier edition preserves a contemporary narrative of England's first colonial venture in North America. Gilbert, founder of the first English colony on the continent, was born about 1539, son of a Devonshire gentleman.

His mother, widowed, afterward married the father of Sir Walter Raleigh, binding the two ventures by family as well as by sea. Hayes writes of ships, storms, and a claim staked on a rocky shore. The voyage ended in wreck, but the claim endured. Readers get the Elizabethan age of discovery in a participant's prose, hopeful, pious, and doomed.
33416-rambles-in-womanland:
Max O'Rell's Rambles in Womanland, in a second edition from London in 1903, offers witty thoughts. Its subjects are life, men, and women. O'Rell, author of John Bull and His Island and Her Royal Highness Woman, opens with thoughts on life in general. He then cries oh, you men, and weighs the rose, the lily, and the violet, or how different methods appeal to different women. His chapters ask whether women love better than men.

The book's humor lies in its genial, teasing observation, as O'Rell rambles from topic to topic with a Frenchman's eye for English manners. Its tone is light, not severe, and its aim is to amuse while it observes. For readers who enjoy period essays on society, Rambles in Womanland is a pleasant, easy companion.
33602-the-firebrand:
S. R. Crockett sets this long romance in Spain, where Ramon Garcia, called El Sarria, begins as a crouching outlaw figure. The fifty chapters carry him through an abbey at Montblanch, sanctuary, defiance, and the shadow of execution, with a cast that includes Brother Hilario, Don Tomas, Don Luis, the señorita Concha. Red caps of Navarre, a death cart, and palace intrigue widen the canvas.

Rollo emerges as a rescuer and intermediary, and Concha's waiting and resolve give the story its emotional center. Crockett mixes adventure, religious houses, court life, and popular revolt into a sweeping tale of honor and loyalty. The novel suits readers who enjoy historical romance on a large, colorful scale.
33673-the-king-of-the-golden-river-or-th:
John Ruskin wrote this fairy tale in 1841 for a very young lady, purely to amuse her, with no thought of publication. The publishers of this 1885 Boston edition, illustrated by Richard Doyle, say so. The legend of Stiria follows the Black Brothers, whose agricultural system is interfered with by South-West Wind, Esquire, and little Gluck, who has an interview with the King of the Golden River.

Chapters follow Hans and then Schwartz on expeditions to the Golden River, and how each prospered, before little Gluck sets off in turn, with other matters of interest. Ruskin's tale rewards kindness and punishes cruelty, using a magical river to test character. Young readers will enjoy its humor, its moral clarity, and Doyle's spirited illustrations, while adults will recognize Ruskin's early imagination at play.
33713-alice-cogswell-bemis-a-sketch-by-a:
A friend sketched the life of Alice Cogswell Bemis in this privately printed Boston volume of 1920, from the Merrymount Press. Bemis descended from good British stock through a long line, eighth in descent from John Cogswell. Cogswell was born at Westbury Leigh, Wiltshire, in 1592, a man of standing with considerable inherited property including mills called Ripond in the parish of Frome Selwood.

John Cogswell married Elizabeth Thompson, daughter of the vicar of Westbury, and after twenty years emigrated to America, embarking on May 23, 1625, with eight children aboard the Angel Gabriel. The ship wrecked off Pemaquid, Maine, in the gale of August 15, 1625, as told by the Reverend Richard Mather. The sketch uses that family history to frame Bemis herself, connecting a modern life to a colonial founding story.
33714-the-wreckers-of-sable-island:
J. Macdonald Oxley writes a sea adventure of wrecking and winter in this 1897 book. The story opens in 1799, when a voyage across the Atlantic was no everyday affair. These include no ocean greyhounds existed, passage in clumsy craft was long and trying, and travel for mere pleasure was rare. Eric Copeland, only son of Dr. Copeland, surgeon-in-chief of the Seventh Fusiliers at Halifax, sets out from Oakdene Manor in Warwickshire to join his father in Nova Scotia.

Ten chapters follow the setting forth, rough weather, the wreck, Eric alone among strangers, Ben Harden, a Sable Island winter, anxious times, farewell to the island, and release and retribution. The frontispiece shows a survivor's greeting: so you're not dead after all, my hearty. Oxley writes sturdy boys' adventure with attention to ships, islands, and the hard ethics of wreckers and rescued men.
33755-a-short-history-of-england-ireland:
Mary Platt Parmele writes a short history of England, Ireland, and Scotland in this illustrated Scribner volume, first copyrighted in 1895 and reissued in 1907. The frontispiece shows Magna Charta in 1215, with King John submitting to the barons and signing the Great Charter of British liberties. English chapters run from ancient Britain and Caesar's invasion through Roman rule, Boadicea, the Angles and Saxons, and the consolidation of English kingdoms.

Later chapters follow Augustine, Alfred, Canute, William the Conqueror, the guilds and boroughs, the Crusades, Becket's death, Magna Charta, the first true parliament, the conquest of Wales and Scotland, and Agincourt. Later chapters also follow the Wars of the Roses, and the introduction of printing. Parmele writes clear, compact narrative history for general readers, and the volume suits students seeking a single-volume survey of the British Isles.
33758-derby-day-in-the-yukon-and-other-p:
Yukon Bill, writing from the trail in 1910, gathers poems of the Northland in this Toronto volume. It is dedicated to his partners B. and B., who helped him carry his pack over life's trail. The contents run from a greeting and Derby Day in the Yukon through the Malamute, Red-Jacket, Up Against It, How Slippery Played the Game, Heroes, Lower-Flat Annals, the Trail.

The opening verses ask a little broken song to carry light laughter to hearts in bitter pain, strengthen the weak, and bid them smile again. Yukon Bill writes in the hearty, popular manner of Klondike verse, celebrating dogs, trails, miners, and comradeship. Readers of Robert Service's era will recognize the same northland humor and sentiment.
33980-in-story-land:
Elizabeth Harrison, principal of the Chicago Kindergarten College, wrote this book of stories, entered in 1895 in a fifth edition. Harrison dedicates the book to her friend Kate Tiffany Richardson, with whose four children she often journeyed into story-land. A preface warns that kindergarten teachers should reshape each story to suit their own children.

Mothers may read the tales at home, and primary teachers may use them for Friday afternoon readings. Harrison writes for the young with warmth and a teacher's eye. The book remains a gentle classic of kindergarten storytelling.
34192-the-glaciers-of-the-alps-being-a-n:
John Tyndall's 1896 book on Alpine glaciers joins a travel tale with a science lesson, in two clear parts. The first part follows his climbs and walks among Swiss peaks, with guides, huts, ice falls, and nights spent high on the ice.

The second part turns to how glaciers form, move, crack, and melt, and sets out the physical laws behind what climbers see. Tyndall wrote for keen readers with no special science training, so the book still works as both a mountain memoir and a plain account of ice in motion. The narrative also gives full credit to the guides whose local skill made the high routes passable.
34210-cathedral-cities-of-england:
George Gilbert's Cathedral Cities of England, with drawings by W. W. Collins, tours twenty-four English cities through their great churches. Canterbury opens the tour, and the road runs on through Durham, York, Lincoln, Norwich, Winchester, and Westminster, among others.

Each chapter pairs a short history of the place with notes on the church fabric: towers, naves, gateways, and tombs. The volume carries a 1905 copyright, and it suits travellers who want to know what to look at and why it stands, city by city, across England. Collins's drawings show the churches from without and within, tower, nave, and gateway.
3429-st-george-for-england:
George Alfred Henty sets this boys' adventure novel in the fourteenth century, opening on a bitter November night in 1330. A woman carrying a child enters the village of Southwark in pouring rain, having traveled far. The story grows from that arrival into the wars and courts of Edward the Third's England. The hero, Walter Somers, rises through service, fighting, and loyalty.

Henty argues in his preface that tales of fighting can still teach lessons. He praises determination, courage joined to gentleness, and honor kept under pressure. Young readers get battles, sieges, and chivalry, while older readers will note the Victorian values behind the tale. The book remains a classic of the old adventure school.
3532-my-discovery-of-england:
Stephen Leacock, a Canadian humorist, writes about his first lecture tour in England in this comic travel book. The volume opens with an introduction by Sir Owen Seaman, who presents Leacock to a London audience and jokes about lecturers and chairmen. Leacock then compares English and American humor, noting that each side accuses the other of missing the joke.

Leacock writes about trains, hotels, audiences, and English manners with friendly teasing rather than scorn. He plays the innocent colonial abroad, puzzled by customs he half understands. The book suits readers who enjoy light travel humor and a Canadian view of England between the wars.
3544-how-he-lied-to-her-husband:
George Bernard Shaw writes a one act comedy about a young man who must lie to a husband to protect a married woman's reputation. Shaw explains that he wrote the piece in four days of rain during a Scottish holiday in 1905, for the actor Arnold Daly. Daly needed a short companion piece in New York, since Shaw's Man of Destiny was too long for second billing and too short to fill an evening alone.

The comedy turns on love, honor, and the lies polite people tell to save face. A poet, a wife, and a husband trade clever talk until truth and flattery tangle. Shaw keeps the action brisk and the wit sharp. The play suits readers who enjoy Shaw in miniature, with romance treated as a game of manners.
3612-john-bull-s-other-island:
George Bernard Shaw sets this play in Ireland in 1904, opening on a summer afternoon in the London rooms of Doyle and Broadbent, civil engineers. The partners, Lawrence Doyle and Thomas Broadbent, are bachelors and close friends who live above their office. Broadbent, a cheerful Englishman, decides to buy land and improve Ireland, while Doyle, an Irishman, knows the country far better and dreads the result.

Shaw turns the Irish question into comedy and argument. Broadbent's plans for progress collide with Irish priests, farmers, and local politics, and Doyle watches his friend blunder with affection and despair. The play suits readers interested in Shaw on empire, Home Rule, and the gap between English good intentions and Irish reality.
3679-getting-gold-a-practical-treatise-f:
J C F Johnson writes a practical treatise for prospectors, miners, and others interested in gold mining, in a second edition revised in 1898. Johnson, a fellow of the Geological Society and member of the Australian Institute of Mining Engineers, draws on thirty years of experience. His preface says the information, original or compiled, will be found useful by men in every branch of the gold industry.

The book covers finding gold, testing ore, crushing, washing, and working claims, with drawings and diagrams in the print edition, omitted here. Johnson writes plainly for working miners rather than for scholars. The treatise suits readers interested in gold rush history and in the practical science of prospecting.
3722-a-daughter-of-the-land:
Gene Stratton-Porter follows Kate Bates, a farm girl who takes the minister's text about the wings of the morning as a personal call. Kate grows up on an Indiana farm, fights for schooling, and sets out to teach, determined to earn her own way rather than marry for shelter. Her grit carries her into a schoolhouse at Walden, where she cleans the rooms herself and readies the winter term with her own hands.

Love complicates the plan, since John Jardine courts her and then crosses her, and Kate answers with a telegram ending the affair and a long walk to clear her head. Stratton-Porter fills the novel with cornfields, country schools, and family quarrels. Readers who like heroines who work for their freedom will find Kate a sturdy companion across a long and eventful story.
3750-letters-of-franz-liszt-volume-2-fro:
Franz Liszt's later letters, collected by La Mara and translated by Constance Bache, cover his years in Rome through to the end of his life. The composer writes to friends, pupils, and fellow musicians about scores, church music, concerts, and the daily business of an artist who has also taken holy orders. One long letter weighs a Mass movement bar by bar, praising its fire while asking whether a celebrant standing still at the altar can survive three hundred slow bars.

The letters show Liszt as teacher, critic, and friend, placing a new work between Bach and Beethoven with easy confidence. They also record an old man's faith, travel, and failing strength without self pity. Music lovers will find the volume a close view of a great career winding down, told in the composer's own busy and generous voice.
3799-landholding-in-england:
Joseph Fisher expanded a paper read to the Royal Historical Society in 1875 into this history of English landholding. He begins from the principle that tillage is the most useful art, since a nation draws its food and its surest riches from the soil. From there he follows that thread through centuries of tenure, law, and custom. The book quotes Vattel on the duties of government toward the soil and Proverbs on food in the tillage of the poor.

Later passages trace statutes of Edward the Third that freed buyers of land from royal seizure, and De Lolme's remark that such laws stripped the king of power over alienation. Fisher writes for readers shut out from the costly Transactions of the Society. Students of English history will find a compact guide to how land passed, who held it, and why it mattered.
4245-a-history-of-the-early-part-of-the-:
Charles James Fox, the eighteenth-century statesman, began this history late in life. He left it unfinished at his death in 1806, and it first appeared in 1808. The narrative opens with the reign of Charles II. It carries the story into the early years of James II. It breaks off at the execution of Monmouth.

Fox worked from papers he had gathered in Paris after the Peace of Amiens. The book reads as a statesman's view of a monarchy sliding toward crisis. An introductory section traces the Fox family itself. It runs from a royalist grandfather under Charles I to the author's own birth in 1749.
4333-studies-from-court-and-cloister-bei:
J. M. Stone gathered these historical and literary essays under the title Studies from Court and Cloister. The first part treats Margaret Tudor, a notable Englishman, the Catholic Reformation in Germany, Jesuits at court, Giordano Bruno in England, and Charles I and the Popish Plot. The second part turns to runic crosses, a missing page of the Idylls of the King, and Foxe's Book of Errors.

Later essays cover the spoils of the monasteries, the royal library, and the Harleian manuscripts. Stone writes as a Catholic historian with an eye for archives and for the human detail inside great events. The book appeals to readers of Tudor and Stuart history, and of the history of books.
4356-sky-island-being-the-further-exciti:
L. Frank Baum wrote this Oz-related fantasy as a sequel to The Sea Fairies. It follows Trot and Cap'n Bill to an island in the sky. A magic umbrella lifts them to a strange place divided between the Blues and the Pinks. The place holds a Boolooroo, six snub-nosed princesses, and a blue city.

A pink country ruled by Queen Mayre completes the map. Later chapters bring Button-Bright and the blue wolf. They bring the sunrise and sunset tribes, Rosalie the witch, and a war of Pinks and Blues. Baum's invention is cheerful and crowded, with new creatures on every page. Young readers who know Oz will enjoy this separate adventure.
4508-south-wind:
Norman Douglas published South Wind in 1917, opening with a bishop travelling by sea and feeling wretchedly sick. The bishop, who serves in equatorial Africa, hates inefficiency and ill health, and he prides himself on getting through any task in a businesslike way. His arrival on an island resort throws him among a mixed company of exiles, artists, and talkers, far from his ordered African duties.

Douglas uses that clash for satire, letting long conversations test morals, religion, art, and English respectability. The island air loosens rules that seemed fixed at home, and the bishop must judge people he would rather dismiss. Readers get a witty, talkative novel of ideas, where character shows itself in argument, and where a holiday island becomes a stage for serious questions about how to live.
4527-the-story-of-the-soil-from-the-basi:
Cyril G. Hopkins wrote The Story of the Soil to teach soil science through farm life, joining exact science with real work on the land. Rather than a dry textbook, the book follows farming practice through the year, showing how soil, crops, and feeding of the land fit together. Its full subtitle promises a story built from absolute science on one side and lived experience on the other.

Readers learn why fertility falls when land is cropped without return, and how careful management of plant food, rotation, and care can rebuild it. Hopkins speaks to farmers, students, and country readers who want reasons they can test in their own fields. The book pairs well with his Farm That Won't Wear Out, and it gives a clear, early twentieth-century account of why good soil is a farm's true capital.
4586-danger-or-wounded-in-the-house-of-a:
T. S. Arthur published Danger, or Wounded in the House of a Friend, at Philadelphia in 1875, as a temperance novel about drinking that begins at home. His preface argues that bars and saloons are less the cause of intemperance than its effect, since the appetite is first formed in the home. It is easier, he says, to kill a weed an inch high than after it has set a hundred rootlets in the soil.

Arthur had already exposed the liquor traffic in Three Years in a Man-Trap, and here he follows the harm done inside families and friendships, where a host's glass can wound a guest. The book preaches plainly, and it aims to warn parents and hosts before ruin starts. Readers get an earnest nineteenth-century moral tale, useful for temperance history, and for seeing how reformers argued to ordinary households.
4606-it-is-never-too-late-to-mend:
Charles Reade dedicated It Is Never Too Late to Mend to the president, fellows, and demies of St. Mary Magdalen College, Oxford. He signs as a grateful son of that ancient house. He calls the book an attempt at solid fiction. It opens with George Fielding, who cultivates a small farm in Berkshire. Farming, Reade says, is less enviable than it was, and a farmer must now be as sharp as his neighbours, or, like them, he will break.

Some soils and situations, Reade adds, break even the intelligent and sober, just as shops in a great street change names wave upon wave, however lively, severe, industrious, or lazy their keepers. From Fielding's farm grows a novel of crime, punishment, prison reform, and second chances. Readers get a vigorous Victorian reform novel, with a title that states its hope: it is never too late for a life to mend.
4623-the-son-of-my-friend:
T. S. Arthur published The Son of My Friend as the first of his New Temperance Tales, identifying himself as the author of Ten Nights in a Bar-Room. The tale opens in a household planning a party, after the couple have accepted many winter invitations and feel they should return social entertainment. The wife suggests hiring a professional caterer, who will supply the table and furnish waiters, leaving the hosts only to receive their guests.

From that easy, fashionable start grows a temperance story about drink at social gatherings, and about a young man, the son of a friend, whose path crosses the party world. Arthur writes to warn parents and hosts, in the plain moral style of his day, that hospitality can become a trap. Readers get a short, earnest tale about social drinking, friendship, and responsibility, useful for the history of temperance fiction.
4637-angel-island:
Inez Haynes Gillmore opens Angel Island the morning after a shipwreck, with five men lying where they slept, bruised, bloodless, and almost corpse-like in their stillness. A long time passes without speech or movement, until Frank Merrill breaks the silence in a level, metallic voice. He cannot forget the scream of the Norton child on seeing the great wave, nor the way the child's mother pressed the boy's head to her breast.

The men have reached an island inhabited by winged women, and their story turns on what shipwrecked men do when they meet beings freer than themselves. Gillmore uses the fantasy to probe power, love, and the treatment of women, with wit and feeling. Readers get an early feminist fantasy, strange and readable, about captivity, wings, and the price of trying to tame what was made to fly.
4747-the-river-s-end:
James Oliver Curwood opens The River's End with a striking resemblance between Conniston, of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, and Keith, the outlaw he has hunted. Both have observed it, and it gives them a sort of confidence in each other. It hovers as a subtle presence, tempting Conniston toward a line of action that would make him a traitor to his oath. For nearly a month he has crushed down those whisperings.

Conniston represents the law, and for twenty-seven months he has followed Keith, under orders not to return until he gets his man, dead or alive. A racking cough splits his thoughts, and at a gasping cry of pain, with blood on his lips, Keith goes to him and supports his shoulder with a strong arm. Readers get a northern tale of law, loyalty, and likeness, where hunter and hunted must reckon with each other as men.
4769-young-folks-history-of-england:
Charlotte M. Yonge wrote Young Folks' History of England as a history for young readers, moving through the island's story. It opens with Julius Caesar in 55 B.C., the Romans in Britain from A.D. 41 to 418, the Angle children in 597, and the Northmen from 858 to 958. The Danish conquest, the Norman conquest, and William the Conqueror follow, with William II, called Rufus, and Henry I, Beau-Clerc.

Stephen, Henry II, Richard I, and John carry the story through the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Henry III of Winchester, Edward I, called Longshanks, Edward II of Caernarvon, and Edward III follow. Richard II, Henry IV, Henry V of Monmouth, Henry VI of Windsor, Edward IV, Edward V, Richard III, and Henry VII come next. Later chapters continue the line of kings and queens in the same clear, short form. Readers get Yonge's history, written for young folks but useful to any beginner.
4910-the-magic-pudding-being-the-adventu:
Norman Lindsay's comic fantasy follows Bunyip Bluegum, a koala who leaves his tree-top home after a quarrel over his uncle's whiskers, and soon meets a pudding that never runs out. The magic pudding regrows as fast as it is eaten, which makes it a prize for every thief and scoundrel on the road.

Bunyip joins Bill Barnacle the sailor and Sam Sawnoff the penguin, and the three defend their pudding through a string of absurd adventures, courtroom farces, and songs. Lindsay's verse and prose keep the tone mischievous throughout. Young readers get a tall tale about friendship and appetite, told with Australian humor and nonsense logic.
505-history-of-the-warfare-of-science-wi:
Andrew Dickson White traces the long clash between science and church dogma in this two-volume history, combined here. From creation to evolution, from comets to medicine, White shows how literal readings of scripture blocked inquiry, then slowly gave way. Ezra Cornell, co-founder of Cornell University, receives the dedication.

White writes as a historian and university builder, marshaling cases with calm, learned force. His ice-barrier image opens the book: truth presses like spring water till old walls break. The work endures as a landmark plea for free inquiry, and for a faith that need not fear fact.
5086-rainbow-s-end:
Rex Beach's Rainbow's End opens with a first view of the Yumuri valley, probably from the Hermitage of Montserrate, where coach drivers take visitors to look over the valley of delight. Chapters follow with a world run backward, capitulation, a woman with a mission, filibusters, a city among leaves, and a city of beggars.

Food, a sick man from San Antonio, El Demonio's child, treasure, the trocha, and a city of death carry the Cuban adventure forward, toward a haunted garden and three travelers coming home. Beach writes the island's wars and beauties with adventure-story energy. Readers get a romance of Cuba in revolt, colorful, crowded, and fast-moving.
51-anne-of-the-island:
Anne Shirley leaves Green Gables for college in this third Anne book. Lucy Maud Montgomery's Anne of the Island follows Anne to Redmond College with friends old and new. Letters from home, Patty's Place, and first proposals fill her terms.

Gilbert Blythe waits in the background while other suitors press their cases. Anne learns what she wants in work, friendship, and love. The novel closes with spring and a return to the island. It bridges Anne's schoolgirl years and her adult life. Montgomery balances college comedy with quiet scenes of home, loss, and growing resolve.
5248-the-dock-rats-of-new-york-or-the-sm:
Old Sleuth's Dock Rats of New York, published in 1908 as Adventure Series number seventy-six, is an early pulp tale of smugglers on the New York waterfront. It opens with a cry of Hold, Stranger, as a young man seizes a boat's tiller rope on a shore of white drift sand, and the chase is on.

Old Sleuth was the pen name of Harlan Page Halsey, a pioneer of American dime-novel detective fiction. The novel offers readers a fast, sensational story of a smuggler band's last stand, with disguises, dangers. Dockside intrigue fills the tale, in the breathless style of the pulp era.
5254-four-little-blossoms-on-apple-tree-:
