Mabel C. Hawley's children's book follows the four little Blossoms on a summer adventure that begins with a new car and Bobby's plan. Chapters move from Twaddles' grasshopper and errands in town to a journey, old Brookside friends. The story reaches Apple Tree Island itself, where a damp adventure, sunny days, a signal for help, and a rescue follow.

Hawley writes gentle, old-fashioned family stories for young readers, with illustrations by Walter F. Rodgers. The book offers simple pleasures — siblings, pets, picnics, and small dangers safely overcome — in a world where children are resourceful and kind.
5406-afoot-in-england:
W. H. Hudson records his walks across the English countryside in this travel book. The contents run from guide books and the pleasures of walking to Salisbury and its doves, Stonehenge, Bath and Wells, and summer days along the River Otter. Hudson moves on foot, stopping to watch birds, study old roads, and talk with people he meets.

Chapters on Roman Calleva, a cold day at Silchester, and an old road leading nowhere show his mix of natural history and quiet reflection. He writes with patience and close attention, finding interest in a cow, a hill, or a ruined wall. Readers get an unhurried walking companion and a portrait of rural England before modern roads changed it.
5675-the-holiday-round:
A. A. Milne's Holiday Round, published in London in 1912, gathers light pieces about holidays, housewarmings, games, and small accidents of leisure. Its contents run from Holiday Time and The House-Warming through At Play, Two Stories, An Odd Lot, and Little Plays for Amateurs, ending with an epilogue. The opening piece finds the narrator woken from a pleasant dream by a voice insisting that everyone must bathe at once.

The charm lies in Milne's gentle comedy of friends at ease: plans go slightly wrong, meals loom large, and a simple outing becomes a small drama. Readers who know Milne only from children's books will meet the same wit turned on grown-up holidays, with dialogue that carries most of the fun. It is an easy, companionable book, best read a piece at a time, like a holiday itself.
5678-heroic-romances-of-ireland-translat:
Leahy presents early Irish heroic tales in English, with a preface, introductions, and notes that argue for their place beside the literatures of Greece and Rome. He insists these old legends are not mere curiosities for scholars. They carry some of the oldest stories of modern Europe. They were written in a land outside Roman rule, by a people who kept Celtic legend alive. The volume draws on old manuscripts, including the Book of Leinster version of the great cattle raid, the Tain bo Cuailnge.

Readers meet heroes, queens, cattle raids, and fierce loyalties, told in prose with verse renderings nearby. The notes explain where each tale came from and how its manuscripts differ, so a newcomer can follow the story while a careful reader can see the sources. For anyone curious about Irish myth before modern retellings, this is a direct route to the tales themselves.
5679-heroic-romances-of-ireland-translat:
Volume two of Leahy's Heroic Romances of Ireland gathers five shorter tales that lead up to the great Tain: the Tain bo Dartada, Flidais, Fraich, Regamon, and Regamna. Each tale is given in verse with a literal prose rendering set beside it, and a short introduction explains its manuscript source. The last four are called remscela, or preludes, to the Tain, while the longer Fraich tale stands well on its own.

Readers meet Queen Maev and King Ailill planning a raid, young princes sent to harry Regamon, and the cattle, daughters, and honor at stake in Cualnge's war. One ending even differs from the main Tain account, claiming Cuchulain was defeated and Connaught gained ground, which shows how freely these tales varied. The volume suits readers who want the Irish cycle in its early, many-voiced form.
5680-heroic-romances-of-ireland-translat:
Leahy's translation of early Irish heroic romance returns in this companion portion of the first volume, again pairing verse renderings with literal prose so readers can compare the two. Its manuscript notes give weight to the Book of Lecan. That fourteenth-century source stands beside the older Book of Leinster. The text is arranged in parts, so the great Tain material and its related tales stand in clear order. Introductions before each tale explain the manuscripts behind it.

The tales themselves concern cattle raids, champions, and kings, with Cuchulain at the center of the Cualnge war. Reading them in this form shows both the story and the scholarship. The verse carries the drama, while the prose keeps the meaning plain. The notes mark where manuscripts agree or part ways. It suits readers who want Irish myth in its early shape, not smoothed into a single modern novel.
586-religio-medici-hydriotaphia-and-the-:
Thomas Browne meditates on faith, death, and friendship in this volume of three seventeenth-century works, edited by J. W. Willis Bund. Religio Medici sets out Browne's personal religion with learned wit; Hydriotaphia, or Urn Burial, reflects on Roman urns dug in Norfolk; a Letter to a Friend counsels a sick man.

Browne writes in vigorous, rugged prose, a tissue of many tongues, as Johnson later put it. His style strikes more than it soothes, yet it rewards slow reading. The book serves as a classic of English meditation, where a physician-philosopher weighs belief against the grave.
5897-castle-richmond:
Anthony Trollope sets Castle Richmond in Ireland, opening with a direct address to novel readers. He wonders whether readers will be offended if he lays his plot in Ireland, noting a strong feeling against things Irish that cannot be denied. Irish servants need not apply, he observes, and Irish acquaintances are treated with limited confidence, yet he proceeds to tell an Irish story anyway.

Readers follow the barony of Desmond through famine, landlords, and family secrets, with Trollope's steady attention to character and society. The novel favors domestic drama over political tract, letting Irish life speak through its people. It suits readers of Trollope, Irish historical fiction, and novels that face prejudice while telling a compelling family tale.
5992-station-amusements-in-new-zealand:
Lady Barker continues her account of settler life in New Zealand, turning from practical matters to the idler hours. Her earlier Station Life had pleased readers with a simple, true picture of everyday days, and this sequel answers friends who kept asking how she amused herself up at the station.

The book opens with a bush picnic in a valley of the Malvern Hills of Canterbury, where picnics ranked among favorite amusements. Barker writes for readers with friends and relations in those distant islands, eager to know what sort of life their absent dear ones led. The tone is cheerful and unforced.
6039-stories-by-english-authors-england:
Seven English tales open with Charles Reade's Box Tunnel, where the 10:15 train glides from Paddington on 7 May 1847. In a first-class carriage sit four passengers, two worth description, including a lady with a smooth white brow, strongly marked eyebrows, and eyes that seem to change color.

The volume adds F. W. Robinson's Minions of the Moon, Amelia Edwards's Four-Fifteen Express, Angelo Lewis's Wrong Black Bag, Thomas Hardy's Three Strangers, Wilkie Collins on Mr. Lismore and the widow, and Anthony Hope's philosopher in the apple orchard. Each story offers a compact English scene, from railways to country houses.
6040-stories-by-english-authors-ireland:
Irish tales open with Samuel Lover's Gridiron, where an old gentleman in the west of Ireland loves the ridiculous as much as claret and fox-hunting. On festive occasions he draws out a servant fond of his travels, a trusty domestic who will correct his master, saying plainly, throth you won't, sir, when a rash dismissal is threatened.

George Jessop's Emergency Men, Jane Barlow's Lost Recruit, John Banim's Rival Dreamers, William Carleton's Neal Malone, and the anonymous Banshee follow. The collection favors humor, talk, and country character, with servants and squires trading wit across the Irish countryside.
6045-the-hollow-of-her-hand:
George Barr McCutcheon opens in March, as a train roars through a withering gale of sleet up from New York and halts with ear-splitting sighs beside a little station. A reluctant porter steps down, and the chapters that follow promise Hetty Castleton, a mob waiting, a faithful crayon point, and Hetty weighed.

Later come Hawkwright's model, the ghost at the feast, a man named Smith, Mr. Wrandall's perjury, and Sara Wrandall finding the truth. The hollow of her hand gives the book its title and its central image. McCutcheon mixes society drama with mystery, letting a woman's hand hold the clue.
6104-station-life-in-new-zealand:
Lady Barker writes Station Life in New Zealand as letters from the wife of a sheep-farmer, aware they incur reproach for egotism and triviality. She insists the fault could not be avoided without lessening their value as an exact account of a lady's experience of the brighter, less practical side of colonization.

The letters are no guide for the intending emigrant, who already has his own literature and will find scarcely a statistic here. They record expeditions, adventures, and emergencies of daily life, written while novelty stayed fresh. Barker gives England a picture of delight and freedom far from highly wrought civilization.
6336-the-misuse-of-mind:
Karin Stephen, formerly fellow of Newnham College, Cambridge, writes a study of Bergson's attack on intellectualism, with a prefatory letter from Bergson himself. She argues that no prior philosophy is needed to understand Bergson, and indeed the less a reader knows of current metaphysics, the easier the required mental attitude may come. Bergson holds that philosophical tradition is all wrong and must be broken with, by a reversal of the intellect's usual work.

That usual work is analysis and classification, asking what a thing is and fitting it to a known class, as one stumbles in a dark room and feels for texture. Stephen follows Bergson through explanation, fact, and matter and memory, showing how qualities, once distinguished, crowd out the whole fact. The 1922 book is a clear guide to a hard thinker, respectful, critical, and plain in its examples.
649-ancient-poems-ballads-and-songs-of-t:
Robert Bell edits this collection of old English poems, ballads, and songs of the peasantry, gathered from broadsides and oral tradition. The Plain-Dealing Man, The Vanities of Life, and The Life and Age of Man lead the poems. Ballads follow, like The Three Knights, The Blind Beggar of Bednall Green, and The Bold Pedlar and Robin Hood.

Bell's notes place each piece in its folk setting, from harvest to highway to churchyard. The verses speak of work, love, death, and jest in plain, sturdy lines. The volume serves as a treasury of English folk verse, where the voice of common people survives in song.
6599-the-letters-of-norah-on-her-tour-th:
Norah, writing as special correspondent to the Montreal Witness, sends home letters from a tour through Ireland. The volume opens with a long list of subscribers who paid to print the letters, from Montreal, Toronto, Belleville, and even Paris. That roll of names shows how keen Canadian readers were to hear news from Ireland.

The letters that follow report towns, people, and Irish life as Norah saw them on the road. Her voice is that of a traveler writing for a paper, keen, personal, and close to daily fact. The Letters of Norah give a lively, first-hand Irish tour through Canadian eyes, in the form of news from abroad.
6659-history-of-king-charles-the-second-:
Jacob Abbott tells the life of Charles the Second with a strict vow: no tales dressed as history, no embellishment, no drift from truth as far as it can be found. His preface stresses that he used the best sources at hand and checked the annals written when the events themselves took place. Some error, he admits, is bound to slip into any history.

The narrative that follows covers the king's exile, return, court, and reign, in Abbott's plain, schoolroom style. Young readers were his first audience, but the tale holds for any reader who likes a straight story. History of King Charles the Second is a clear, honest introduction to a witty, troubled king.
666-the-gutenberg-webster-s-unabridged-d:
This section of Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary, published in 1913 by Merriam under Noah Porter, covers words beginning with P. Entries give spelling, pronunciation, part of speech, etymology, and numbered senses, from P, the sixteenth letter, through Pa, a short form of Papa, and Paage, a toll for passage, and onward. Notes trace Latin, Greek, and Phoenician roots.

P is a letter of passages and payments: tolls, papers, and parcels fill its early pages, with plants and proverbs close behind. The entries show how prefixes like pa- and pre- built whole families of words. For a reader of old law, letters, or trade, this slice is a practical key.
6681-sganarelle-or-the-self-deceived-hus:
Molière's one-act comedy from 1660, six months after the hit of Les Précieuses Ridicules, turns on a husband who thinks himself a cuckold. Sganarelle, or the Self-Deceived Husband, owes its first idea, some say, to an Italian farce never printed, so the debt cannot be proved. Old writers like Noël du Fail and Rabelais also fed the plot.

The joke is all in Sganarelle's own mind: he reads guilt into innocent acts and torments himself. Molière keeps the verse brisk and the farce tight, with no room for slack. Sganarelle is a short, sharp comedy of jealous fancy, still funny in its picture of a man fooled by himself.
6682-nets-to-catch-the-wind:
Elinor Wylie opens Nets to Catch the Wind with a poem on Beauty, warning that beauty is neither good nor bad, but wild as a gull's wings. Love her not too much, she warns, for that is even worse than calling her wicked. The set that follows runs from The Eagle and the Mole and Madman's Song to Wild Peaches, Velvet Shoes, and a Valentine.

Wylie's verse is taut, bright, and full of strange images, with a formal grace that never feels stiff. She writes of love, loss, and the natural world with a cool, clear eye. Nets to Catch the Wind is a fine, early modern poetry book, still sharp and lovely today.
6702-life-of-harriet-beecher-stowe-compi:
Charles Edward Stowe compiles his mother's life from her letters and journals, in a volume issued in 1890. Harriet Beecher Stowe herself opens with a note on why she wished to leave recollections behind, though failing strength had long held her back. Her son then lets her own words carry much of the tale.

From a New England childhood to Uncle Tom's Cabin and world fame, the letters show a writer, reformer, and mother at close hand. The life that emerges is busy, devout, and deeply human. Life of Harriet Beecher Stowe is a warm, first-hand biography, built from the author's own pen.
6803-algonquin-legends-of-new-england:
Charles Leland gathers Algonquin legends of New England, myths and folk lore of the Micmac, Passamaquoddy, and Penobscot tribes. A frontispiece shows Mik um Wess, the Indian Puck, in a red cap like a Norse goblin, scraped on birch bark by Tomak Josephs. Leland began collecting in the summer of 1882 among the Passamaquoddy at Campobello, expecting very little.

Surrounded by whites and converted to Catholicism, these few Indians yet kept scanty remains of old heathen lore, which Leland saved with care. The tales that follow are vivid, strange, and humane. Algonquin Legends of New England is a precious record of Native story, told close to its sources.
6827-boy-scouts-of-the-air-on-lost-islan:
Gordon Stuart sends the Boy Scouts of the Air to Lost Island. The tale opens at dawn in Ring's back yard. Three boys kick dew off tall grass and peer toward cedars hiding the Fulton house. No light shows yet, grumbles the short, stocky boy; their friend is not up. Over the dam, a hopeless search, and Lost Island itself follow.

More thrills, a startling clue, a rescue, a voyage in the dark, and a mid-air miracle fill the chapters, with the Flying Eagle Scouts in the air. Stuart keeps the action brisk and the scout spirit high. Boy Scouts of the Air on Lost Island is a lively, early aviation adventure for boys.
6872-the-battle-ground:
Ellen Glasgow sets this novel in Virginia, where the Montjoy kin and their neighbors live out golden years before war breaks them apart. Dan and Betty grow up amid open doors, school days, and college talk, and the early books follow courtship, temper, and pride in a house proud of its name. Love scenes at firesides and on night roads sit beside the first signs of storm.

The later books carry the same people into the Civil War, with marches, battle, and the hard lot of women left behind. Ragged armies, cabins in the woods, and a long march home close the tale. The vanquished return to a place changed by guns and by loss, and try to live in peace again.
699-a-child-s-history-of-england:
Charles Dickens wrote this history of England for young readers, in plain, story-like prose. It runs from ancient Britain and the Romans through Saxon kings, the Norman conquest, and the long line of later monarchs. Each chapter takes a reign or an age and tells its chief events as a tale, with heroes, villains, and turning points.

Dickens speaks straight to children, praising good kings and blasting cruel ones, and he does not hide his views on power and pride. The book was meant to give the young a first, vivid sense of their country's past. It still reads as a lively, if partisan, tour of English history, and as a window on how Victorians taught that past.
7081-the-motor-girls-on-cedar-lake-or-th:
The Motor Girls on Cedar Lake opens with Cora Kimball welcoming Bess and Belle Robinson to camp, where talk turns at once to a new motor boat. Cora, the camp hostess, has just received the boat, and no boy stands ready to show her how to run it. Jack, expected to help, has not arrived, and Cora refuses to wait until evening to start her new craft.

Belle, her twin sister fears, may fall prey to white birches and want to paint pictures on bark. Cora fancies she will take to the pines, strong and dependable like big boys. The hermit of Fern Island waits in the title, promising mystery on the lake. The tale that follows mixes camp fun, motors, and a lakeside secret.
7095-malayan-literature-comprising-roman:
Malayan literature, translated into English for the first time with an introduction by Chauncey Starkweather, gathers romantic tales, epic poetry, and royal chronicles. The introduction calls the Epic of Bidasari easily the most charming poem of the collection, with all the absorbing fascination of a fairy tale. Readers glide into haunted palaces and beauteous gardens, through languorous nature into shadowy realms of the supernatural.

Sturdy bowmen and lithe lancers hurry in column, while mystic sentinels, djinns, demons, and spirit princes watch from another world. Starkweather praises a wealth of imagery and luxury of picturesqueness, shadowy, vague, mysterious, and entrancing. The volume opens Malay story and verse to English readers for the first time.
7143-the-strange-cabin-on-catamount-isla:
Lawrence Leslie sends Max and his friends to the strange cabin on Catamount Island, opening with a dare from Herb Benson. Max must camp on the island, bad name and all, and stay a full week, though Benson doubts they have nerve even for the try. Contents promise Bandy legs in trouble, a sudden awakening, exploring the island, and what the ashes told Max.

The mystery of the cabin, an unwelcome discovery, and being watched from the shore follow, with the builder of the strange cabin, what happened on the second night, and a bold plan. Unseen perils hover near as the scheme works out, with unexpected allies and a last camp fire on the island. Leslie writes a boys camp mystery of dare, island, and secret.
717-chita-a-memory-of-last-island:
Lafcadio Hearn wrote this tale of Last Island, a pleasure resort off Louisiana that a great hurricane swept away. A small girl named Chita is found after the storm, alone among the wreck, and taken in by a Creole household. The book opens with the legend of the island, then follows Chita's rescue and her new life.

Hearn writes the Gulf coast with lush, musical prose, full of sea, heat, and Creole custom. Beneath the beauty lies the storm's terror and the fragility of a gay, careless world. The book is both a memorial to a lost place and a tender story of a child saved from the sea, told by a master of atmosphere.
7460-how-sammy-went-to-coral-land:
Emily Paret Atwater, author of Tommy's Adventures, wrote this little volume for children spending time by the sea. The framing comes from a family holiday. Little Bob had been very ill in the spring, and the doctor ordered sea air and sea bathing to bring color back to his pale cheeks. Grandma, Bob, and Eleanor are all part of the seashore party.

Sammy's own tale carries the book. He goes out to see the world, escapes from a shark, and reaches Coral-Land, where the wonders of the sea unfold. Atwater mingles fiction with facts, drawing the natural history from Cooke's Toilers of the Sea and Hartwig's Denizens of the Deep. Young readers learn about coral and sea creatures while following a boy's adventure.
7520-snow-blind:
Katharine Newlin Burt, author of The Branding Iron, sets this novel in a snow country under a noon sun. The vast, flat land lies buried deep in snow, like a paper hoop rimmed by dark primeval forest, its surface shining with an unbearable brightness as of sun-struck glass. To the north, a single blunt mountain head breaks the horizon, and Hugh Garth drops down into the small space shoveled clear before his hidden cabin door.

Inside, a solid table stands in the center of the floor, and a woman sets heavy earthenware plates, nicked and discolored. She herself seems heavy and discolored, yet like the stove she has a dull glow. Burt writes the winter West as a place of glare, cold, and stubborn human warmth, where the snow blinds the eyes but not the heart.
754-the-story-of-mankind:
Hendrik Van Loon wrote this history of the world for young readers, from early man to his own day. He tells the story in short, vivid chapters, with maps and drawings by his own hand, moving from Egypt and Greece through Rome, the Middle Ages, and the modern age. His voice is that of a lively teacher, not a dry scholar.

Van Loon links great events to the lives of ordinary folk and to ideas that changed the world, from writing to steam. The book won the first Newbery Medal and taught generations their first world history. It still charms as an old-fashioned, humane tour of mankind, even where later research has revised its facts.
7843-the-happy-end:
Joseph Hergesheimer's The Happy End gathers stories written, he says, for one purpose only: to give pleasure, at the request of friends he had pleased. He dedicates them not to critics, middlemen, or academies, but, with a joke, to his grocer, who fed him in hard times.

Contents include Lonely Valleys, The Egyptian Chariot, The Flower of Spain, Tol'able David, Bread, Rosemary, Roselle, and The Thrush in the Hedge. The first tale opens in a rectory where a maid doubts a visitor's welcome. Warm, polished, and humane, the stories seek a happy end.
7882-the-life-of-kit-carson-hunter-trapp:
Edward S. Ellis's The Life of Kit Carson, hunter, trapper, guide, Indian agent, and colonel, opens by saying Carson's real worth was known only to close friends and careful students. More than his titles, he held mental and moral gifts that would have raised him in any calling.

Cast on the far western frontier as a youth, he won respect from tough, often lawless men through integrity, bravery, loyalty, quick judgment in danger, woodcraft, and daring leadership. As friend and counselor to Fremont the Pathfinder across the Rockies, Father Kit became a frontier legend.

7963-the-eskdale-herd-boy-a-scottish-tal:
Mrs Blackford wrote this Scottish tale for young readers, following John Telfer, a boy who loses his parents and is taken up by Mr Martin, the local minister. Engaged as a herd-boy by Mr Laurie, John learns his work on the hills of Eskdale while the minister's daughter Helen learns her own lessons in perseverance and self-command. The chapters mix farm life, country excursions, and visits to neighbours' cottages.

The story teaches by example: honesty, patience, and steady effort are rewarded, while affectation and carelessness bring trouble. Its Border setting, with rustic manners, dogs, and moorland scenery, gives it charm beyond its moral. As an early children's book it shows how the nineteenth century liked to instruct its young readers, through adventure close to home rather than lectures.
7981-synthetic-tannins-their-synthesis-i:
Georg Grasser, lecturer in tanning chemistry at the German Technical College in Brünn, wrote this technical book on synthetic tannins: how they are made, produced at industrial scale, and used. He builds on Emil Fischer's outline of the synthesis of natural tannins, then turns to the chemical industry. Notably the Badische Anilin und Soda factory at Ludwigshafen, which found ways to make production practical. No full list of synthetic tannins had yet been published.

The book serves tanners and chemists who needed a reliable survey of a fast-moving field. Its chapters move from laboratory synthesis to factory and finished leather, keeping the science tied to use. As a record of early twentieth-century industrial chemistry, it shows how a laboratory discovery became a working material.
8109-early-bardic-literature-ireland:
Standish O'Grady wrote this study of early bardic literature in Ireland, beginning from the monuments scattered across Europe: cromlechs and dolmens, great earthen tumuli, flagged sepulchres, and enclosures of tall pillar-stones. He argues that the makers of those works were not strangers but our own ancestors, and that out of their rude civilisation our own has slowly grown. Of that elder phase, he says, no record or tradition survives except through the bards.

The book introduces the Irish bardic tradition as the voice of a prehistoric world, carrying history in poetry. O'Grady, a key figure in the Irish literary revival, wrote to recover that heritage for modern Ireland. For readers interested in Celtic literature, it is a pioneering, romantic study, and a window onto how Ireland reimagined its past.
8537-lonesome-land:
B. M. Bower, author of Chip, of the Flying U, wrote Lonesome Land as a western novel, with four illustrations by Stanley L. Wood. Contents open with the arrival of Val, well-meant advice, a lady in a temper, the shivaree, and Cold Spring Ranch, as the hero enters ranch country and its rough customs.

Bower, the most popular western novelist of her day, writes of ranch life with humor and romance, and her heroines hold their own among cowboys. Readers get a classic western, brisk and good-humored, where a newcomer learns the land's ways. The novel suits fans of ranch fiction, and of Bower's Flying U world.
858-stage-land:
Jerome K. Jerome wrote this comic guide to the world of the stage, as seen by the earnest student of the drama. He sorts stage folk into types: the hero, the villain, the heroine, the comic man, the lawyer, the adventuress, and the servant. Each type behaves by fixed rules that real life rarely follows.

Jerome mocks the gap between stage manners and common sense, with jokes on swoons, asides, and sudden fortunes. His dedication, to that retiring student of the drama, sets the teasing tone. The book delights theatre lovers, for it names every cliché they have laughed at, and it still reads as a witty tour of Victorian melodrama.
8659-sabbath-in-puritan-new-england:
Alice Morse Earle describes how Puritans in New England kept the Sabbath, from the meeting-house itself to the long services inside it. Chapters cover the plain building, the old pews, the seating order, the tithingman who watched sleepers, the icy winter cold, and the noon-house where families ate between sermons. Psalm books get close attention too, from the Pilgrims' book through the Bay Psalm Book and the Sternhold and Hopkins version.

Earle draws on old records, diaries, and church practice to show a day ruled by drums, horns, and shells calling people to worship. The book's charm lies in small, concrete detail: foot warmers, dog whippers, and children kept awake through hours of preaching. Readers gain a vivid sense of a stern but human Sunday, and of how much ordinary New England life bent around the church bell.
883-our-mutual-friend:
Charles Dickens wrote his last completed novel about John Harmon, heir to a fortune in dust heaps, who is supposed drowned on his return to London. The Boffins, his father's servants, inherit instead, and the tale follows their rise, the Wilfer family, and the river folk who found Harmon's body. Money, marriage, and murder intertwine.

Dickens fills the novel with rogues, lawyers, and schoolmasters, and with the Thames as a dark mirror of the city. Lizzie Hexam, Bella Wilfer, and Bradley Headstone carry a story of love and obsession. The book stands as a rich, sombre masterpiece, and a fitting close to Dickens's great career.
885-an-ideal-husband:
Oscar Wilde wrote this play about Sir Robert Chiltern, an ideal husband and rising statesman, whose past holds a secret sale of a state secret. Mrs Cheveley, a schemer with a letter as proof, blackmails him, while his wife, Lady Chiltern, holds him to a standard no man can meet. Lord Goring, the witty friend, must save the day.

Wilde's dialogue dazzles, but the play turns on forgiveness: Lady Chiltern must learn that ideals need mercy. First staged in 1895, the play was a triumph before Wilde's fall. It remains a brilliant comedy of politics and marriage, where wit and feeling share the stage.
8884-travels-in-syria-and-the-holy-land:
John Lewis Burckhardt, the late Swiss explorer, records his travels in Syria and the Holy Land in this 1822 volume. Published by the Association for Promoting the Discovery of the Interior Parts of Africa. The editor's preface hopes little apology is needed for an Asiatic volume from an African society: the Association, having secured a man of Burckhardt's education and talents. Spared neither time nor expense to teach him the language and manners of an Arabian Muslim so perfectly that his real character would escape detection in Africa's interior.

Burckhardt's Syrian journeys, made in that disguise and with a scholar's eye, describe Damascus, Palmyra, the Hauran, and the holy places with detail unmatched in his day. He died before publication, and his notes became a classic of exploration.
8887-marjorie-s-new-friend:
Carolyn Wells, author of the Patty books, writes Marjorie's New Friend, illustrated with scenes including Miss Hart holding a book and asking how many leaves it has. Contents move from a bothersome bag and a welcome Christmas gift, through merry Christmas and happy new year. To a tearful time, the going of Gladys, and the coming of Delight. A visit to Cinderella, a straw-ride, making valentines, Marjorie captive, and Miss Hart's help follow, with goldfish and kittens, a pleasant school, and a sea trip.

A valentine party, a jinks auction, honest confession, a visit from Gladys, and chessy cats close the year. Marjorie, a lively American schoolgirl, learns friendship, honesty, and kindness through small adventures rather than grand ones. Wells writes for young girls with humour and warmth, and the book belongs to the wholesome series fiction of its era.
8993-the-mysterious-island:
Jules Verne's novel, first put out in French in the 1870s, strands five men and a dog on a wild Pacific island after their balloon crashes. The castaways, led by engineer Cyrus Smith, have almost nothing, yet they build shelter, tools, and a small working world from scratch. A hidden hand seems to aid them at key turns.

Bit by bit they learn that Captain Nemo, the lone sea captain from Verne's earlier sea tale, has watched over them from his craft below the waves. The book pairs clear how-to detail with mystery and a final reveal, and it still stands as one of Verne's most loved tales of skill, hope, and survival.
9297-the-orange-yellow-diamond:
J. S. Fletcher wrote this detective novel in 1921 around an orange-yellow diamond and a pretty pawnbroker. Mrs. Goldmark's eating-house, a dead man, and a platinum solitaire open the case. Two letters, a Spanish manuscript, and a member of Parliament deepen it, with an inquest asking whose rings these were.

Melky intervenes, a back door opens, and a friend from Peebles calls for help. A private laboratory, a mortuary, and a five-hundred-pound note carry the plot to midnight secrets. Fletcher keeps clues fair and pace brisk. The novel is a solid golden-age mystery, neat and satisfying.
9332-georgie-s-present-or-tales-of-newfo:
Miss Brightwell wrote these tales of Newfoundland for children, under the title Georgie's Present. The book opens on a beautiful May morning, when George Green rises early for his birthday. Ten years old at last, he awaits his father in the breakfast parlor, eager for a whole holiday and a secret afternoon at Aunt Baker's.

Four chapters follow George's birthday gift and the tales it prompts, of Newfoundland life, sea, and shore. Brightwell, known for Annals of Industry and Genius, writes plainly for young readers. The book remains a charming Victorian gift book, warm and instructive.
9459-indian-legends-of-vancouver-island:
Alfred Carmichael wrote the text of these Indian legends of Vancouver Island, illustrated by J. Semeyn. His introduction warns that the unsophisticated native of British Columbia is almost a memory, leaving no monuments or ruins. Frame houses replaced old dwellings, and only slate carvings, stone hammers, and spear points remain as mementos.

Two tribes of the Alberni district, the Seshaht and Opitchesaht, anchor the tales, with winter villages on commanding sites. Carmichael preserves their stories with respect. The book remains a valuable record of coastal legend, and of a world already fading when it was made.
9503-seeing-europe-with-famous-authors-v:
Francis W. Halsey edited Seeing Europe with Famous Authors, a ten-volume travel set built from great writers' own pages. This second volume, part two of Great Britain and Ireland, tours literary shrines and famed scenes. Writers inside include Emerson, Hawthorne, Goldwin Smith, and Mrs. S. C. Hall. Each stop pairs a place with a pen that knew it well.

Stops include Stoke Pogis, Haworth, Gad's Hill, Rydal Mount, Stonehenge, Oxford, Cambridge, and Chester. The Eddystone Lighthouse and the home of the Pilgrim Fathers also appear. A reader gets a guided tour of Britain through its authors, rich in lore, and a fine way to plan a trip or to travel from an armchair.
9832-the-crimson-blind:
Fred M. White wrote The Crimson Blind in 1905, a mystery of voices, blinds, and hidden schemes. Chapters promise a voice in the darkness, a house of silent sorrow, and a medical opinion. Margaret sees a ghost, Rollo shows his teeth, and a man with a thumb returns. Hatherly Bell, Frank Littimer, and Enid cross the plot, with a crimson blind at its heart.

White builds suspense from whispers, figures, and a frame of picture, till the scheme works out. His prose favors brisk Edwardian thrills. A reader gets a lively, old-style mystery, full of blinds, bells, and a villain's patient plot.
9870-war-is-kind:
Stephen Crane wrote War Is Kind in 1899, a book of poems on war's bitter irony, with drawings by Will Bradley. The title poem tells a maiden not to weep, for war is kind, though her lover threw wild hands to the sky and his steed ran on alone. Drums boom, men born to drill and die march, and a field of corpses waits. A babe's father tumbles in yellow trenches, and a mother mourns her son.

Crane's short, sharp lyrics strip war of glory, praising slaughter only to damn it. The sea, a shell, and a splendid shroud close the images. A reader gets Crane's fierce anti-war verse, brief and haunting, from the poet of The Red Badge of Courage.
9948-the-banner-boy-scouts-afloat-or-the:
George A. Warren's 1913 scout story sends the Banner Boy Scouts afloat in search of the secret of Cedar Island. It opens with mysterious boxes and glorious news, then sets the boys cruising after laying in stores, ghost or no ghost.

On the swift Radway river they dodge snags and snares and get stuck fast in the mud. They read a water gauge, camp on Cedar Island, and find footprints in the sand, while a bursting meteor deepens the mystery. Warren writes brisk, earnest adventure. Young readers get boating, camping, and a ghost story that may have a plain explanation.
9983-wylder-s-hand:
J. Sheridan Le Fanu's novel, first published in 1864, opens with a narrator riding through the village of Gylingden carrying Mark Wylder's letter in his valise. Dinner parties at Brandon Hall follow, where Dorcas Brandon speaks and a London gentleman appears in Redman's Dell.

Captain Lake, a Persian magician's ring, and an ace of hearts deepen the mystery, as old secrets stir around the Brandon family. Le Fanu, master of the sensation novel, builds dread from drawing rooms and night walks. Readers get a slow, atmospheric puzzle of inheritance, villainy, and a hand reaching from the past.
9996-tis-sixty-years-since-address-of-ch:
Charles Francis Adams gave this Founders' Day address on January 16, 1913, taking as his text the words 'Tis Sixty Years Since. The phrase is the second title of Walter Scott's first novel, Waverley, which brought Scott fame when it appeared in 1814.

Adams, allotted a single hour, covers much ground in brief compass, looking back sixty years and more to the world that made Scott and his readers. His address suits listeners interested in history, literature, and the Adams family's long public life. Readers get a reflective talk on how a nation remembers its writers.
a-child-s-history-of-england:
Charles Dickens wrote this history of England for young readers, and the contents show its march reign by reign. It begins with ancient England and the Romans. It passes the Saxons and Alfred, then the Normans and the Conqueror. From there it goes through the Plantagenets: Henry the Second, Richard the Lion-Heart, John Lackland, and the long line of Edwards and Henrys.

Dickens tells each reign as a story of character — proud kings, wicked uncles, battles, and murders in towers — with his sympathies plainly engaged. He admires Alfred and Edward the First, scorns John and Richard the Third, and treats the Tudors and Stuarts at the same brisk pace, ending with the later Stuart kings. The history was written to be read aloud in a family, and its judgments are a novelist's, not a scholar's.
a-christmas-garland: Max Beerbohm parodies the great writers of his day in this Christmas garland. His pieces take off Henry James, Rudyard Kipling, H. G. Wells, G. K. Chesterton, Thomas Hardy, and Shakespeare among others. Each pastiche copies the victim's style while turning it to Christmas subjects. Beerbohm, himself a master stylist, makes imitation into a form of witty criticism.
a-daughter-of-the-land:
Gene Stratton-Porter opens in a small country church, where the minister takes his text: take the wings of morning. Outside, tall Kate Bates bends low along the footpath to keep her head below the windows. She is the youngest of a land-rich, cash-poor family, and the land that should have been her portion has gone to her brothers.

Twenty-eight chapters follow Kate through teaching, a contract quarrel, courtship, marriage, and the long work of winning a farm of her own, ending with blue ribbon corn. Chapter titles like Kate Takes the Bit in Her Teeth state her character plainly. Stratton-Porter writes farm life from inside knowledge, in praise of work and independence.
a-history-of-the-early-part-of-the-reign:
Charles James Fox's History of the Early Part of the Reign of James the Second, printed here in Cassell's 1888 National Library edition, is the great Whig orator's unfinished monument. Fox collected his materials in Paris in 1802, after the Peace of Amiens, and worked on the history in his last years. He died in 1806; the book appeared in 1808. It begins with his view of Charles II's reign and ends with Monmouth's execution in 1685, the early part only, as the title honestly warns.

Fox writes as a parliamentarian judging a king who meant to rule without parliaments. James's designs on the army and the law are traced from inside Whig memory. Sedgemoor and the Bloody Assizes end the fragment in tragedy. Readers get two books in one: a primary voice of English liberalism, and a history of 1685 written by the statesman who most feared its lessons being forgotten.
a-journey-to-the-western-islands-of-scot:
Samuel Johnson left Edinburgh on August 18, 1773, with James Boswell, to see the Hebrides he had long wished to visit, as his opening pages tell. This text follows the 1775 edition with the 1785 corrections. Johnson crosses the Firth of Forth to Inch Keith and works north along the coast before turning to the islands.

He records inns, roads, lairds, language, second sight, and the remains of the clan world after its breaking. Johnson judges schools, churches, and poverty with his usual force, and praises what earns praise. The book is travel writing of a high order: sturdy, curious, and full of sentences built to last.
a-knight-of-the-cumberland:
John Fox, Jr. wrote this short novel of the Cumberland mountains. That is the coal and feud country along the Kentucky and Virginia line. The narrator leads his small sister and a fashionable young visitor on horseback. The visitor is nicknamed the Blight. They cross the crest of the Big Black mountain. Their goal is country of moonshiners and feudsmen, where, he says, an older way of life still holds. The contents list eight chapters.

The visitors meet mountain customs head-on. They join a wild dog hunt. They pass a shooting scrape at close quarters. Election day counts as a great day. At last comes a tournament in the old style, where local men ride as knights. The Blight's presence tests both worlds. Fox made the Cumberlands his subject, and wrote the tale as both romance and report.
a-prisoner-in-fairyland:
A Prisoner in Fairyland is a 1913 novel by Algernon Blackwood, one of the most prolific writers of ghost stories in the history of the genre. Blackwood, also a journalist and broadcasting narrator, earned high praise from critics of the weird tale. Here he turns from ghosts to fairyland, and traps his hero among the fairies in an odd, gentle fantasy.

The mortal man dwells in the enchanted realm as a captive, and the story unfolds softly rather than as a tale of terror. Blackwood's gift was for atmosphere, for the thin border between the everyday world and a stranger one beside it. This novel applies that gift to fairyland, making captivity itself a dreamlike state the reader drifts through.
a-short-history-of-scotland: Andrew Lang writes this short history of Scotland, opening when Romans under Agricola crossed the border in the year 81. A magic mirror, he suggests, would show familiar hills above overflowing rivers. Thick oak and pine woods roaming with deer, elks, and boars covered land now arable, and lakes stood where fields of corn now stand. Clay and wattle huts, stockaded houses of tribal princes, and crannog villages on lochs held a people already far beyond the savage stage of culture.
a-wanderer-in-holland: Edward Verrall Lucas wanders in Holland in this volume, with twenty illustrations in colour by Herbert Marshall and thirty-four after old Dutch masters. The contents run from Flushing through sunrise on the Maas, Rotterdam, Gouda, Dort, Utrecht, and Scheveningen beach to Leyden, Haarlem's turf market, and Amsterdam's canals. Volendam, Alkmaar's cheese market, Hoorn, Enkhuizen, Harlingen, Kampen, Arnheim, Nymwegen, and Middelburg follow, with Vermeer, Steen, and Cuyp among the masters.
a-woman-of-the-world-her-counsel-to-othe: Ella Wheeler Wilcox, a woman of the world, counsels other people's sons and daughters in this 1904 volume, in a fourth impression of April 1910. Her letters address a law student of twenty-three, a Vassar girl, a bride on honeymoon, and a young woman facing the necessity to earn a living. A shop girl concerning her oppressors, a teacher of three years, and a would-be journalist receive counsel in turn. A former maid and a clergyman's son and daughter follow.
about-ireland: Elizabeth Lynn Linton writes about Ireland in this 1890 volume, apologizing for rushing into print on a subject she does not half know. She knows a little more than when she was an ardent Home Ruler, influenced only by sentiment and abstract principle. She hopes the process by which her own blindness was couched may clear the vision of others. Lay folk, she argues, must follow leaders their temperaments affiliate them to, since life is too short to examine every question from the beginning.
addresses-by-henry-drummond:
Henry Drummond's spoken addresses open with Love, the Greatest Thing in the World, his famous talk on the thirteenth chapter of First Corinthians. He asks what the supreme good is, and answers against the common view: not faith, but love, is the greatest thing. The contents add Lessons from the Angelus, Pax Vobiscum, and First, an address to boys.

Later talks treat the changed life and dealing with doubt. Drummond, a Scottish scientist and evangelist, spoke to students across Britain and America, and his manner here is plain, warm, and direct. The love address alone was printed in huge numbers and carried his name around the world.
aesop-fables-townsend:
Aesop, a storyteller of ancient Greece, gave his name to hundreds of short animal fables. George Fyler Townsend translated the full body of tales into English prose. Foxes, hares, tortoises, and farmers crowd his pages.

Each brief story ends by teaching its lesson plainly. The tortoise beats the hare, and the boy who cried wolf loses his flock. Townsend's version became the standard English Aesop for generations of children. Adults still quote these morals without knowing their source. Few books so short have shaped so much everyday wisdom. Townsend's edition first appeared in 1867 and was reprinted many times.
afoot-in-england:
W. H. Hudson's Afoot in England opens by refusing guide-books, in a chapter that introduces his own. Hudson counts England's guides by the library and finds them never out of date, only superseded. On Going Back and Walking and Cycling state his method: slowly, on foot, returning. Seeking a Shelter and Wind, Wave, and Spirit follow.

Roman Calleva and a cold day at Silchester explore the buried Roman town under Berkshire fields. Salisbury and its doves, Whitesheet Hill, and Stonehenge with its tillage fill the Wiltshire chapters. In Praise of the Cow honours the animal of the downs. Hudson, the Argentine-born naturalist, walked England as an exile in love with a second home. His prose lingers where guide-books hurry: a road leading nowhere, an Abbotsbury swannery, a river followed for its own sake. The book is a classic of English walking.
after-london-or-wild-england: Richard Jefferies imagines England after London has fallen, as forest reclaims the land and people relapse into barbarism. The first part traces wild animals, woodland men, and invaders around a great lake, while the second follows life in this wild England. A landmark of speculative fiction, it asks what survives of civilisation when cities fail and nature returns.
algonquin-legends-of-new-england:
Charles G. Leland tells in his preface how the work began in the summer of 1882 among the Passamaquoddy at Campobello. He expected scanty remains of heathenism there. He found instead a whole mythology kept by oral tradition. His book gives the myths and folk lore of the Micmac, Passamaquoddy, and Penobscot tribes, as the title page states. A birch-bark frontispiece shows Mikumwess, the Indian Puck.

The contents center on Glooskap, the great hero: his birth, his making of elves, men, and beasts, his deeds, his family, and his battles with sorcerers and giants. Leland prints the tales with notes comparing Norse and other traditions. The collection preserved stories that might otherwise have been lost within a generation.
alice-s-adventures-in-wonderland:
Lewis Carroll wrote this children's novel about Alice, a girl who follows a waistcoat-wearing White Rabbit down a rabbit hole. She lands in a world that runs on nonsense and wordplay. The contents list twelve chapters, from the fall itself through the pool of tears, the caucus-race, and the mad tea-party, to a final trial over stolen tarts.

Alice grows and shrinks, argues with a Caterpillar, and meets the Cheshire Cat and the Mock Turtle. She also plays croquet with a flamingo under the Queen of Hearts, who orders heads off at every turn. Carroll plays with logic, verse, and riddles all through. The book's dream logic and puns made it a landmark of children's literature, read by adults as much as by children.
american-cookery-the-art-of-dressing-via: Amelia Simmons writes American Cookery, the art of dressing viands, fish, poultry, and vegetables, with the best modes of making pastes, puffs, pies, tarts, puddings, custards, and preserves. From imperial plum cake to plain cake, her recipes are adapted to this country and its ingredients. As the first American cookbook, it marks the birth of a national kitchen.
american-historical-and-literary-curiosi: John Jay Smith begins a second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities with part eleven, again built from illustrations and page images of literary antiquities. The editor's note repeats the scanning caveat and points readers to the HTML file for the plates. A new sequence thus opens on the same visual terms as the first.

John Jay Smith's second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities continues in part twelve, a plate book of American antiquities. Text here is sparse because the original is images, and the editor directs readers to the HTML presentation for the full effect. The instalment extends the antiquarian survey into fresh material.

John Jay Smith offers part thirteen of the second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities, another gathering of facsimile plates. The note inside explains that few sections could be scanned as text, so the HTML file is the recommended route to the images. Viewed in sequence, the parts build a visual archive of American letters.

John Jay Smith's fourteenth part in the second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities maintains the series' focus on reproduced pages and relics. The text file's thin content reflects the book's nature as a plate volume, a point the editor makes while pointing to the HTML edition. It serves best as a pointer to the richer visual original.

John Jay Smith continues the second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities with part fifteen, presenting further plates of American literary antiquities. Scanning limits mean only a few passages appear as text, and readers are directed to the HTML file to see the plates. The instalment adds another sheaf of visual documents to the collection.

John Jay Smith's part sixteen of the second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities rounds out another set of illustrated antiquities. As before, the book lives in its page images, with the text file carrying only what scanning could rescue, and the editor's note pointing to HTML. The series as a whole preserves Americana in facsimile for later readers.

John Jay Smith's seventeenth part of the second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities adds another sheaf of plates to the antiquarian sequence. The text file again carries only the passages scanning could capture, with the editor's note sending readers to the HTML edition for the images. In order, the parts form a long visual survey of American historic papers.

John Jay Smith continues the second series with part eighteen of American Historical and Literary Curiosities, a volume of facsimile plates and page images. Because the original is pictorial, this text holds little continuous prose, and the editor points readers toward the HTML file. The instalment keeps the series' steady accumulation of Americana going.

John Jay Smith's nineteenth part in the second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities presents more reproduced pages from the American past. The editor's note explains the thin text, a result of scanning a plate book, and recommends the HTML version for viewing. Each part stands alone, yet all belong to one antiquarian collection.

John Jay Smith offers part twenty-one of the second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities, another volume of page images and plates. Scanning rescued only a few text sections, so the editor directs readers to the HTML file for the full plates. The late parts of the series continue its work of preserving historic papers in sight.

John Jay Smith's part twenty-two of the second series of American Historical and Literary Curiosities brings the sequence near its close with further illustrated antiquities. The text file, thin by the nature of a plate book, is accompanied by an editor's note pointing to the HTML edition. The volume completes another stage of the visual archive.
american-negro-slavery-a-survey-of-the-s: Ulrich Bonnell Phillips surveys American Negro slavery through the supply, employment, and control of Black labour under the plantation regime. The study examines how the system worked in economic and social terms, drawing on plantation records. Though later scholarship has challenged its views, the book long shaped historical debate on slavery.
an-account-of-some-of-the-principal-slav: Joshua Coffin gives an account of some of the principal slave insurrections, and others attempted, in the United States and elsewhere during the last two centuries. Addressed to the reader from New York, the work lists risings and plots with sober, abolitionist purpose. It is an early attempt to record Black resistance to slavery as history.
an-ideal-husband:
Oscar Wilde's play centers on Sir Robert Chiltern, a respected government official whose career rests on a secret from his youth. The cast list places the action in his London house and in Lord Goring's library. A visitor, Mrs. Cheveley, arrives holding proof of the old wrong and demands a price for her silence.

Four acts mix drawing-room wit with blackmail, a stolen brooch, and a friend who seems lazy but thinks clearly. Lady Chiltern must weigh the perfect husband she imagined against the flawed man she has. Wilde uses the plot to question public purity and private forgiveness, and the dialogue sparkles throughout.
ancient-poems-ballads-and-songs-of-the-p:
Robert Bell edited this anthology of the poems, ballads, and songs of England's rural poor, printed in London in 1857 as the title page shows. His subtitle states the sources: pieces taken down from oral recitation and transcribed from private manuscripts, rare broadsides, and scarce publications. The contents divide the harvest into poems, ballads, and songs.

The poems moralize on life, age, and death, with dialogues between an exciseman and Death and between husbandman and servingman. The ballads tell of Robin Hood, Lord Bateman, the blind beggar of Bednall Green, and Sir John Barleycorn. The songs praise the plough and the farmer's boy. Bell prints the material as literature worth keeping, with an introduction on its origins, preserving a working-class song culture that print was about to scatter.
anecdotes-of-painters-engravers-sculptor: Shearjashub Spooner gathers anecdotes of painters, engravers, sculptors, and architects, with curiosities of art, in volume three of three. The book collects lively stories of artists' lives, tricks, and masterpieces, drawn from his biographical history of the fine arts. It remains a browsable store of art lore for general readers.
angel-island:
Inez Haynes Gillmore opens Angel Island on the morning after a shipwreck. Five men lie bruised and speechless on a Pacific beach, haunted by the drowned. Frank Merrill, Honey Smith, Pete Murphy, and Billy Fairfax count their losses. No ship, no women, and no rescue are in sight.

The island's wonder arrives on wings: a company of flying women descends from the sky. The men fall in love with creatures who can leave whenever they choose. Courtship turns into a struggle over freedom, as the men plot to clip the women's wings. Gillmore, a feminist writer, built her fantasy as an argument. Angel Island uses a desert-island romance to ask who owns a woman's body and movement. Its serene prose carries a radical charge that still startles.
animal-carvings-from-mounds-of-the-missi: Henry Wetherbee Henshaw studies animal carvings from mounds of the Mississippi Valley, in the second annual report of the Bureau of Ethnology to the Smithsonian, covering pages 117 to 166. The paper describes carved pipes and figures, and what they tell of mound-builder art and belief. Henshaw's work remains a key source on Native American archaeology.
anne-of-the-island:
Lucy Maud Montgomery continues Anne Shirley's story in this novel, which opens with Anne leaving Green Gables for Redmond College. The dedication speaks to girls everywhere who wanted more about Anne. Forty-one chapters follow her college years: rooms at Patty's Place with friends, stories sold and rejected, proposals accepted and refused, and letters carrying news from home.

At home, Avonlea changes without her: Diana marries, old neighbors die, and Gilbert Blythe waits through Anne's confusion about what love should look like. A brief glamour with another suitor clears her mind. The final chapters bring degrees, weddings, and Anne's recognition of where her heart has been all along. The book balances campus comedy with a quiet growing-up.
at-the-back-of-the-north-wind:
George MacDonald's fairy tale appears here in an illustrated Children's Classics edition, marked as an eleventh impression. MacDonald tells of Diamond, a poor London boy who sleeps in a hayloft above the stable where his father works as a coachman. The North Wind visits him as a beautiful lady and carries him to the country at her back, where the dead children play.

Diamond learns to drive from the stable men, sprawling tired across old Diamond, the horse he is named for. Between his flights with the Wind, he helps his struggling family and a little street girl. MacDonald blends dream journeys, city poverty, and gentle theology into a story about goodness that puzzled some child readers and charmed generations of others.
bede-ecclesiastical-history-england:
Bede, a monk of Jarrow in Northumbria, finished his Ecclesiastical History of the English People in 731. The translation here is the version revised from J. A. Giles's standard English text. Bede's history is the founding work of English history, and our main source for the island's conversion.

In five books he runs from Caesar's invasion to his own day. The heart of the work is the coming of Augustine's mission from Rome, the kings who accepted or refused baptism, and the saints of the young English church. Bede's care with sources and dates set a standard few medieval writers matched. The book made the English a people with a story.
beggars-bush-a-comedy-from-the-works-of-:
Beggars Bush, a comedy from the Beaumont and Fletcher folio, opens its plot in Flanders, where Wolfort has usurped the earldom. Gerrard, the rightful earl, lives disguised as Clause, king of the beggars, while his son-in-law Florez passes as Goswin, a rich merchant of Bruges. Bertha, called Gertrude, is the Duke of Brabant's daughter and Florez's mistress in the cast list's blunt terms.

Three knavish beggars — Higgen, Prigg, and Snapp — give the play its famous canting scenes, the beggars' bush itself being their trysting tree. A hunting speech in the middle reels off polecat, marten, and lucerne, stag and wild sounder, in a huntsman's brag. Fletcher builds romance on the double disguise: beggary as a kingdom in exile, waiting for one recognition scene to restore earl, daughter, and fortune together.
beyond:
John Galsworthy built his novel Beyond around Gyp, the daughter of retired lancer Charles Clare Winton, whose story opens at a registry office. Gyp has just married a foreign violinist her father calls the fiddler fellow, against his judgment and her own better knowledge. The marriage fails in the way Galsworthy marriages do: quietly, through temperament, selfishness, and the slow discovery that love was appetite.

What follows tests what a woman may claim beyond the rules. Gyp finds real love where the law and divorce courts of Edwardian England will not let her marry again. Galsworthy, who wrote The Forsyte Saga of property and marriage, here asks what fidelity means when the legal bond is the false one. The tone is tender and unsparing at once.
bowser-the-hound:
Thornton W Burgess wrote Bowser the Hound, copyrighted by Little, Brown in 1920, with pictures by Harrison Cady. Burgess dedicates the tale to the dog, the child's playmate and staunch ally. Old Man Coyote opens the plot by leading Farmer Brown's hound astray.

Bowser spends bad nights lost and hurt, while Blacky the Crow takes pity and flies for help. Reddy Fox dreams of chickens and gets drawn into the search. Verse tags head the chapters, in Burgess's Green Meadow manner. Bowser at last falls prisoner in a strange yard, and his great voice carries far. Blacky's wits, not Reddy's, do the real work of rescue. Young readers learn woods law: kindness counts, and mockery of the lost comes back on the mocker.
boy-scouts-of-the-air-on-lost-island:
Gordon Stuart's The Boy Scouts of the Air on Lost Island is a boys' adventure story built around flying, a dam and a mysterious island. Three boys wait at dawn in a back yard, watching for their friend Tod, while the sky lightens over the cedars.

Chapters promise a hopeless search, more thrills, a startling clue, a rescue, a voyage in the dark, and a mid-air miracle. The scouts patch their machine, the Skyrocket, and play a big game against rivals who trick them again and again. Stuart writes in the brisk serial manner of the period, and young readers who enjoy scouting tales with aeroplanes will find the pace unflagging.
brandes-main-currents-4-naturalism-in-en:
England's writers come under Brandes's eye in the fourth book of Main Currents, here in English, under the head of naturalism. He traces the turn toward plain truth in fiction and verse. A Dane's view of Victorian letters can startle English readers even now.

Brandes praises force and honesty while faulting prudery and cant. He sets English books beside French and German ones to test their worth. His judgments are bold, clear, and often still argued over. The volume shows how an outsider with wide reading could see a nation's writing more clearly than many of its own critics.
britannica-1911-aalesund:
Aalesund receives a port entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Norwegian seaport stands in Romsdal amt on two outer islands, Aspö and Nörvö, which enclose a fine harbour. Founded in 1824, it serves Söndmöre and the herring fishery as a chief station.

Steamers call between Bergen, Hull, Newcastle, Hamburg, and Trondhjem, and tourists pass through for the Jörund and Geiranger fjords. Ruins south of town are said to be Rollo's castle, Rollo being founder of the Norman dukes. The entry closes in grief: a gale-driven fire in January 1904 burned nearly the whole wooden town in one night. Few lives were lost, but aid poured in from Norway, Germany, and Britain. Its people counted 11,672 in 1900.
britannica-1911-abscond: Abscond is the headword of a very short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives the word, from Latin abscondere, to hide or put away, as departing in a secret manner. Law narrows the sense: to remove from the courts' jurisdiction, or to hide so as to escape it. A person may abscond to dodge arrest for a crime, the entry states. Fraud supplies the other great case, flight meant to cheat creditors. Cross-references send the reader onward to Arrest and to Bankruptcy for the working detail.
britannica-1911-almond:
Almond is the fruit of Amygdalus communis, a plant of the rose family. It is closely allied to the plum and cherry. The entry opens with the word's tangled history. Greek, Latin, and Old French forms all played a part. In a plum, soft pulp clings to the stone. In the almond, a leathery coat covers the hard shell instead. That coat can be separated. The seed inside the shell is the edible kernel.

The tree seems native to western Asia, Barbary, and Morocco. It spread across the warm-temperate Old World. It ripens fruit even in the south of England. It flowers early in spring. The entry links that habit to its Hebrew name Shaked, meaning hasten. A passage in Jeremiah makes the same point. Trade varieties follow, with Jordan almonds from Malaga most esteemed. Notes on blanching sweet almonds for the table close the account.
britannica-1911-amsterdam-holland:
Water cuts Amsterdam into islands, and the likeness to Venice is often drawn. A half-circle outer canal guards the landward side, while four crescent canals inside it trace the old lines of wall and moat, and smaller canals cross them all. The city is Holland's chief, in North Holland province, on the south side of the Y, an arm of the Zuider Zee. Its name means the dam of the Amstel, the canalised river running through it to the Y.

Railways and canals tie it to every quarter, and 523,557 people lived there in 1900. The Dam square, old towers, churches, museums, markets, and industries are toured at length. History then runs from the medieval core through the Dutch Republic to 1810, when France ranked Amsterdam the empire's third town, after Paris and Rome.
britannica-1911-amsterdam-island:
Shipwreck and solitude give Amsterdam Island its human story. In 1871 the British frigate Megaera wrecked on its shore, leaving some four hundred people ashore for over three months. Longer still was Captain François Péron's stay: his memoirs tell of three years marooned on the island, from 1792 to 1795.

Also called New Amsterdam, the island is an extinct volcano in the Indian Ocean, rising 2,989 feet from the sea, empty of people and hard to reach. It lies about sixty miles north of St Paul Island, about halfway on the line from the Cape of Good Hope toward Tasmania. Anthony van Diemen found it in 1633, and France annexed it in 1893. Earlier sightings are weighed with care: Magellan's companions may have seen it in 1522, and a Dutch vessel, the Zeewolf, may have seen it in 1617.
britannica-1911-annapolis-maryland:
Annapolis is the capital city of Maryland. It is also a seaport. Anne Arundel county has its seat there. The United States Naval Academy sits there too. The Severn river flows past the city. Chesapeake Bay lies two miles away. Baltimore is twenty-six miles north. Washington is about the same distance west. Population in 1910 was 8,609.

The state house dominates the city centre. Its white dome rises 200 feet. Its cornerstone was laid in 1772. A colonial treasury building stands close by. Statues honour Taney and Baron de Kalb. Street names recall colonial days vividly. King George and Prince George both appear. Eighteenth-century residences survive in numbers. The Naval Academy was founded in 1845. The entry closes with colonial histories of the ancient city.
britannica-1911-back-bond:
Back-Bond, or Back-Letter, is a Scots law term for a deed that qualifies the terms of another deed, or declares the purposes for which that other deed was granted. One paper thus limits or explains what a second paper seems to say on its face.

The entry's example makes the point concrete. A disposition may look absolute on its face, yet a back-bond can state the limited nature of the right actually held by the person receiving it. Put together, the two deeds amount to what England calls a deed of trust. So the back-bond is the private key to a public-looking grant, recording the true, narrower bargain behind it.
britannica-1911-balfour-francis-maitland:
Francis Maitland Balfour (1851–1882) was a British biologist, younger brother of Arthur James Balfour. Born at Edinburgh, he found at Harrow a master, George Griffith, who backed his love of natural science. At Trinity College, Cambridge, he took second place in the Natural Science Tripos of 1873.

Lectures on embryology by Sir Michael Foster turned Balfour toward animal morphology, the study of animal form and growth. Work at the Naples zoological station won him a fellowship at Trinity in 1874. The 1911 Britannica entry highlights his monograph of 1878 on the Elasmobranch fishes, which shed new light on how organs such as the urinary and nervous systems develop in vertebrates.
britannica-1911-band:
Band is a word for something that binds or fastens one thing to another: a cord, a rope, or a tie. Bookbinders use the straps that fasten sheets to the back of a book. The word is a variant of bond, from the Teutonic stem bindan, to bind, and bend comes from the same root.

Other senses fill the 1911 Britannica entry. In building, a band is a flat frieze running round a tower or wall, often with bold mouldings and carved circles or shields. The two small linen strips worn at the neck in legal, clerical, and academic dress are called bands, survivors of the falling collar of the 17th century. Later parts treat further uses of the word.
britannica-1911-barere-de-vieuzac-bertra:
Bertrand Barère de Vieuzac (1755–1841) was a member of the French National Convention, born at Tarbes in Gascony on 10 September 1755. His surname came from a small fief of his father, a lawyer at Vieuzac, and he kept it long after feudal rights were renounced in August 1789. He began practice as an advocate at Toulouse in 1770.

Barère won a name as an orator and a flowing essayist, and Bigorre sent him to the states-general in 1789. In the Assembly he was known less as a speaker than as a journalist, through his paper the Point du Jour. The 1911 Britannica entry, a long one, follows the career that made him, in its opening words, one of the most notorious members of the Convention.
britannica-1911-barren-island:
Barren Island, a volcanic island in the Bay of Bengal, gets a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The island is roughly circular and about two miles across. An outer rim rises between 700 and 1000 feet, and inside that rim stands a central cone reaching 1015 feet. The whole mass rises steeply from water about 800 fathoms deep.

Volcanic activity is the other fact the entry records. The cone was active during the years from 1789 to 1832, a span of more than four decades. After 1832 it had gone quiet, and the entry describes it as dormant since that time. Readers get the island's shape, heights, depth of surrounding sea, and active dates, with no claim that the volcano had finished for good.
britannica-1911-barry-sir-redmond:
Sir Redmond Barry (1813–1880), a British colonial judge closely tied to Melbourne, Australia, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Son of a major-general from County Cork, he was educated in Kent and at Trinity College, Dublin, and called to the Irish bar in 1838. He emigrated soon after, stayed briefly in Sydney, and then settled in Melbourne, the city that shaped the rest of his life and career.

Law came first, then public building of another kind. Barry became Victoria's first solicitor-general in 1851, later a supreme court judge and acting chief-justice. Knighted in 1860, he represented the colony at exhibitions in London and Philadelphia. His lasting mark, the entry stresses, was education. He founded the University of Melbourne in 1853 as its first chancellor. He also led the public library, gallery, and museum, and pushed government to spend heavily on learning.
britannica-1911-bartlett-paul-wayland:
Paul Wayland Bartlett (1865– ), an American sculptor born in New Haven, Connecticut, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. He was the son of Truman Bartlett, an art critic and sculptor. At fifteen he went to study in Paris under Frémiet, modelling animals at the Jardin des Plantes, the city's botanical garden and menagerie. He won a medal at the Paris Salon of 1887, an early mark of standing in the French art world.

Public monuments dominate the list of his works. Named pieces include The Bear Tamer in New York and the equestrian Lafayette in Paris, presented by American schoolchildren. Strong figures of Columbus and Michelangelo for the Congressional Library in Washington are also listed. The Ghost Dancer, a Dying Lion, an equestrian McClellan for Philadelphia, and a Joseph Warren for Boston are also listed. The entry adds his remarkable bronze patinas of reptiles, insects, and fish.
britannica-1911-basin-stand:
Basin-stand is a piece of furniture described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a small stand, usually carried on three legs and most commonly made of mahogany or rosewood, made to hold a wash-hand basin. Before fixed plumbing in bedrooms, such a stand was a room's washing place. It was a standard article of furniture through much of the eighteenth century.

Two sizes served two purposes. The smaller stands were used for rose-water ablutions, light washing with scented water, or for the operation of powdering the hair. The larger ones carried sockets for soap-dishes, holding the soap within reach of the basin. Those larger stands were the direct predecessors of the ample modern wash-hand stand. Both kinds were often very elegant, and were widely used in their period.
britannica-1911-bazard-amand:
Amand Bazard (1791–1832) was a French socialist born at Paris. He helped defend Paris in 1815, then held a minor post in the prefecture of the Seine. Around 1820 he drew friends into the Amis de la vérité, from which a French form of Carbonarism grew, with Bazard at its head.

A failed rising at Belfort broke the society, and Bazard turned from politics to social change. He joined the school of Saint-Simon, wrote for Le Producteur, and lectured in public on its teaching from 1828. A quarrel with Enfantin over the freeing of women left him near alone, and he died in July 1832.
britannica-1911-ben-lomond:
Ben Lomond is a mountain in the north-west of Stirlingshire, Scotland, near the east bank of Loch Lomond. It rises 3,192 feet, about nine miles from the head of the loch. Granite, mica schist, diorite, porphyry and quartzite make up its rocks, the quartzite gleaming white at a distance like snow.

Grass covers the hill to the top, and climbers favour it, coming from Rowardennan, Inversnaid or Aberfoyle. The summit view runs north to the Grampians with glimpses of Ben Nevis, west to Jura, and south to Arran and Tinto Hill. Eastward it reaches as far as Edinburgh Castle and Arthur’s Seat, which gives the climb its fame.
britannica-1911-bend:
Bend is really three words wearing one spelling. From Old English bendan comes a bending or curve, as in the bend of a river, or the ribs, the “wales,” of a ship. From bindan, to bind, comes the sailor’s bend, a knot, as in the cable bend or the fisherman’s bend.

From Old French bende, a ribbon, heraldry takes its bend: a diagonal band across a shield, running from the dexter chief to the sinister base. Tanners use the word too, for the half of a hide after the thin parts are trimmed away. Bend-leather, from that half, is the thickest and best leather for soles.
britannica-1911-bergschrund:
Bergschrund is a German word, from Berg, mountain, and Schrund, a cleft or crevice. It names the gaping crack found near the top of a snowfield or glacier, close against the rock wall. The split runs roughly parallel to the rock face at the glacier basin’s upper edge.

The crack opens because the glacier, settling downward, pulls its whole mass away from the mountainside. It can run down to the solid rock beneath the ice. At its bottom lie blocks of ice and chunks of rock torn from the wall and floor by the glacier’s lower part. For climbers the bergschrund is often the last hard step before the rock of a high peak, though the entry stays with the crack’s cause and shape.
britannica-1911-berkeley-england:
Berkeley is a market town of Gloucestershire, England, near the river Severn in the Vale of Berkeley. It counted just 774 people in 1901 and stands on a gentle rise in rich pasture country. The vale’s dairies make the famous cheese called “double Gloucester,” and the town trades in coal, timber, malt and cheese.

Dr Edward Jenner, pioneer of vaccination, was born at Berkeley in 1749 and lies buried in its handsome church. South-east of the town stands Berkeley Castle, one of England’s noblest baronial castles and one of the few still lived in. The manor gave its name to the great Berkeley family, and the Berkeley Ship Canal joins Gloucester to the docks at Sharpness, dodging the hard upper Severn.
britannica-1911-berry-charles-ferdinand:
Charles Ferdinand, Duke of Berry (1778–1820), was the younger son of Charles X of France. He was born at Versailles. At the Revolution he left France with his father. He served in the army of Condé from 1792 to 1797. He then joined the Russian army. From 1801 he lived in England for thirteen years. There he married Anna Brown, an Englishwoman.

The marriage was cancelled in 1814 for political reasons. The 1911 Britannica entry then follows his return to France. Louis XVIII made him commander in Paris during the Hundred Days. In 1816 he married a Neapolitan princess, Caroline. A saddler named Louvel stabbed him at the Paris opera in February 1820. His widow's later plots and secret marriage close the article.
britannica-1911-berthoud-ferdinand:
Ferdinand Berthoud (1727–1807) was a Swiss chronometer-maker, born at Plancemont in Neuchâtel. He settled in Paris in 1745. There he won a great name for the excellence and accuracy of his chronometers. Those instruments, used to find longitude at sea, had to keep near-perfect time. He became a member of the Institute in Paris. He was also a fellow of the Royal Society of London.

This short 1911 Britannica entry names one book among his works. It is Essais sur l'horlogerie, published in 1763, a treatise on clock and watch making. Berthoud died in 1807 at Montmorency, in Seine et Oise. His nephew Louis Berthoud (1759–1813) succeeded him in the business. The entry gives no list of his inventions or patrons. It rests on his reputation for precision.
britannica-1911-birjend:
Birjend is the capital of Kain, a sub-province of Khorasan in Persia. It stands at 32 degrees 53 minutes north and 59 degrees 10 minutes east. Its height above the sea is 4,550 feet. The population is about 25,000 people. The town lies 328 miles from Meshed by the direct road. A fertile valley running east and west holds the town. Barren hills, the Kuh i Bakeran range, bound that valley on the south.

The Khusp river runs through the valley but is generally dry. Water supply for the town and its 70 or 80 villages is very scanty, the 1911 Britannica entry stresses. A ruined fort stands east of the town at a hill's foot. Birjend holds six good caravanserais, a college, and some mosques. Post and telegraph offices opened there in 1902. The entry is a compact gazetteer note on a dry Persian valley town.
