britannica-1911-birmingham-england:
Birmingham, England, is a great industrial city in the north-west of Warwickshire. The 1911 Britannica article, one of the longest city pieces in the volume, gives 522,204 people in 1901. It lies 113 miles north-west of London, served by three railway companies. The town stands on New Red Sandstone in the valleys of the Rea and Tame feeders. Ground rises from 200 to 600 feet across the site. The Lickey hills skirt it to the south-west.

The article works through site, history, government, churches, and trades in deep detail. Birmingham's metal trades and workshops anchor its fame as a manufacturing metropolis. Suburbs spill into Staffordshire and Worcestershire beyond the county line. Riots mark its history at points, including church-and-king mobs and the Murphy riots of 1867. Long lists of local histories, from Hutton in 1783 onward, close the piece. It is a full civic portrait, not a gazetteer note.
britannica-1911-bishop-auckland:
Bishop Auckland is a market town in County Durham, England, 11 miles south-south-west of Durham city. Several North Eastern railway branches join at the town. Its urban district held 11,969 people in 1901. The town stands beautifully on a height near where the Wear and Gaunless rivers meet. The parish church lies a mile off, at Auckland St Andrew. That fine cruciform church was once collegiate, mostly Early English in style.

The palace of the bishops of Durham stands at the town's north-east end. It is a spacious, splendid, if irregular, pile on five acres, set in a park of 800 acres. Bishop Anthony Beck first chose the site under Edward I. Up the Wear stands tiny Escomb church, massively built and thought to date from the 7th century. Its stones include Roman work from nearby Binchester fort. Collieries and iron works employ most of the town's workers.
britannica-1911-blantyre-nyasaland:
Blantyre was the chief town of the Nyasaland protectorate in British Central Africa when the entry was written. It stands about 3000 feet above the sea in the Shiré Highlands, 300 miles by river and rail north-north-west of the Chinde mouth of the Zambezi. About 6000 Africans and 100 whites lived there.

Scottish missionaries founded the town in 1876 and named it after David Livingstone's birthplace. It housed the head offices of the main trading firms and mission bodies in the protectorate, and the trans-continental telegraph line passed through it. Its pride was the Church of Scotland church, a red brick building mixing Norman and Byzantine styles, built wholly by local labour and fronted by an avenue of cypress and eucalyptus trees.
britannica-1911-blantyre-scotland:
Blantyre is a coal parish in Lanarkshire, Scotland, a few miles south-east of Glasgow, with 14,145 people in 1901. Its name is Gaelic for the warm retreat. High Blantyre, Blantyre Works, Stonefield, and smaller villages make up the parish, and coal mining was carried on across the whole district.

Blantyre Works is remembered as the birthplace of David Livingstone (1813–1873) and his brother Charles, who both worked as piecers in a local cotton mill as boys. The entry notes the scant remains of Blantyre Priory, founded late in the 13th century, on the Clyde opposite Bothwell Castle. Stonefield, the largest place in the parish, was given over wholly to mining, and rail links tied the villages to Glasgow.
britannica-1911-blashfield-edwin-howland:
Edwin Howland Blashfield (born 1848) was an American painter known for large wall decorations in public buildings. Born in New York City, he studied in Paris under Bonnat. He joined the National Academy of Design in 1888. He began with genre scenes. Later he turned to decorative work praised for fine, soft colour.

His murals filled domes and halls across the country. The entry lists work at the Chicago Exposition of 1893. It names the Library of Congress dome in Washington and the Minnesota capitol. It names the Baltimore court-house too. New York sites run from the Waldorf-Astoria ballroom to the Vanderbilt and Huntington houses. With his wife he wrote Italian Cities (1900) and edited Vasari's Lives. He led the societies of mural painters and of American artists.
britannica-1911-bolton-edmund:
Edmund Bolton (born 1575, still living in 1633) was an English historian and poet of Catholic faith. By his own account he was born in 1575, schooled at Trinity Hall, Cambridge, and later lived at the Inner Temple in London. In 1600 he gave poems to the collection England's Helicon.

As a follower of the duke of Buckingham he won a small post at the court of James I. His plan for an English academy won the king's favour but died with him. Bolton wrote a life of Henry II for Speed's Chronicle, dropped because his sympathy for Becket showed his faith too plainly. His key works are Hypercritica, a short critical essay rich in notes on living writers, and Nero Caesar (1624), a study of depraved monarchy.
britannica-1911-bond:
Bond, in English law, is a duty taken on by deed, and the entry sets out how such an instrument works. The giver of the bond, the obligor, binds himself to pay money, or to do or not do some act, and backs the promise with a penalty. A condition is added to undo the bond if the duty is met.

That undoing clause is called the defeasance. The sum secured is usually half the penalty named. A full model money bond is printed, with blanks for names, dates, and sums, followed by its condition for payment of £1000 against a £2000 penalty. Later pages treat the kinds of bonds, how they are enforced, and how the penalty could be claimed or relieved in court.
britannica-1911-bonner-edmund:
Edmund Bonner (about 1500–1569) was bishop of London under the Tudors, remembered for his part in the Marian persecution. The entry opens with a quarrel over his birth: Strype printed a detailed account making him a natural son, which a contemporary disputed on weak proof. He was schooled at Broadgates Hall, Oxford, and took degrees in civil and canon law.

Ordained about 1519 and a doctor by 1525, he became Wolsey's chaplain and was with the fallen cardinal at Cawood. Passing into Henry VIII's service, he was sent to Rome in 1532 to block the king's case in the papal court. At Marseilles in 1533 he delivered Henry's appeal from the pope to a general council. Later pages trace his embassy work, his bishopric, his fall under Edward, his return under Mary, and his death in prison.
britannica-1911-bridgend:
Bridgend is a market town in southern Glamorganshire, Wales, standing on both sides of the river Ogwr, from which its Welsh name Penybont-ar-Ogwr is drawn. The urban district held 6062 people in 1901. Rail puts it 165 miles from London on the Great Western trunk line, with a branch toward Barry.

Farming trade fills its market, but coal gives the town its weight. The mining valleys of the Llynvi, Garw and the two Ogwr streams meet about 3 miles north and drain through Bridgend as their natural outlet. Local work includes joinery, a brass and iron foundry, a tannery, a brewery, brick-works and stone quarries. Ruined castles at Newcastle and Coity, the county lunatic asylums at Angelton and Parc Gwyllt, and a parish formed only in 1905 complete the picture.
britannica-1911-brighton-england:
Brighton is a borough of Sussex, England, and one of the best-known seaside resorts in the United Kingdom, 51 miles south of London by rail. Its people numbered 123,478 in 1901. Easy reach from the capital is named as the chief cause of its fame, and the town climbs the seaward slope of the South Downs in mild, sheltered air.

The sea front runs nearly 4 miles from Kemp Town in the east to Hove in the west, facing the English Channel. Inland the town, Preston included, spreads some 2 miles. Channel currents push shingle eastward, and the sea once ate at the shore. A massive sea wall, begun about 1830, 60 feet high and 23 feet thick at its base, at last held it back. Churches, the old parish church of St Nicholas with its Norman font. The pulpit once held by the preacher F. W. Robertson from 1847 to 1853 fill out the survey.
britannica-1911-bristol-england:
Bristol is a city and seaport of England, chiefly in Gloucestershire but partly in Somersetshire, 118 and a half miles west of London, with 328,945 people in 1901. The river Avon, marking the county boundary, runs confined between hills through a narrow valley floor where the old city core rests, reaching the Severn estuary 8 miles below.

Between city and channel the valley pinches into a gorge crossed at one stride by the famous Clifton Suspension Bridge. Above Bristol the hills close in again at Keynsham, leaving the city in a basin-like hollow some 4 miles across that spreads up northern heights. Railways fill the account: the Great Western from London, a link to South Wales by the Severn tunnel, outports at Avonmouth and Portishead. A Midland trunk line north through Gloucester, Worcester, Birmingham and Derby, both companies sharing one central station.
britannica-1911-bristol-rhode-island:
Bristol is the shire-township of Bristol county, Rhode Island, about 15 miles south-south-east of Providence, forming a peninsula between Narragansett Bay on the west and Mount Hope Bay on the east. It covers 12 square miles and held 6901 people in 1900, rising to 8565 in 1910, with ferries and two railways linking it outward.

Mount Hope, 216 feet high on the eastern side, commands fine views, while the gently rolling land suits farming, above all onion growing. The chief village, also Bristol, is a port of entry with a deep, roomy harbour, makes rubber and woollen goods. Is famed for yacht building: America's Cup defenders Columbia and Reliance came from the Herreshoff yards there. At the close of King Philip's War in 1676, Mount Hope Neck, the beaten sachem's seat, passed to Plymouth Colony, and the township followed in 1680.
britannica-1911-brunetiere-ferdinand:
Ferdinand Brunetiere (1849–1906) was a French critic and man of letters born at Toulon on 19 July 1849. Schooled at Marseilles and at the Lycee Louis-le-Grand in Paris, he aimed at teaching and sat the examination for the Ecole Normale Superieure but failed. The war of 1870 barred a second attempt. Private tuition and literary criticism became his path instead.

Successful articles in the Revue Bleue brought him to the Revue des Deux Mondes, first as contributor, then secretary and sub-editor, and finally in 1893 as principal editor. In 1886 he was made professor of French language and literature at the Ecole Normale, a singular honour for one who had not passed through the academic mill. He presided over conferences at the Sorbonne. The Legion of Honour came in 1887 and the Academy in 1893.
britannica-1911-carlisle-england:
Carlisle is a city of Cumberland, in northern England. It is the county town of that shire. It stands 299 miles north-north-west of London. The Scottish border lies only 8 miles north of it. Its population in 1901 was 45,480. This long 1911 Britannica article surveys the city. Carlisle lies on the south bank of the river Eden. Two tributaries, the Caldew and the Petteril, join there.

The suburb of Stanwix stands across the Eden to the north. A handsome bridge of 1812–1815 joins it to the city. The rivers at Carlisle are not navigable. A canal to Port Carlisle, opened in 1823, failed. It was converted into a railway in later years. Silloth, 21 miles away, is the nearest real port. Carlisle is one of Britain's great railway centres, though. Lines from England and Scotland meet at its stations. The article covers its castle, cathedral, trades and history.
britannica-1911-carrel-jean-baptiste-nic:
Jean Baptiste Nicolas Armand Carrel (1800–1836) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French publicist born at Rouen, the son of a well-off merchant. He studied at the college of Rouen and at the military school of St Cyr. His bold, upright, and independent temper marked him out, and he joined the army as a sub-lieutenant with deep admiration for Napoleon's generals.

Carrel took a secret part in the failed Belfort conspiracy, and when war with Spain broke out in 1823 he resigned and escaped to Barcelona. There he joined the foreign legion and fought against his old comrades until the legion surrendered near Figuières. A council of war condemned him to death, but a flaw in the process saved him, and he was acquitted and freed. With his soldiering over, he moved to Paris and trained as a writer under the historian Augustin Thierry.
britannica-1911-cartwright-edmund:
Edmund Cartwright (1743–1823) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English inventor born at Marnham in Nottinghamshire. He studied at Oxford, took a fellowship at Magdalen, and published poems before settling as a country clergyman at Goadby Marwood in 1779. In 1784 his attention turned by chance to the problem of weaving by machinery.

The result was the power loom, patented in 1785 and improved under later patents in 1786 and 1787. His weaving factory at Doncaster failed and passed to his creditors in 1793, and a Manchester mill using his machines was burned in 1791. He also patented a wool combing machine in 1789. The entry shows a clergyman poet whose invention reshaped textile work while bringing him little profit.
britannica-1911-chatham-england:
Chatham is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a port and borough of Kent, England. It stands on the right bank of the Medway, 34 miles east south east of London by rail. Its population in 1901 was 37,057. To the west it joins Rochester and to the east Gillingham, so the three boroughs form one town of over 110,000 people. Apart from the dockyards and fortifications, the entry finds few objects of interest.

St Mary's church opened in 1903 on a site that bore a church in Saxon times. St Bartholomew's chapel belonged to a leper hospital founded in 1070 by Bishop Gundulph, one of the first in England. An almshouse founded in 1592 by Sir John Hawkins for decayed seamen still stands. The Chatham Chest, a fund begun by Hawkins and Drake in 1588, was merged into Greenwich Hospital in 1802. Statues honour General Gordon and Thomas Waghorn. Brickyards, lime kilns, and flour mills work in the district.
britannica-1911-clermont-ferrand:
Clermont-Ferrand is a city of central France, capital of Puy-de-Dôme, 113 miles west of Lyons on the Paris-Lyon railway, with 58,363 people in the commune in 1906. It sits on an eminence at the western border of the fertile plain of Limagne. Hills surround it on three sides, with the Puy-de-Dôme standing out among the mountains behind. Since 1731 it has joined the two towns of Clermont and Montferrand.

Old Clermont streets by the cathedral are narrow and sombre, bordered by old houses built of lava. Boulevards divide them from the modern quarters of the joined city. The cathedral, a Gothic edifice begun in the 13th century, was completed only in the 19th under Viollet-le-Duc. Its stained glass runs from the 13th to 15th centuries. A Crusades monument with a statue of Pope Urban II stands in the square.
britannica-1911-cockburn-sir-alexander-j:
Sir Alexander James Edmund Cockburn (1802–1880) rose to be lord chief justice of England. He was born on 24 December 1802, of old Scottish stock. His father served Britain as envoy to the state of Columbia. His mother came from a French family. Birth and schooling gave him strong French, of use all his life.

He read at Trinity Hall, Cambridge, and became a fellow there. He entered the Middle Temple in 1825 and was called to the bar in 1829. Work on the western circuit came slowly at first. Lord John Russell made him solicitor-general in 1850 and attorney-general in 1851. The entry praises the care he gave to every case, great or small. No counsel or suitor, it says, left his court unheard.
britannica-1911-coney-island:
Coney Island is an island about nine miles south-east of the south end of Manhattan, on the south shore of Long Island. Bays, a tidal creek and broad salt marshes split it from the main shore. It lies within the Borough of Brooklyn in New York city. The island is the west end of a chain of sandbars near 100 miles long.

The island itself runs about five miles long. Its width runs from a quarter mile to one mile. Rail lines, electric lines and summer steamboats all serve it. The entry calls it the most popular sea resort in the United States. Four districts mark its length. Sea Gate, at the west end, holds summer homes and a yacht club house. West Brighton draws the crowds with side-shows, booths and dance halls. Luna Park and Dreamland stand there. Brighton Beach and Manhattan Beach lie east.
britannica-1911-cumberland-england:
Cumberland is the most north-western county of England, bounded by Scotland, Northumberland, Westmorland, Lancashire, and the Irish Sea. Its area is 1,520 square miles. The south holds about half of the Lake District, with Scafell Pike, at 3,210 feet the highest mountain in England. Derwentwater, Wastwater, and Ullswater stand among its lakes. Valleys run out from the fells to a flat coastal belt, widest on the Solway Plain.

The Eden valley parts the Lake District from the Pennine face, where Cross Fell rises to 2,930 feet within the county. Salmon fisheries enrich the Eden, and trout fill many streams and lakes. The long entry works through geology, rivers, and the county's antiquities in turn. A heavy list of authorities closes the survey, from Ferguson's History of Cumberland to the Victoria County History. The whole is a full county portrait of land, water, and past.
britannica-1911-cumberland-maryland:
Cumberland is a city in Maryland and the county-seat of Allegany county, on the Potomac river about 178 miles west of Baltimore. Its population grew from 12,729 in 1890 to 21,839 in 1910. Five railways serve it, and the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal ends there. The city sits about 635 feet above the sea, shut in by high hills. A deep gorge called the Narrows cuts those hills to the west as a natural gateway.

Coal mined nearby drives Cumberland's large trade, and in 1905 it ranked second among Maryland's manufacturing centres. Iron, steel, bricks, flour, cement, silk, and leather lead its products, and factory output rose over half between 1900 and 1905. The city owns its water-works and electric light plant. First settled in 1750, the place gained Fort Cumberland in 1754, which Braddock occupied the next year. It was laid out in 1763 and chartered as a city in 1850.
britannica-1911-cumberland-rhode-island:
Cumberland is a township of Providence county, Rhode Island, in the north-east of the state, with the Blackstone river along most of its west border. Its area is 27.5 square miles, and its people rose from 8,090 in 1890 to 10,107 in 1910. Many villages crowd its borders, from Cumberland Hill and Diamond Hill to Valley Falls. The land is mostly hilly and rocky. Granite, limestone, and some coal, iron, and gold are found there.

That mineral wealth won Cumberland the name of the mineral pocket of New England. The Blackstone and its branches give strong water power. Cotton goods, silk goods, and horse-shoes lead its manufactures, whose value grew faster than in any like town in the state. William Blackstone, the first lasting white settler in Rhode Island, built his Study Hall there about 1635. The township was formed in 1747 from the old Attleborough Gore and named for William Augustus, duke of Cumberland.
britannica-1911-dortmund:
Dortmund is the chief commercial town of the Prussian province of Westphalia, standing on the Emscher 50 miles east of Dusseldorf. Its people grew from 57,742 in 1875 to 175,292 in 1905, and since the old walls came down in 1863 the town has turned modern. Old churches remain, the Reinoldikirche with its stained glass and the Marienkirche with an eleventh-century nave, and the restored thirteenth-century town hall holds the antiquarian museum.

The town's real weight is industrial: it sits in the great Westphalian coal basin with iron ore beds beside it. Steel rails, mining plant, wire ropes and machinery lead its output, with great breweries and a corn and timber trade behind them. The article recalls its Hanseatic supremacy and its passage to Prussia in 1815.
britannica-1911-elland:
Elland is an urban district in the Elland parliamentary division of Yorkshire, England, standing on the river Calder south of Halifax. Its population in 1901 was 10,412. The church of St Mary is built in the Decorated and Perpendicular styles. Cotton mills, woollen factories, and ironworks employ the town's working people. Flagstone quarries at Elland Edge and fire-clay works add to its industry.

Elland Hall, though almost rebuilt, keeps alive the memory of a fierce family feud. The Ellands feuded with the Beaumonts of Crosland Hall, whose site can still be traced nearby. A nephew of Sir John Elland met death in 1342 at the hands of a Beaumont kinsman. Sir John took vengeance on that house and on the allied houses of Lockwood and Quarmby. The children of those families were raised to avenge their parents, and after many years they succeeded, cutting off Sir John Elland and his heir.
britannica-1911-exeter-england:
Exeter is the county town of Devonshire, 172 miles west-south-west of London, with 47,185 people in 1901. The old city rides a broad ridge rising steeply from the Exe's left bank. The castle crowns the ridge on a great British earthwork, now laid out as a promenade. High Street and Fore Street are narrow and picturesque, lined with houses of the 16th and 17th centuries.

The cathedral, though not among England's largest, is praised as unmatched in beauty and detail. Apart from its Norman transept towers, the work is Decorated, from about 1280 to 1369. Inside, one unbroken roof spans nave and choir, with a minstrels' gallery and Bishop Stapeldon's throne of about 1320. Scott restored the whole between 1870 and 1877. The city's woollen trade, begun under Elizabeth, once exported over half a million sterling a year, second only to Leeds, but died out by the early 1800s.
britannica-1911-fogelberg-benedict-erlan:
Benedict Erland Fogelberg (1786-1854), Swedish sculptor, was born at Gothenburg on 8 August 1786. His father, a copper-founder, backed his early taste for design and sent him to Stockholm in 1801 to study at the school of art. There he fell under the influence of the sculptor Sergell, who passed on his own love of antique art and natural grace. Fogelberg worked hard at Stockholm for years, though his instinct for severe beauty rebelled against the rococo taste then ruling the city.

A government pension in 1818 let Fogelberg travel. He studied a year or two in Paris, under Guerin and then the sculptor Bosio. In 1820 he reached Rome, the dream of his life, and spent most of his remaining years there in steady work and close study of the art of the past. In 1854 the king called him home to Sweden, where he was received with honour, as the entry closes his career.
britannica-1911-franz-josef-land:
Franz Josef Land is an Arctic archipelago east of Spitsbergen and north of Novaya Zemlya, running from about 80 to 82 degrees north. Its glacier-covered islands rise to about 2400 feet, and their main rock is basalt pushing through the ice near the shore. Bear and fox are the only land mammals, though the bird life drew scientific interest.

Julius Payer, with the Austrian ship Tegetthof beset in the ice, first saw the land in August 1873 and reached Cape Fligely at 82 degrees 5 minutes north. Leigh Smith charted the south coast in 1881 and 1882. The Jackson-Harmsworth party worked from Cape Flora from 1894, and there Jackson met Nansen in June 1896. The duke of Abruzzi wintered in Teplitz Bay in 1899, and his sledge party reached 86 degrees 33 minutes north the following spring.
britannica-1911-fredegond:
Fredegond (died 597) was a Frankish queen who rose from serving-woman to wife of King Chilperic I. At her urging he put away his first wife Audovera and strangled his second, Galswintha, sister of Queen Brunhilda. Chilperic married Fredegond in 567, and her hold over him proved ruinous to his house and realm.

She pushed him into war with Austrasia and procured the murder of the victorious King Sigebert in 575. His sons by Audovera all died tragic deaths while she fought to secure the throne for her own children. Two sons died in infancy, but a third lived to reign as Clotaire II. After Chilperic death in 584 she governed the western kingdom for the boy, plotted against Childebert II, beat Theudebert at Laffaux, and died in 597.
britannica-1911-frederick-maryland:
Frederick is a city and the county-seat of Frederick county, Maryland, on Carroll Creek, 61 miles by rail west of Baltimore. Its population was 10,411 in 1910. Rich Monocacy valley farmland surrounds it, with Catoctin Mountain west and Sugar Loaf Mountain south, and most buildings are brick or stone.

The Maryland school for the deaf and the Woman College of Frederick stand here. Francis Scott Key and Roger Brooke Taney lie buried in Mount Olivet cemetery, where a monument honours Key. Canning works and makers of flour, bricks, brushes, leather goods, and hosiery drive the trade. Germans settled the place in 1733, named for Frederick Calvert of the Baltimore family. Braddock prepared his ill-fated march here in 1755, and Whittier poem Barbara Frietchie later made the city famed in the Civil War.
britannica-1911-gavelkind:
Gavelkind, in the 1911 Britannica, is a land-tenure custom tied chiefly to Kent, where all land is presumed held by it until the contrary is proved. More exactly, it is socage tenure subject to the custom of gavelkind. The entry sets out its six chief peculiarities in order.

A tenant may grant his land away at fifteen, may always leave it by will, and loses nothing by felony: 'the father to the bough, the son to the plough.' If he dies without a will, all sons share equally, not the eldest alone. A widow's dower is one half, not one third. The entry traces gavelkind to before the Conquest, when it was the general custom, later displaced by primogeniture. Irish gavelkind, a tribal form, is set apart at the close.
britannica-1911-gazaland:
Gazaland is a district of Portuguese East Africa, running north from the Komati river at Delagoa Bay to the Pungwe river. The 1911 Britannica entry calls it a well-watered, fertile country. It is also named as one of the chief recruiting grounds for labour for the Transvaal gold mines.

The name comes from Gaza, a Swazi chief of Chaka's time. His son Manikusa welded refugee clans into one tribe, the Matshangana, and by 1836 mastered the country as far as the Zambezi, taking the Portuguese posts. The entry follows his son Umzila, who ceded the land south of the Manhissa to the Portuguese yet held the north in independence until about 1884. A rival figure, the Goanese prazo-holder Gouveia, closes the account.
britannica-1911-greenland:
Greenland, Danish Gronland, is a large continental island, the greater part of it within the Arctic Circle and the whole arctic in character. The 1911 Britannica opens its long article with the island's isolation. No land joins it to Europe or America, though submarine ridges link it to Iceland, the Faeroes and Scotland, and to Baffin Land across Davis Strait.

Only a narrow strait parts its far north from Ellesmere Land. The entry maps its seas with care: the North Atlantic and the Greenland Sea to the east, Denmark Strait toward Iceland, and Davis Strait and Baffin Bay to the west. Northward the bay narrows into Smith Sound, Kane Basin, Kennedy Channel and Robeson Channel. From that geography the article moves to the ice cap, the coasts, the Norse and Danish settlements, and the exploration of the interior.
britannica-1911-grindal-edmund:
Edmund Grindal (c. 1519–1583) rose through the Elizabethan church. He served in turn as bishop of London, archbishop of York and archbishop of Canterbury. Born at Hensingham in Cumberland, he was a farmer's son. He studied at Cambridge and became a fellow of Pembroke Hall in 1538. He later served as a chaplain to Edward VI.

Under Mary he fled abroad to Strassburg and then Frankfurt. There he tried to settle disputes among the English exiles. The fight was over how far reform should go. Returning in 1559, he helped revise the liturgy. Yet his scruples over vestments and church government set him apart. He also shrank from punishing Puritans harshly. He founded a free school at St Bees. He left money for the poor of several places.
britannica-1911-hamilton-scotland:
Hamilton is a burgh of Lanarkshire, Scotland. Its population in 1901 was 32,775. It stands near the junction of the Avon with the Clyde. Glasgow lies about ten miles north-west by road. Two railway companies serve the town. The town hall is Scottish Baronial, with a 130-foot clock-tower. Queenzie Neuk, where Queen Mary rested before Langside, is a noted spot.

Cotton, lace and embroidered muslins are manufactured there. Carriage-building and market gardens also employ people. The district is famed for its apples. Real prosperity rests on coal and ironstone. The surrounding field is Scotland's richest mineral ground. Hamilton palace stands just east of the town. Its portico pillars are each a single stone block. The palace grounds cover nearly 1,500 acres. Cadzow Castle's ruins lie nearby. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; the Hamilton, Scotland entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-hand:
Hand is a word common to the Teutonic languages. German Hand and Gothic handus are its kin. It names the terminal part of the human arm. The fingers and palm make it up. Some animals have prehensile limbs called hands too. Transferred uses of the word fill most of the account. Hand can mean charge, authority or agency. Phrases like at first hand show that range.

From the hands' position it also means direction. Right hand and left hand come from that use. A given hand symbolises marriage and oaths. Labourers and ships' crews are called hands. So is a person of special skill, an old parliamentary hand. Clock pointers and card deals take the name too. As a measure a hand equals four inches. It survives only in measuring horses. The hand of glory, a hanged man's dried hand, closes the entry.
britannica-1911-helmund:
The Helmund is a river of Afghanistan, about 600 miles long. It is identical with the ancient Etymander. Only the Kabul river rivals it in importance there. It exceeds the Kabul in both volume and length. It rises in the Koh-i-Baba west of Kabul. Its infant stream parts the Unai and Irak passes. No European followed its next fifty miles. Below Girishk it becomes a mountain river no longer.

At Girishk the Herat to Kandahar route crosses it. Forty-five miles lower the Arghandab joins it. Then it runs 300 to 400 yards wide and 9 to 12 feet deep. Even in the dry season it never lacks water. In Seistan it turns north for 70 to 80 miles. It ends in the Seistan swamps by various mouths. Its shifting bed caused repeated frontier squabbles. Persian Seistan, once highly cultivated, is now barren waste.
britannica-1911-hickeringill-edmund:
Edmund Hickeringill (1631–1708) was an English divine who lived an eventful life across the Commonwealth and the Restoration. A junior fellow of Caius College, Cambridge, in 1651–1652, he joined Lilburne's regiment as chaplain. He then served in the ranks in Scotland and in Swedish service, and rose to captain in Fleetwood's regiment. For a time he lived in Jamaica, and published an account of it in 1661.

That same year he was ordained by Robert Sanderson, bishop of Lincoln, having passed through shades of belief named Baptist, Quaker and Deist. From 1662 until his death in 1708 he was vicar of All Saints', Colchester. A vigorous pamphleteer, he clashed with Henry Compton, bishop of London, and paid heavy damages for slander in 1682. He made a public recantation in 1684 and was shut out of his living from 1685 to 1688. His career ended with a conviction for forgery in 1707, a year before his death.
britannica-1911-hill-rowland:
Rowland Hill (1744–1833) was an English preacher, born at Hawkstone, Shropshire, in 1744. Educated at Shrewsbury, Eton and St John's College, Cambridge, he scandalized his friends by preaching before taking orders, fired by Whitefield's example. In 1773 he took the parish of Kingston, Somersetshire, where crowds flocked to his open-air services.

With inherited wealth Hill built Surrey Chapel in London in 1783, keeping always to the forms of the Church of England. His powerful voice and bold manner fitted rude audiences, and Southey ranked his delivery with Kean's. He helped found the Religious Tract Society, the British and Foreign Bible Society and the London Missionary Society. His Village Dialogues (1810) reached a 34th edition by 1839.
britannica-1911-hill-sir-rowland:
Sir Rowland Hill (1795–1879), author of the penny postal system, was born at Kidderminster in 1795. A younger brother of Matthew Davenport Hill, he was named after Rowland Hill the preacher. A spinal complaint kept him lying down as a child, and he passed the time repeating figures aloud to huge totals. At school his gift for mathematics was plain.

At twelve Hill was helping teach mathematics in his father's Birmingham school, and later he chiefly ran it. His system for educating boys in large numbers, printed in 1822, left as much power as possible with the boys themselves. It worked so well that the head master never used his veto in six years. As an educationist he ranks beside Arnold of Rugby. His lasting fame rests on the penny post.
britannica-1911-holy-island:
Holy Island, or Lindisfarne, is an island in the North Sea, 2 m. from the coast of Northumberland. Its population was 405 in 1901. At low water flat sands join it to the mainland, crossed by a track marked with wooden posts and passable for vehicles. The island measures 3 m. east to west and covers 1,051 acres, sandy and barren in the north, fertile in the south.

Rabbits, fish, oysters and farm produce are exported. At the south-west angle stands the fishing village, now a summer watering-place, with a harbour sheltering small vessels. The island takes its name from the monastery St Aidan founded there, restored in 1082 as a cell of Durham. Aidan chose Lindisfarne in 635 as the head of his new diocese, and St Cuthbert was among its bishops. In 793 the Danes landed and burnt the monastery. The castle, on a basalt rock east of the village, dates from about 1500.
britannica-1911-hoyle-edmund:
Edmund Hoyle (1672–1769) was the first systematizer of the laws of whist, and the author of a book on games. He was born in 1672; his parentage and birthplace are unknown, and few details of his life survive. For some time he lived in London, and partly supported himself by teaching whist. For his pupils he drew up a Short Treatise on the game.

That treatise passed hand to hand in manuscript before Hoyle printed it, entering it at Stationers' Hall in November 1742. Hoyle's laws stayed authoritative until 1864, when the Arlington and Portland clubs adopted new rules that slowly replaced them. He also published rules for several other games, and his book on games has passed through many editions. The weight of his name survives in the phrase according to Hoyle, still used for settling any point by the book. The short entry is drawn from the whist article's ground.
britannica-1911-huber-ludwig-ferdinand:
Ludwig Ferdinand Huber (1764–1804) was a German author, born in Paris on the 14th of September 1764. His father, Michael Huber, did much to spread the study of German literature in France. The family moved in his infancy to Leipzig, where the boy was carefully taught modern languages and literature, inclining most to those of France and England.

At Leipzig Huber grew intimate with Christian Gottfried Körner, the poet's father. At Dresden he became engaged to Dora Stock, Körner's betrothed's sister, and fell in with Schiller, one of Körner's staunchest friends. In 1787 he was made secretary to the Saxon legation at Mainz, and stayed until the French occupation of 1792. There he took up the cause of the family of his friend Georg Forster, who had gone over to republican views. The account follows his later work as a writer and editor in Stuttgart and Ulm.
britannica-1911-john-of-england:
John (1167–1216), king of England, was the youngest son of Henry II by Eleanor of Aquitaine, born at Oxford on the 24th of December 1167. Lacking lands granted to his elder brothers, he was nicknamed Lackland. His father still planned great things for him: a Savoy marriage scheme, the earldom of Cornwall in reserve, a Gloucester heiress as bride, and the lordship of Ireland in 1177.

Sent to govern Ireland in 1185, he came home within months in disgrace, having offended loyal chiefs and failed to guard the settlers. In 1189 he joined Richard and the French king in the plot against his dying father. Under Richard he was loaded with lands and income yet barred from the regency during the crusade. He then worked against the chancellor Longchamp and plotted to secure England for himself. The long entry follows his reign to its end and closes with a guide to the record sources.
britannica-1911-jurien-de-la-graviere-je:
Jean Baptiste Edmond Jurien de la Gravière (1812–1892) was a French admiral, son of an admiral who had served through the Revolutionary and Napoleonic wars. He was born on the 19th of November 1812 and entered the navy in 1828. He was made commander in 1841 and captain in 1850, and in the Russian War he commanded a ship in the Black Sea.

He became rear admiral in December 1855. In 1859 he led a squadron in the Adriatic and sealed the Austrian ports with a close blockade. In October 1861 he took command in the Gulf of Mexico, and two months later led the expedition against Mexico, rising to vice admiral in January 1862. In the war of 1870 he held the Mediterranean fleet. He died on the 4th of March 1892. He was also a full writer on naval history, most of whose works first appeared in the Revue des deux mondes.
britannica-1911-kean-edmund:
Edmund Kean (1787–1833) was an English actor, born in London on the 17th of March 1787. His father was probably Edmund Kean, an architect's clerk, and his mother was an actress, Ann Carey. In his fourth year he first appeared on the stage as Cupid in Noverre's ballet of Cymon.

As a child his liveliness and cleverness made him a general favourite. But the harsh facts of his lot, and the lack of firm handling, bred self reliance with wayward ways. About 1794 kind persons paid for his schooling, and he mastered his tasks with striking ease and speed. Finding the restraint unbearable, he shipped as a cabin boy at Portsmouth. He found he had traded one bondage for a harder one. He then feigned deafness and lameness with such skill that he fooled even the doctors.
britannica-1911-kerguelen-island:
Kerguelen Island, Kerguelen's Land, or Desolation Island, is an island in the Southern Ocean, southeast of the Cape of Good Hope and southwest of Australia, nearly halfway between them. It lies between about 48 and 50 degrees south. Its greatest length is about 85 miles, but its area is only about 1400 square miles.

The island is mountainous throughout, and from the sea it can look like a run of jagged peaks. Ridges and mountain masses are parted by steep sided valleys. They run down to the sea and form deep fjords, so that no part of the interior is more than 12 miles from salt water. The chief summits are Mount Ross at 6120 feet, Mount Richards at 4000, and Mount Crozier at 3251. The coast is deeply cut, and the fjords on the north, east, and south form well sheltered harbours.
britannica-1911-kustenland: Küstenland, meaning coast-land or littoral, is a common name for three crown-lands of Austria: Görz and Gradisca, Istria and Trieste. Together they cover 3084 square miles and held 755,183 people in 1900. The three lands are joined for some purposes of government under the governor of Trieste, and the legal and financial officers of Trieste also hold authority over the whole littoral.
britannica-1911-ladybrand:
Ladybrand is a town of the Orange Free State, 80 m. E. of Bloemfontein by rail, with another railway running to Natal by way of Harrismith. Its population in 1904 was 3862, of whom 2334 were whites. The town sits pleasantly at the foot of the flat-topped Platberg, about 4 m. W. of the Caledon river, which parts the province from Basutoland.

It is the centre of a rich arable district and has a large wheat market. It is also a health resort: the nearness of the Maluti Mountains keeps the climate bracing even in the summer months, November to March. Coal and petroleum are found in the neighbourhood. The town is named after the wife of Sir J. H. Brand, president of the Orange Free State.
britannica-1911-limburg-holland: Limburg is the smallest province of Holland and the farthest south-east. Gelderland bounds it north and North Brabant north-west. Belgian Limburg and Liége lie south. Germany lies east. Its ground covers 850 square miles. The count of 1900 gave 281,934 people. The Meuse runs along its south-west edge, then through its north. The Geul and the Roer feed that river. Maastricht is the capital. Roermond names the second of its two parts.
building-a-state-in-apache-land:
Charles D. Poston set down how Arizona came to be, drawn from his pieces in the Overland Express, dated 1894. Part one tells how the land was won. San Francisco in the early 1850s opens the tale. A house at Stockton and Washington, called the Government Boarding House, held senators and high staff.

Night talks in its parlor, over a bottle of Sazerac, turned on a new treaty with Mexico. More land was the aim, though no sharp want drove it. The treaty of 1848 had left a flaw in the line, and a road south was the true prize, as the tale goes on to show. Poston's own hand in the work gave him the tale from inside. Land, law, and Apache ground form the stakes of the whole.
castle-richmond:
Castle Richmond, by Anthony Trollope, is his Irish novel of the great famine, presented here in a 1906 edition with an introduction by Algar Thorold. Thorold reports that Trollope wrote it in 1861, long after leaving Ireland, and judges the plot mechanical and the characterization weak, with one great exception. The book's value, he argues, is documentary: graphic famine scenes observed carefully and, on the whole, impartially.

The exception is Abe Mollett, an unscrupulous blackmailer drawn, Thorold says, with real art and a hunter's loving preoccupation. Around the castle and its family, Trollope sets landlords, priests, and parsons against starvation in County Cork, and the introduction notes that his priest comes off a better man than his parson. Modern readers often come to this novel for exactly what its introducer praised: a major novelist testifying, from memory and conscience, to a catastrophe England preferred to forget.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-croy:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Croyland, or Crowland, describes a Benedictine monastery in Lincolnshire, sixteen miles from Stamford. Ethelbald, King of Mercia, founded it early in the eighth century in memory of St. Guthlac.

Danes destroyed the house and slaughtered its community in 866. After refounding under King Edred it burned again in 1091, was rebuilt by Abbot Joffrid, and burned once more in 1170 before rebuilding under Abbot Edward. Thereafter Croyland prospered almost unbroken to the Dissolution, richly endowed by visitors to Guthlac's shrine and secure in its fenland isolation. The entry names its notable abbots, including Ingulphus.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-mori:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Morimond describes the fourth daughter of Cîteaux, in Champagne. Odelric d'Aigremont and Adeline de Choiseul founded it in 1115, with Arnold as first abbot. Arnold, its first abbot and a member of one of Germany's noblest families, was long counted a column of the Cistercian Order.

Through Arnold's zeal Morimond grew rapidly, planting colonies across France, Germany, Poland, Bohemia, Spain and Cyprus. Celebrated foundations included Ebrach in 1126, Holy Cross in 1134, and Aiguebelle in 1137, and by the late eighteenth century Morimond counted nearly seven hundred daughter houses. Briefs from popes also placed Spain's military orders under Morimond's spiritual jurisdiction.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-absalon-of-lu:
Absalon of Lund, also known as Axel, was a famous Danish prelate born in 1128 at Finnestoe in Seeland. He died at Soroe's Benedictine monastery on 21 March 1201, the house his father founded. A graduate of the University of Paris, he taught briefly at Ste. Genevieve's school. Roskilde gained him as bishop in 1158; Lund gained him as archbishop in 1178, with primacy over Denmark and Sweden, and eventually he served as papal legate.

In that office he laboured for the final extirpation of paganism in Scandinavia, notably on Rugen, its last stronghold. He held great political influence under King Waldemar I and Canute VI. At his request Saxo Grammaticus composed his sixteen books of Danish history, and the fourteenth book carries a tribute to Absalon himself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ancient-see-o:
Ribe, with twenty-nine deaneries and 278 parishes, covered Ribe, Vejle, and Ringkjobing, with part of North Schleswig. Saint Ansgar founded its first church in 860. Saint Rembert served it, and heathens destroyed it after his death in 888. It rose again toward 948, when Saint Leofdag, first Bishop of Ribe, was consecrated by Archbishop Adaldag of Hamburg.

Leofdag is said to have been martyred by heathens at Ribe. Until the death of his third known successor Vale, who ruled from 1044 to 1059, the bishops of Ribe, Schleswig, and Aarhus wandered Jutland on missionary tours. In 1060 Jutland was divided into Ribe, Aarhus, Viborg, and Vestervig. Bishop Thure, from 1125 to 1134, began the Cathedral of Our Lady, finished under Elias, from 1142 to 1166, who founded the chapter in 1145. Radulf, an Englishman, brought Leofdag's relics to the cathedral, though Leofdag was never formally canonized.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-galla:
Antoine Galland, a French scholar of the East born in 1646, gave Europe its first Arabian Nights. Poor after his father's early death, he won patrons who sent him to study at Noyon and Paris. At twenty-four the French ambassador took him east, where he learned Turkish, Persian, and Arabic.

As king's antiquary in the Levant, he gathered coins, inscriptions, and manuscripts for France. In 1709 he took the chair of Arabic at the College de France. His translations ranged from Indian fables to Ottoman and Persian histories, and his Nights, drawn from Arabic tales, made him famous far beyond scholarly circles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auckland:
Auckland is a diocese covering the Auckland provincial district of New Zealand, with its islets and the Kermadec Group, an area of 21,665 square miles. Its story opens in 1835, when Pope Gregory XVI erected the Vicariate Apostolic of the Western Pacific. He chose Jean Baptiste Francois Pompallier as its first vicar. Pompallier reached Hokianga in January 1838 with Marist fathers, at a time when fewer than one hundred white Catholics lived in all New Zealand.

Marist missions to the Maori people grew fast despite hostile rumors spread by Wesleyan trader-missionaries. By April 1846 about five thousand Maori had been baptized, with many more preparing. Pompallier moved his base to Auckland in 1845, and Auckland and Wellington were later split into separate sees. April 1906 figures close the entry: twenty-nine parochial districts, seventy-nine churches, about five thousand Catholic Maori, and two thousand six hundred children in Catholic schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-basutoland:
Basutoland is a mountainous district of South Africa, a prefecture apostolic of 10,293 square miles. It is bounded by the Orange River Colony, Natal, and Cape Colony, with Maseru as chief town. About 700 whites and 309,000 natives live there, ruled by native chiefs under a British Resident Commissioner. The climate is healthful, cold in winter, rainy in summer, and the country has neither railways nor proper roads.

Annexed to Cape Colony in 1871 and a Crown Colony from 1884, it became an independent prefecture on 8 May 1894. The Oblates of Mary Immaculate, present since about 1862, founded Roma, its first mission, that same year. Its first prefects were Monginoux, Baudry, and Cenez, all Oblates. Droughts, locusts, and few priests hamper evangelization, though a settled population keeps missionaries close to their flocks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bequests-for-:
Bequests for Masses in England receive a long legal history in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia. Before the Reformation, gifts of land or money for Masses were valid, save where mortmain laws barred gifts to religious houses. Tenure by divine service even bound land to prayers for the dead, and great wills of the age are full of such gifts.

The break came with the Chantries Act of Edward VI, which dissolved chantries and cast doubt on requiem Mass bequests ever since. Later statutes and court cases, including the Superstitious Uses Act, narrowed what testators could leave. The entry traces that long legal shadow from medieval piety to modern trust law.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-ferdi:
Blessed Ferdinand, Prince of Portugal, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Portugal in 1402, sixth son of King John I and Philippa of Lancaster, he died at Fez in Morocco in 1443. Sickly from youth, bodily weakness never hindered a spirit and intellect of remarkable quality, the entry says.

His mother had nursed a martial spirit in her sons, giving each a sword on her deathbed for widows, orphans, and country. Ferdinand joined the disastrous Tangier expedition of 1437, was left hostage for Ceuta, and died in captivity rather than see the city surrendered. The entry presents a prince-martyr of Portugal's crusading age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-louis:
Louis Allemand, Cardinal and Archbishop of Arles, became the leading voice for council supremacy over the pope at the Council of Basle. Born near Belley about 1380, he rose through papal service to become Bishop of Maguelonne in 1418, Archbishop of Arles in 1423, and cardinal in 1426.

At Basle he headed the party that deposed Eugenius IV and elected Felix V, whom he consecrated and crowned in 1439, while also tending plague victims and promoting the Immaculate Conception decree. After Felix resigned in 1449, Nicholas V restored Allemand's dignities, and he died in 1450, venerated as Blessed from 1527.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-catholic-univ:
The plan for a Catholic University of Ireland took shape at the Synod of Thurles in 1850. Reviving true learning mattered for the well-being of Irish Catholics, and lay students needed higher schooling on Catholic lines. They kept away from the Queen's Colleges, where religion had no official recognition. Pius IX had suggested it, and Louvain offered an inspiring example.

The Holy See approved it in 1852, funds poured in, and property was bought in Dublin. John Henry Newman became rector. He took his oath of office at Pentecost in 1854. The university's work began that November under statutes sanctioned by Rome, with papal authority to grant degrees. The hierarchy, acting through a committee, governed the institution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-christian-bro:
An entry on the Christian Brothers of Ireland, an institute founded at Waterford in 1802 by the merchant Edmund Ignatius Rice. After two centuries of penal laws, a Catholic could not legally school his children as Catholics, nor could a teacher take up the work. The ignorance and misery of Waterford's Catholic boys moved Rice to act. Bishop Hussey backed him, and in 1800 he gave his fortune and his life to the cause.

Rice opened his first school in 1802, and young men soon joined him; the citizens built them a monastery in 1803. Houses followed at Carrick-on-Suir, Dungarvan, and Cork, where the bishop summoned citizens to gain the same benefit in 1811. Dublin gained a community in 1812, and by 1907 ten Dublin communities taught over 6,000 pupils in primary and secondary schools, orphanages, and industrial schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cleveland:
The Diocese of Cleveland, established on 23 April 1847, covers the part of Ohio north of the southern limits of ten counties from Columbiana to Van Wert. Its territory spans thirty-six counties and 15,032 square miles. The first missionaries in Ohio were Jesuit Fathers Potier and Bonnecamp, coming from Quebec in 1749 to evangelise Hurons along the Vermilion and Sandusky Rivers.

Two years later Father de la Richardie joined them from Detroit and settled part of the Hurons near present Sandusky, building a chapel, Ohio's first place of Catholic worship. These Hurons took the name Wyandots on leaving the parent tribe. Drawn into the French and Indian War and then Pontiac's conspiracy, they saw the Jesuits unjustly forced out in 1752, Potier the last among the western Hurons. No systematic mission work followed until 1795, when Father Edmund Burke came as chaplain at Fort Meigs near Maumee, serving there until February 1797.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-commissariat-:
Gregory Cleary's entry defines a Holy Land commissariat in the Order of Friars Minor. It is the district assigned to a commissary gathering alms for Palestine's Holy Places, kept by the Friars Minor. More narrowly it means the convent where that commissary lives. Always a friar, he takes office by letters patent from the minister general. Each year he sends the minister an account of alms received. Those alms may never, without express leave of the Holy See, go to other ends, however pious.

Bishops' annual collections reach Jerusalem's custos through their district commissary. Forty commissariats stood across the Christian world. Naples, founded when Robert of Anjou redeemed the Holy Places from Egypt's sultan, ranks as the oldest. Seven served English-speaking lands. The United States commissariat sits at Washington's Mount Saint Sepulchre, with new houses in California and Saint Louis.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Ernest Salmon's entry covers the Congregation of Saint Edmund, founded in 1843 by Jean-Baptiste Muard at Pontigny, France, for popular missions. Members also give themselves to parish work, youth education in seminaries and colleges, direction of pious associations, and foreign missions. The motherhouse stands at Pontigny, but since the expulsion of religious orders the superior general lives at Hitchin, England.

In the United States the congregation holds two houses. Swanton, Vermont, hosts a missionary house and apostolic school training young men for priesthood and religious life. Winooski, Vermont, holds a college with twelve fathers, eight scholastics, and one hundred pupils. Short as the entry is, it maps a missionary congregation's French roots, English exile, and American classrooms in a single compact sketch.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-damaraland:
A mission entry describes Damaraland, the middle part of German South-West Africa between latitudes 19 and 23 south. From the Atlantic coast the traveller crosses a 42-mile sand belt of giant dunes. Next come ninety miles of barren desert with bare mountains. Then Hereroland proper rises to 7,000 feet, and finally the rolling Omaheke plain runs toward the Kalahari. Rain is scarce, and only cattle-raising thrives.

Its peoples were the Hill Damara, about 20,000 original possessors robbed of pastures by the invading Herero, and the Herero themselves, Bantu immigrants of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Down to modern times the Damara lived among the Herero as slaves, but sided with Germany in the Herero rising and improved their lot. Catholic missions, schools, and the region's peoples are surveyed in turn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-didymus-the-b:
Didymus the Blind of Alexandria was born about 310 and lost his sight at the age of four. Yet in time he ranked among the best-read scholars of his day. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he learned by listening, turning over at night what readers had read aloud by day. In time he seemed to have written it all on the pages of his memory.

Saint Jerome called him not the blind man but the Seer. Saint Anthony told him to rejoice in a spiritual sight shared with saints and apostles. The entry surveys his biblical commentaries and his place among the teachers of Alexandria. It also weighs which works are truly his, giving a vivid life of learning without eyes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dietrich-gres:
Dietrich Gresemund was a German humanist born at Speyer in 1477. His father, a court physician to the Elector of Mainz, gave him a thorough classical schooling. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry notes that by 1493 the youth was already linked with Wimpfeling and Abbot Trithemius. In 1494 he printed his first work, and Trithemius praised him as a youth who had outstripped many grown men, even doctors.

Gresemund studied medicine at Speyer like his father and moved in the learned circles of Mainz. He died there in 1512, only thirty-five years old. The entry gathers the scant sources for a short life that still shows how early German humanism prized Latin letters and new learning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-education-of-:
Blindness and its teaching are the subject of this long survey, which opens by noting that organised schooling for blind pupils dates only from 1784. Drawing on census figures, it puts the share of blind people at about one in five hundred in Asia. In Africa the share is about one in three hundred. In Europe it is about one in eleven hundred. In all, it reckons near two and a half million blind people alive in the world.

Heat, glare, snow light, and disease help explain why blindness clusters in hot lands and near the poles. The entry then traces teaching methods. These include raised print, the Moon system, and Braille, with its dots read by touch. It surveys schools and workshops country by country, and notes Catholic care for blind pupils. Readers get both the scale of the need and the slow craft of meeting it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ermland:
Ermland, or Ermeland, is a district of East Prussia and an exempt bishopric. Saint Adalbert of Prague, dead in 997, and Saint Bruno of Querfurt, dead in 1009, converted the heathen Prussians of this region to Christianity. Two centuries later Teutonic Knights and Cistercians brought civilization into the land as well. In 1243 the possessions of the Teutonic Knights were divided into the dioceses of Culm, Pomesanien, Ermland, and Samland.

Albert of Suerbeer, a Cologne man and former Archbishop of Armagh in Ireland, was appointed Archbishop of Prussia. In 1251 he chose Riga as his see, confirmed by Alexander IV, who in 1255 made Riga metropolitan over the four dioceses. It was not until 28 August 1251 that the first actual bishop was consecrated. Anselm of Meissen, also a Teutonic Knight priest, was consecrated at Valenciennes by the papal legate Pietro of Albano.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-established-c:
The Established Church of Scotland dates from August 1560. In that month the Scottish Parliament decided that the Protestant Confession of Faith should be the established, and only authorized, creed of the kingdom. Papal jurisdiction fell to the same Parliament's abolition, and hearing or celebrating Mass drew a death penalty under its ban. Yet appointing or maintaining the new clergy got no provision from it.

December 1560 brought the first General Assembly, and there the First Book of Discipline won approval. Doctrine, worship, the election of ministers, and their generous support from the confiscated revenues of the ancient Church all fell under its legislation. Ten districts divided Scotland, each with a travelling superintendent who instituted ministers and set the Church in order. A scheme for popular and higher education, much praised, was sketched by the Reformers, but they never carried it out.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-finland:
Finland was then a grand duchy of the Russian Empire, a land of lakes and forests. Its people, about 2,900,000 souls, were chiefly Finns, with Swedish settlers on the coasts. Christianity came from both east and west: Russian missionaries reached Karelia, and Erik of Sweden crusaded in 1157. An independent church order grew under Bishop Thomas, whose see later moved to Åbo.

The last Catholic bishop resigned in 1523, and Gustavus Vasa pressed Lutheranism on the land. By the sixteenth century's end the Catholic Church in Finland had ceased to exist. Under Russian rule from 1809, Catholics regained the right to exist, but numbered only about 1,000 souls. Most Finns belonged to the Lutheran National Church, in four dioceses with 512 parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francis-patri:
Francis Patrick McFarland, born at Franklin, Pennsylvania, on 16 April 1819 and dead at Hartford, Connecticut, on 2 October 1874, was the third Bishop of Hartford. His parents, John McFarland and Mary McKeever, had emigrated from Armagh, and from childhood he leaned toward the priesthood. After teaching in a village school he entered Mount St. Mary's College, Emmitsburg, graduated with high honours, stayed on as teacher, and was ordained at New York by Archbishop Hughes on 18 May 1845.

Hughes set him to teach at St. John's College, Fordham, but McFarland longed for parish ministry and made missionary journeys among scattered Catholics. After a year he became pastor at Watertown, New York, then in 1851 at St. John's, Utica, where seven years of saintly labour won notice as far as Rome. He declined the vicariate of Florida in 1857, was elected Bishop of Hartford, consecrated at Providence in 1858, and resided there until his diocese was divided in 1872.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-rene:
Francois-Rene de Chateaubriand, born at Saint-Malo in Brittany on 4 September 1768 and dead at Paris on 4 July 1848. He was a French writer whose Genius of Christianity helped restore Catholic imagination after the Revolution.

When the monarchy fell he sailed for America on 8 April 1791, and the wilderness gave his poetic mind inexhaustible imagery. But on Louis XVI's arrest at Varennes he felt duty-bound to serve imperilled royalty, returned to France on 2 January 1792, married, and emigrated. He joined Conde's army, was wounded and left for dead before Thionville, and escaped to England in 1793. There he lived in abject misery in London until 1800, returning under an assumed name. His Genius of Christianity, published in 1802, made him famous at once, winning him a Rome embassy secretaryship from Bonaparte and a place in the French Academy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-free-church-o:
The Free Church of Scotland broke from the established Church in 1843 over who should control the Church's own life. Known since 1900 as the United Free Church, it counted more than half a million of Scotland's Presbyterians by 1908. The entry traces a long fight over patronage, the right of private patrons to name parish ministers.

Scottish Presbyterians had claimed freedom from civil meddling since 1560, but the 1712 act restored private patronage. The Assembly's Veto Act of 1834 let congregations refuse an unwanted presentee, yet civil courts struck it down in the Auchterarder case of 1838. After a Ten Years Conflict, the evangelical party walked out in 1843 rather than yield the Church's spiritual freedom to the state.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-garland:
Garland means a wreath of flowers or evergreens once worn at baptism, weddings, funerals, and solemn processions. The earliest sure baptismal garland comes from seventh-century Alexandria, where the priest crowned the newly baptized after communion. The custom lingered there into the eighteenth century. A Gallican phrase about the baptized and crowned in Christ likely speaks in metaphor instead.

Bridal crowns began with pagan Greeks, passed to Romans, and by Chrysostom's day crowned Christian couples as victors over fleshly temptation. The Greek Church keeps the rite with silver crowns. Funeral wreaths first honored virgin martyrs, then all martyrs, and in England maids' garlands hung above graves into recent times, notably in Devon and Cornwall. Clergy too wore rose garlands in procession.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-george-of-tre:
George of Trebizond, a Greek scholar born in Crete in 1395, carried Greek learning into Renaissance Italy. Named for his family's Trebizond origin, he arrived about 1420, before Constantinople's fall, and swapped lessons with Vittorino da Feltre at Mantua, Latin for Greek. After Venice and Florence he reached Rome, where Eugenius IV gave him a leading professorship at the restored university in 1431.

Nicholas V prized him as a translator of Ptolemy and Eusebius, but arrogance and quarrels with Bessarion, Gaza, and Poggio drove him to Naples. His former pupil Paul II restored him as papal abbreviator, yet fresh quarrels followed. Siding with Aristotle against Plethon's Plato, he lost Bessarion's friendship, whose reply counted 259 errors in his translation of Plato's Laws. He died resenting obscurity in 1486.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-greenland:
Greenland is an island stretching from within the Arctic Circle south to about 59 degrees north latitude, between 20 and 75 degrees west longitude. Roughly triangular with its apex pointing south, it is bounded by the Arctic Ocean, Smith Sound, Baffin's Bay, Davis Strait, and the Atlantic. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a land of ice, fiords, and hard winters.

The interior is a plateau rising toward the east, with peaks above 13,100 feet. Immense ice fields launch glaciers to the sea. Only the southwestern valleys and south-facing hills grow vegetation, and farming is out of the question, though lettuce and cabbage thrive comparatively well. Ivigtut, outside Siberia, is the only known source of kryolite, used in making aluminum.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-guitmund:
Norman Benedictine Guitmund, later Bishop of Aversa, defended the doctrine of Transubstantiation against Berengarius of Tours in the eleventh century. A pupil of Lanfranc at Bec alongside St. Anselm, he refused a bishopric from William the Conqueror in 1070 and boldly called the Norman conquest of England robbery.

Between 1073 and 1077 he wrote his dialogue treatise On the Truth of the Body and Blood of Jesus Christ in the Eucharist, answering Berengarius point by point. His account of how Christ is present stays unclear, and he treats the decay of the species as a trick of the senses. Taking the name Christianus in Rome, he was made Bishop of Aversa by Urban II in 1088 and died there between 1090 and 1095.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-helinand:
Flemish-born poet and chronicler Hélinand, born at Pronleroi about 1150, won Philip Augustus's favour as a worldly courtier before turning Cistercian at Froidmont about 1190 and becoming a model of piety. Whatever hours monastic duty left, he gave to study, preaching after ordination, and writing, and Beauvais honours him as a saint on 3 February.

Surviving works fill a large stretch of Migne. There are twenty-eight sermons in neat Latin steeped in pagan poets and Fathers, two ascetic treatises, a letter recalling a renegade monk, and a passion of Theban Legion martyrs. A world chronicle to 1204 follows, its early part lost and its history too uncritical for much weight. A French poem on death survives in only four broken stanzas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-harland:
Henry Harland, a novelist born at St. Petersburg in 1861 to New England parents, studied theology briefly at Harvard and spent a year in Italy, returning a Catholic at heart. Rising at four before his day's work at the Surrogate's Court, he wrote As It Was Written and a Jewish trilogy signed Sidney Luska, a name he later wished forgotten. In London from 1887 he wrote stories collected in Mademoiselle Miss, Grey Roses, and Comedies and Errors.

Harland founded The Yellow Book in 1894 with Aubrey Beardsley. It made both men lions of the hour until failing health ended it in 1897, the year he and his wife entered the Church. His later novels, The Cardinal's Snuff Box, The Lady Paramount, and My Friend Prospero, are pervaded by Catholic faith. A physician gave him two years at thirty; he lived fourteen fruitful ones, dying at San Remo in 1905.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-henry-ii-king:
Henry II, king of England from 1154, was born in 1133 to Matilda, daughter of Henry I, and Geoffrey Plantagenet, from whom he inherited Anjou, Touraine, and Maine. Knighted at sixteen, ruler of Normandy and Anjou at eighteen, husband of Eleanor of Aquitaine at nineteen, he forced Stephen to terms at twenty and took the crown a year later. With his chancellor Thomas Becket he crushed feudal resistance, surrendered castles, and reorganized the exchequer and royal justice, reforms later embodied in the Assizes.

Prosperity broke on his quarrel with Becket, raised to Canterbury in 1162. Henry's attack on the jurisdiction of church courts produced the Constitutions of Clarendon, six years of persecution. Becket's murder in 1170, followed by Henry's barefoot penance at the martyr's shrine in 1174. The rebellions of his sons, probably stirred by Eleanor, embittered his closing years. He died on 6 July 1189, a king whose legal reforms outlasted his personal tragedies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hucbald-of-st:
Hucbald of St. Amand was a Benedictine monk, born in 840 and dead in 930 or 932, whose birthplace is unknown. He entered the order at St. Amand near Tournai and added music to his studies, then completed his general and artistic education at St. Germain d'Auxerre. By 883 he taught at St. Bertin, and with Rémi d'Auxerre he restored the old church singing schools in the diocese of Reims in 892.

Hucbald worked to improve neumatic notation, which showed melody's rhythm but left intervals to tradition. After trying Greek notation again, he invented the Dazia signs, which mark intervals and church modes plainly. Those signs proved clumsy and never won lasting favour, so he later fixed the scale's intervals with lines and the Latin alphabet's first letters, a step toward modern notation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-iceland:
Iceland is a North Atlantic island, counted with Europe by population and history though really part of America. It lies between set northern latitudes, separated from the New World by the ice-bound Strait of Greenland. Much indented by fjords on northern and western shores, it covers about forty thousand square miles, only two-fifths of it habitable.

From a barren, rocky plateau averaging two thousand feet high rise glaciers, broad summits, and volcanic mountains such as Hecla and Oeraefa. Those peaks have belched lava and mud to great havoc in eruptions like those of 1783, 1845, and 1873. Earthquakes are frequent, rivers short but full, and inland lakes many. The climate is oceanic, with moderate temperature swings and frequent fogs, and the entry goes on to Iceland's people, history, and church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ireland:
Ireland, set in the Atlantic west of Great Britain, is surveyed here on the encyclopedia's largest scale, from its coasts to its saints. At most it is 302 miles long and 174 miles wide. It covers 32,535 square miles in four provinces and thirty-two counties. Its center is a level plain ringed by coastal mountains. Many rivers and bays cut it. Its climate is mild yet very moist. Its soil suits farming and pasture better than mining.

Ancient names — Ierna, Juverna, Hibernia, Ogygia, Inisfail — open a history that runs through early kings, missionaries, Norse raids, Norman conquest, and later centuries of penal law and revival. Geography, peoples, church organization, schools, and literature each get their section. Readers find a whole country in one entry, written just before the political upheavals that would soon reshape it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-sirmo:
Scholar Jacques Sirmond ranked among the greatest of the seventeenth century. He was born at Riom in Puy-de-Dôme in October 1559. He died at Paris on 7 October 1651. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1576. In 1581 he became professor of classical languages at Paris. There he counted St Francis de Sales among his pupils. Called to Rome in 1590, he served sixteen years as private secretary to Superior General Aquaviva.

During those years he spent leisure moments studying antiquity's literary and historical treasures. He kept close ties with learned men then at Rome, including Bellarmine and Baronius. He helped Baronius compose the Annales. In 1608 he returned to Paris. In 1637 he became confessor to King Louis XIII. His first literary work appeared in 1610. From then until life's end, almost every year saw a new publication. The entry presents a Jesuit antiquarian at Europe's scholarly center.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-allemand: Jean Allemand, a French priest and scholar of Eastern languages born in 1799 and dead in 1833. He taught Scripture at the Roman Seminary and served as a consultor and censor in Rome. He also edited a journal of religious science. His known writings defend purgatory against an English critic and warn against Champollion's reading of Egyptian hieroglyphs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-baptiste:
Jean-Baptiste-Antoine Ferland, a French-Canadian historian born at Montreal in 1805 and dead at Quebec in 1865, spent his youth gathering notes on Canada's past before he ever wrote a book. Ordained in 1828, he served country parishes, then directed studies and later led the college of Nicolet.

Ferland turned to print only near forty, answering a rival church history in 1853 and publishing notes on Quebec parish registers. Named professor of Canadian history at Laval in 1855, he gathered fresh papers in France and drew large crowds to his public lectures from 1858 to 1862. Those lectures, printed as his Course of Canadian History, fixed his name as a founder of the field.

Jean-Baptiste Marchand, a Sulpician priest born at Verchères in 1760 and dead at Sandwich, Ontario, in 1825. He led Montreal College and then served the Hurons at Detroit for nearly thirty years. Ordained in 1786, he joined the Montreal Sulpicians in 1788. He soon headed their college, then Saint Raphael's.

In 1796 Marchand succeeded to the Huron mission at Assumption parish opposite Detroit, now Sandwich. A bishop's first recorded visit there in 1801 confirmed some five hundred people, and an assistant came, though he was recalled in 1806. Marchand laboured on mostly alone, tending a frontier flock through war, change, and distance from Quebec.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jocelin-de-br:
Jocelin de Brakelond, a late-twelfth-century English chronicler, was the Bury Saint Edmunds monk. His abbey history under feeble Abbot Hugh and energetic Abbot Sampson gave Carlyle material for the second book of Past and Present. Entering the abbey in 1173, Jocelin learned under novice-master Sampson, who made him chaplain and constant companion when he became abbot in 1182.

Jocelin served as chaplain to 1188, guest-master a decade later, and almoner in 1212, last heard in April 1215 advising Abbot Hugh II on manors. His chronicle runs from 1173 to 1202, including Henry of Essex's tale, and was first edited for the Camden Society in 1843, the edition Carlyle used. Shrewd, kindly, and plainly truthful, Jocelin won Carlyle's warm praise.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-almond:
John Almond was a Cistercian monk counted among the confessors of the faith under Elizabeth I. A native of Cheshire, he had been a monk in Henry VIII's reign. The name of his abbey is not known. His fate during and after the suppression of the monasteries cannot be traced.

His closing sufferings are known from an account printed by Foley. It tells of an aged priest worn down by imprisonment, left in Hull Castle to pine away under revolting neglect until his death on 18 April 1585. The supplementary process of the English martyrs included his case. It stands as a stark example of what Elizabethan prisons did to Catholic priests who would not conform.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-england:
John England was the first Bishop of Charleston and a leading voice for Catholic emancipation in Ireland and America. Born at Cork in 1786, he entered Carlow College in 1803 and preached to crowded congregations. He founded poor schools from which the Presentation Convent grew, and was ordained in 1809. His pen and tongue assailed the Veto measure of 1814, and next to O'Connell his influence was greatest in the agitation for emancipation.

Consecrated Bishop of Charleston at Cork in 1820, he refused the customary oath of allegiance to Britain. He reached Charleston that December to find a diocese of three states with Catholics scattered in little groups. He built up churches, schools, and a seminary, and edited a diocesan paper. He defended the Church in public controversy until his death at Charleston in 1842, leaving a model of an American bishop in a missionary age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-garland:
John Garland was an English poet and grammarian who spent most of his life teaching in France. Born in England, he studied at Oxford under John of London, one of Roger Bacon's masters, then was fostered in France, a land he cherished above his birthplace. He studied at Paris, and grammar and belles-lettres were his subjects at Toulouse and later at Paris.

Reaching Toulouse near the close of the Albigensian war, he wrote about 1229 an epithalamium for the Virgin. He also wrote his epic On the Triumphs of the Church, celebrating crusading victories and the crushing of heresy. Back in Paris by 1234, he composed a poem on accent in over fourteen hundred hexameters and a poem on the liturgy. He also wrote schoolbooks in verse: glossaries, a grammar compendium, lists of homonyms, a rhetoric, and a collection of versification examples. He took his name from Paris's Rue Garlande.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-olivie:
Joseph Olivier Briand was the seventh Bishop of Quebec and a second founder of Canada's Church. Born at Plérin in Brittany in 1715 and ordained in 1739, he secretly left home to follow Bishop Pontbriand to Canada. As vicar-general he ran the diocese during the siege of Quebec in 1759 and tended the dying at Ste-Foy in 1760.

After the British conquest, Briand judged that allegiance must change and worked to secure the Church under London. Consecrated at Paris in 1766, he won the Quebec Act of 1774, which let Catholics hold public office and confirmed religious freedom. He declined clergy gifts for his support and lived at the Quebec Seminary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-kaiserwilhelm:
Kaiserwilhelmsland was the German portion of the island of New Guinea, some 460,000 square miles with about a million inhabitants. The first Catholic missionaries arrived in August 1896, three priests and three brothers, and twelve stations soon lined a coast some four hundred miles long. The little mission steamer Gabriel linked them. An apostolic prefecture set up in 1896 passed to the Society of the Divine Word.

By 1909 the mission counted twenty-two priests, seventeen lay brothers, and twenty-nine sisters, though no native priests yet, and a cathedral, St. Michael's at Alexishafen, was already planned. Thirteen parochial schools taught six hundred pupils, and some 1,960 baptisms had taken place since the start. Language was the great difficulty: about 120 pupils at St. Michael's spoke twenty-five different tongues.
