Adults also learned trades like carpentry, smith-work, boat-building, and tailoring, in hopes the mission might one day support itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lincoln-engla:
The diocese of Lincoln was founded by St. Theodore of Canterbury in 678, when he moved the Lindiswaras out of Lindisfarne's diocese. The bishop's first seat was at Sidnacester, now Stow, until in 870 the Northmen burnt St. Mary's church, and eighty years passed with no bishop.

But this stood in the extreme corner of what was England's largest diocese. The Norman bishop, Remigius of Fécamp, chose Lincoln for his cathedral after the Council of 1072 ordered bishops into walled towns. In 1185 the earthquake damaged the cathedral, and when St. Hugh became Bishop of Lincoln the next year he rebuilt it from the foundations. The nave rose during the next half century, when Robert Grosseteste was bishop. In 1255 St. Hugh's choir came down for the Angel Choir, designed to hold his shrine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-francoi:
Louis Wolowski was a Polish-born French jurist and economist, born at Warsaw in 1810 and dead at Gisors in 1876. His father served the provisional government of the Polish rising of 1830, and sent the young Louis to Paris as a legation secretary. The family settled there, and Louis became a French citizen in 1836.

His Revue de legislation et de jurisprudence, founded in 1834, built his name, and a chair of industrial law at the Conservatory of Arts and Crafts held him for thirty-two years. Elected to assemblies in 1848, 1849, and 1871, he shaped finance, backed the Credit Foncier land bank, defended bimetallism and free trade, and helped limit child and women's labour in 1871.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-louis-legrand:
Louis Legrand was a French theologian and Sorbonne doctor, born in Burgundy in 1711 and dead at Issy in 1780. After St. Sulpice he taught at Clermont, joined Saint-Sulpice in 1739, and took his Sorbonne doctorate in 1746, later directing studies at St. Sulpice.

No major Sorbonne judgment, it was said, passed without his counsel. He drafted the condemnation of Rousseau's Emile, praised as learned, exact, and clear, though Rousseau's genius outlived it. He also framed censures of Marmontel's Belisaire and Berruyer's history, and spared Buffon's Epoques after the author's retraction, winning esteem from both writers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lund:
Lund is an ancient Catholic diocese in Scania, now the capital of that former Danish province, set on wooded heights eight miles from the Sound and twenty-four east of Copenhagen. Its university holds about 200,000 volumes and over 2,000 manuscripts, beside schools, observatory, gardens, museum, and hospitals.

Its Romanesque cathedral, crypt from the eleventh or twelfth century, was restored between 1833 and 1878, and St. Peter's alone survives of thirty medieval churches. In the Middle Ages Lund stood as metropolis of Denmark, yet fire, war, and Swedish destruction in 1452 wore it down. Ceded to Sweden in 1658, it regained life only with its university, founded in 1666.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maitland:
Maitland was a diocese in New South Wales, named for the chief settlement on the Hunter River. It began as a bishop's title in 1848. William Henry Davis then became coadjutor to Archbishop Polding of Sydney. It became a residential see only in 1865, alongside Goulburn and Bathurst.

James Murray, once secretary to Cardinal Cullen, was consecrated at Dublin on 14 November 1865. He took possession on 1 November 1866. His territory was wide at first, then trimmed in 1887 at his own request. The diocese then ran from Camden Haven to Red Head, west to Wollar and Cassilis, over about 12,000 square miles. Among some 150,000 people, 30,000 Catholics, mostly Irish, were served by 40 priests in twenty districts. Thirty convents, schools for about 4,000 children, a Redemptorist house at Waratah, and Australasia's only Catholic institute for deaf mutes completed the picture.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-maryland:
Maryland was one of thirteen English colonies that became original states of the American Union after the 1776 Revolution. It covered 13,327 square miles, 3,386 of water, with 1,275,434 people in 1906, of whom 37.1 per cent claimed church membership: 23.7 per cent Protestant, 13.1 per cent Catholic, and 0.3 per cent others. Baltimore, chief city, grew nine per cent in 1900 to 1910, reaching 558,485.

George Calvert, converted to Catholicism in 1625, withdrew from office with son Cecilius and sought a colony, and on 25 March 1634 Jesuit Andrew White's Ark and Dove party celebrated landing. The colony's genial climate, fertile soil, liberal plantation terms, and security drew settlers, but Richard Ingle's 1644 raid, aided by Claiborne, struck at the Catholic colony. In 1649 the Assembly passed the celebrated Toleration Act. Puritan usurpation later made Catholics suffer greatly, and a 1692 Act of Religion enforced England's penal laws in the colony.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mind:
Mind, in Greek nous, Latin mens, German Geist or Seele, and French ame or esprit, has been used in a variety of senses in English. The corresponding terms in other languages show a similar want of fixity. Aristotle reports that Anaxagoras, compared with other early Greek philosophers, seemed like one sober man among drunken men. He introduced nous, mind, as the efficient cause of the universe's general order.

Aristotle himself, treating the soul, identifies nous with the intellectual faculty, conceived as partly active and partly passive. The article then examines mind and consciousness, the origin of mental life, mind and matter, and mind and mechanism. It sets scholastic teaching against modern materialist and mechanist accounts of thought.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-moritz-von-sc:
Moritz von Schwind, born at Vienna in 1804 and dead at Munich in 1871, was a painter of inexhaustible invention. He was a leading ornament of the Munich school, above all a draughtsman and painter of small detail. He made little pictures harmonious in colour and composition. Romantic by nature, he deepened that bent in the studio of Ludwig Schnorr von Carolsfeld and through his Catholic schooling.

After a journey to Rome, fresco work at Karlsruhe and a short stay at Frankfurt, he reached Munich in 1847. There Cornelius strongly influenced him. His spirit recalls the minnesingers, Eichendorff and Brentano. His material was nature and life, above all child life, lyrically conceived in watercolour. He prized religious painting, and at the Wartburg castle he painted fine frescoes of the works of mercy and the life of Saint Elizabeth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-new-zealand:
New Zealand, formerly a colony, became a Dominion by royal proclamation in September 1907, remaining under British sovereignty. It consists of three main islands, North, South or Middle, and Stewart, plus smaller groups. Those groups are Chatham, Auckland, Campbell, Antipodes, Bounty, Kermadec and Cook Islands, with half a dozen atolls beyond the Cook Group. Its total area, 104,751 square miles, runs about one-seventh less than Great Britain and Ireland.

Good grazing land has made it a great wool, meat and dairy country, with considerable farming, excellent timber, and valuable though little developed minerals. Volcanoes mark the North Island's centre, Ngauruhoe erupting in 1909, and the North Island holds the boiling geysers, said to be the world's oldest except one group. The entry covers the islands' peoples, towns, government, and the Catholic Church's dioceses, missions and schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-newfoundland:
Newfoundland, a British North American colony of 42,734 square miles, is bounded north by the Strait of Belle Isle, separating it from Labrador. It faces the Atlantic east and south and the Gulf of Saint Lawrence west, between 46 and 51 degrees north and 52 to 59 degrees west. It was North America's first portion discovered by European voyagers.

The Cabots sailed from Bristol in 1497, landing on 24 June, Saint John the Baptist's festival, in the harbour they named Saint John's, its name to this day. Seeking new lands, power, wealth and territory, they also sought the Gospel's spread and heathens' conversion. They brought priests and missionaries, Augustinians or Black Friars, so Mass was surely celebrated on those shores in 1497. Portuguese, French and English settlement, fisheries, and the Catholic Church's growth follow in the entry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-newport-engla:
Newport in England is a diocese named for Newport, a town of about 70,000 at the Usk's mouth in Monmouthshire. Before Pius IX restored hierarchy in England in 1850, the old Western District had since 1840 split into two vicariates. The northern one, twelve Welsh counties with Monmouthshire and Herefordshire, was called the Vicariate of Wales.

When an Apostolic Brief of 29 September 1850 divided the country into dioceses, six South Welsh counties with Monmouthshire and Herefordshire became Newport in England and Menevia. Menevia, Latin for Saint David's, signalled two future dioceses. Its first bishop was Thomas Joseph Brown, Benedictine, who had ruled the Vicariate of Wales for ten years. In March 1895 Leo XIII split off five South Welsh counties into a new vicariate, leaving Newport as Glamorganshire, Monmouthshire and Herefordshire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oliver-almond: Oliver Almond, an English priest and writer educated at Rome from 1582 to 1587 and at Valladolid. He worked as a missionary in England and gave a precious chalice to the English College at Rome. Foley thought him brother of the martyr John Almond, but Gillow showed that link probably mistaken, and Gillow conjectures Oliver wrote The Uncasing of Heresies, printed around 1623.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-berlan:
Pierre Berland was Archbishop of Bordeaux from 1430 to 1457, born in the Médoc in 1375. Of humble birth, he studied humanities at Bordeaux and canon law at Toulouse only through friends' generosity. Ordained priest, he served as the archbishop's secretary, canon of St. Andrew's, and pastor of Soulac before his own elevation. Education absorbed him: he founded Bordeaux University and endowed St. Raphael's College with twelve scholarships for poor students.

His archbishopric sat delicately inside the Hundred Years' War, Guyenne favouring England while Joan of Arc's martyrdom and Henry VI's Paris coronation as King of France repelled him. Twice he travelled north to moderate his suzerain, failed, and transferred his allegiance to Charles VII, helping bring the whole province under the French crown as the war ended. Old and infirm, he resigned in 1457 and died soon after, honoured still: St. Andrew's tower of 1440 bears his name, Pey Berland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-bertra:
This entry covers two French cardinals named Pierre Bertrand, uncle and nephew. The elder, born at Annonay in 1280, studied and taught law at Avignon, Montpellier, Orléans, and Paris, rose high in Parliament, the King's Council, and the Queen's Chancery, then took orders. He became Dean of Puy, Bishop of Nevers, then of Autun, and cardinal under John XXII in 1331.

His best title to fame is defending the Church's rights at the 1329 Conference of Vincennes and in writings like his Libellus against Pierre de Cugnières. He founded charities at Annonay and Paris's Collège d'Autun for fifteen poor students. The younger Bertrand, born at Colombier in 1279, followed the same path to Nevers, Autun, and Arras, became cardinal in 1344, served Avignon's popes on delicate missions, and crowned Charles IV emperor. Both died at Montaud priory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-plegmund:
Plegmund was a Mercian hermit who became Archbishop of Canterbury under King Alfred. He spent his early life as a hermit on an island near Chester that took his name, Plegmundham, now Plemstall. His fame for piety and learning drew Alfred to summon him to court to help with the king's literary work.

Chosen archbishop in 890, he travelled to Rome for the pallium, the woollen band of office, from Pope Formosus. When Formosus' acts were condemned in 897 and the condemnation confirmed in 905, Plegmund's own position grew doubtful. In 908 he returned to Rome, and the next year he consecrated seven bishops in a single day, five for Wessex, before his death in 914.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poland:
Poland covers the former kingdom that stretched across the western Sarmatian Plain and the northern slopes of the Carpathians. Its area was about 435,200 square miles, twice the size of Germany, and its name likely comes from pole, the Polish word for field or plain, the mark of its landscape. Until 1772 it was bounded by the Baltic, Russia, Tatar lands and Hungary, Bohemia, and Prussia.

Its rivers run north to the Baltic, the Oder, Vistula, Niemen, and Düna, or south to the Black Sea, the Dniester, Bug, and Dnieper. Farming always led its industry. The entry divides the kingdom into its historic lands, from Great Poland and Masovia with Warsaw to Silesia, Pomerania, Volhynia, and Podolia, each with its chief cities.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prebend: A prebend is the right of a chapter member to his share of a cathedral's revenues. The word also means the share itself. In a wider sense it marks any slice of cathedral revenues set aside to keep the clergy tied to it, even those outside the chapter, in semi prebends. Prebends count as benefices and follow the same laws.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-providence-rh:
The Diocese of Providence covers the whole State of Rhode Island, and this encyclopedia entry traces its story from the first Masses on its soil to its early twentieth-century shape. It was erected on 17 February 1872, at first taking in part of south-eastern Massachusetts as well, until that district became the Diocese of Fall River in 1904. Catholic worship first appeared in the colony in late 1780, when French chaplains with Rochambeau's army said Mass openly at Newport and Providence.

Bishop Harkins, consecrated on 14 April 1887 in the still unfinished Cathedral of Saints Peter and Paul, dominates the later pages. A lover of order and method, he organized the diocese and made its charities his own, above all the orphan asylum begun in 1851. By the entry's count, sixty-one parishes stood in Providence county against eighteen small ones in the state's other four counties, a picture of a strongly Catholic little state.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rhode-island:
Rhode Island and Providence Plantations, one of the thirteen colonies, is the smallest state in the union, at 1,054 square miles. It takes in the Island of Rhode Island, Block Island, and the lands around Narragansett Bay. It is bounded by Massachusetts to the north and east, the Atlantic to the south, and Connecticut to the west. The 1910 census counted 542,674 people, and Providence, the capital at the bay's head, counted 224,326 as the industrial centre of a wealthy, dense district.

Long chiefly a manufacturing state, Rhode Island drew many Canadian Catholics after the Civil War, and in recent years Italians and Poles in great numbers. Its Catholic population counts about 65,000 Canadians and French, 40,000 Italians, 10,000 Portuguese, 8,000 Poles, and 1,000 Armenians and Syrians. A government report on religious bodies puts Catholics at 76.5 per cent of Providence, served by 199 priests in the diocese.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-i-kin:
Richard I of England, later famed in song as Coeur-de-Lion, or the Lionheart, reigned while spending most of his life outside England. Born at Oxford in 1157, the second son of Henry II, he was raised among the southern French lands of his mother, Eleanor of Aquitaine. He was made Duke of Aquitaine before he was sixteen. As a young prince he joined his brothers in revolt against their father, then made peace and waited for the crown.

King from 1189, he won renown for knightly daring and for his part in the Third Crusade, yet the entry stresses how little he governed England itself. It follows his campaigns, his captivity in Germany on the way home, his ransoming, and his death from a wound in France in 1199. Readers meet a warrior king whose legend, the article suggests, owes more to later minstrels than to his own subjects.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richmond:
The Diocese of Richmond is a suffragan see of Baltimore. It covers most of Virginia and part of West Virginia. This entry traces its story from the first Spanish landings to its organization in 1820. Richmond was erected on 11 July 1820, originally embracing Virginia and the territory that later became the Diocese of Wheeling. Its extent, measured at over 31,000 square miles in Virginia alone, is set out county by county.

Colonial beginnings came long before the diocese itself. In 1526 Lucas Vasquez de Ayllon led a Spanish party of 600 to the James River. Dominicans said Mass in a chapel, only the second Catholic place of worship on American soil. Fever killed Ayllon, and the settlement failed within a year. A Jesuit mission on the Rappahannock in 1570 ended in the martyrdom of its members. From these fragile starts, the entry follows Catholic life in Virginia down to the diocese's formal founding.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roermond:
Roermond is a diocese in Holland, suffragan of Utrecht, covering the province of Limburg. In 1909 it counted 332,201 people, among them 325,000 Catholics, with a chapter of nine canons, fourteen deaneries, 173 parishes, and 197 churches with resident priests. Its institutions included a seminary at Roermond and a boys' preparatory seminary at Rolduc. They included about seventy primary schools, two gymnasia, and schools for philosophy and theology. There were thirty-five higher schools for girls, sixty charities, forty-five men's houses with 2,400 members, and 130 convents with 3,900 sisters.

The see was erected in 1559 under Philip II, when the Netherlands dioceses were reorganized after long talks with the papacy. Roermond, its bounds fixed in 1561, became suffragan of Mechlin. The reorganization met fierce opposition from bishops who lost territory, abbots whose abbeys were absorbed, and a fast-growing Calvinism. Its first bishop, Lindanus, consecrated in 1563, could not take up his duties until 1569 and later retired amid revolution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-margare:
Margaret of Scotland, queen to Malcolm III, was born about 1045 and died in 1093. Daughter of the exiled prince Edward and granddaughter of Edmund Ironside, she reached Scotland after a storm drove her family's ship north while they fled the Norman conquest. Her entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows an English princess who became a Scottish queen.

Marriage, delayed by her wish to enter religious life, took place between 1067 and 1070. As queen she poured her energy into reforming church practice, founding religious houses, and caring for the poor, while raising children who would shape both Scotland and England. The entry weighs what can be known against what rests only on tradition, and shows why she stayed a beloved figure long after her death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scotland:
Scotland, as the term is now used, covers the whole northern part of Great Britain, divided from England by the Cheviots, the Tweed, and smaller streams. It spans about 30,000 square miles, 292 miles long and 155 broad, mostly mountainous, with only a quarter of its land cultivated. Its great entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia opens with geography before history.

The Grampians form the chief range, Ben Nevis the highest hill at 4,406 feet, and rich coalfields run east to west along the Forth and Clyde. The climate runs colder and, except on parts of the east coast, wetter than England's. Romans called the land beyond Forth and Clyde Caledonia, its people later Picts, and the country Pictland, until the name Scotland came into use. The entry then follows church, clan, and crown through the centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-shrines-in-gr:
This entry is a gazetteer of sanctuaries of Our Lady and of the saints across England, Scotland, Wales, and Ireland. In England it moves from Abingdon, where Saints Edward the Martyr and Dunstan encouraged pilgrimage, to Canterbury and Caversham. At Coventry, Leofric and Godgifu founded a splendid abbey church in 1043. Images plated with silver and rich offerings from queens and kings recur through the list.

Scotland and Ireland add their own sanctuaries. They run from Our Lady of Loreto at Musselburgh, destroyed by reformers, to Dublin, Muckross, Navan, and Trim. Trim, the most celebrated Irish shrine, saw its image publicly burnt in 1539. Shrines of saints follow, above all Thomas Becket at Canterbury. His gold-plated tomb drew pilgrims from across Christendom until Henry VIII despoiled it. Edward the Confessor, Patrick, Wulstan, and Gilbert of Sempringham stand beside him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-siam-thailand:
Siam, the land of the White Elephant and country of the Muang Thai, the Free, lies in the southeast corner of Asia between French and British possessions. It stretches some 1,130 miles north to south and covers about 242,580 square miles, near the size of Spain and Portugal together, divided into 41 provinces. Its people, estimated between six and nine million, include a third Siamese, a quarter Chinese or of Chinese descent, and Burmese, Cambodians, Laotians, Malays, and Europeans besides.

The Siamese are praised as polite, hospitable, and light-hearted, skilled as goldsmiths, painters, and carvers, living under a perpetual summer on rich rice and pepper harvests. The entry's second half is mission history. A vicariate came in 1662, the Paris Foreign Missions took charge in 1669, King Phra-Narai welcomed the missionaries, and later persecutions in 1729, 1755, and 1764 tested a church that kept growing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sigismund:
Sigismund, King of Germany and Emperor of the Holy Roman Empire, was born at Nuremberg on 15 February 1361 and died at Znaim in Bohemia on 9 December 1437. Second son of Emperor Charles IV, he was betrothed to Maria, eldest daughter of the King of Hungary and Poland. During his elder brother Wenceslaus's reign, he pressed his claim to Hungary after its king died, and on 31 March 1387 he was crowned King of Hungary.

In 1389 he had to defend his new kingdom against the Turks, after Sultan Murad I crushed the Serbian kingdom at Kosovo. Murad's son Bayezid beat a Christian army under Sigismund at Nicopolis. Bohemian clergy and nobles rebelled against Wenceslaus's favorites in 1389, backed by Sigismund and Jost of Moravia. When electors deposed Wenceslaus as emperor in 1400, he named his brother imperial vicar for Germany and governor of Bohemia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-somaliland:
Somaliland, the triangular territory at the north-eastern tip of Africa jutting toward Socotra, is the subject of this wide-ranging entry on land, people, and exploration. Bounded by the Gulf of Aden, the Indian Ocean. And the hills of Harrar and Shoa, it covered about 356,000 square miles with roughly a million inhabitants. And Greek sailors once knew it as the country of aromatic gums.

Exploration began with sixteenth-century Portuguese in Ethiopian service, stalled for centuries, and resumed in the nineteenth with Burton and others, yet knowledge stayed patchy. Harsh climate, dry soil, poor transport, and hostile inhabitants, the entry says, made it one of the least welcoming places on earth. And its frank, period tone is itself part of the historical record.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-alcmund:
St. Alcmund, or Alchmund, was bishop of Hexham, dying in 781, and this entry admits that almost nothing of his life is known beyond the veneration he drew. Hexham's church, founded by St. Wilfrid, had become an episcopal see, and Alcmund, succeeding as bishop in 767, lived in remarkable piety until his death on 7 September 781, buried beside St. Acca outside the church.

Two and a half centuries later, after Danish ravages had erased all memory of his tomb. The saint reportedly appeared in a vision, bidding a Hexham man tell Alured, sacrist of Durham, to translate his body. Alured found and exhumed the remains, pocketed one bone for Durham, and found the shrine immovable until the bone was restored, a tale the entry tells with straight-faced charm.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-brigid-of-:
St. Brigid of Ireland, incorrectly known as Bridget, was born in 451 or 452 to princely ancestors at Faughart near Dundalk in County Louth. She died on 1 February 525 at Kildare. This entry follows a girl who refused many offers of marriage, took the veil from St. Macaille as a nun, and settled with seven other virgins at Croghan Hill's foot, but moved thence to Druin Criadh in the plains of Magh Life.

There, under a large oak, she erected her famous convent of Cill-Dara, the church of the oak, now Kildare. It is exceedingly difficult to reconcile the statements of Brigid's biographers. The Third, Fourth, and Fifth Lives agree in assigning her a slave mother in the court of her father Dubhthach, an Irish chieftain of Leinster. Probably the most ancient life of Brigid, by St. Broccan Cloen, who is said to have died on 17 September 650, is metrical in form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-clair-augu:
St. Clair Augustine Mulholland was born at Lisburn in County Antrim, Ireland, on 1 April 1839. He died at Philadelphia on 17 February 1910. This entry follows a boy who emigrated to Philadelphia with his parents while still young. His youthful tastes inclined him to military affairs, and he became active in the militia ranks. At the Civil War's outbreak he was commissioned lieutenant-colonel of the 116th Pennsylvania Volunteers, attached to Meagher's Irish Brigade, and later made its colonel.

He was wounded in the Irish Brigade's famous charge up Marye's Heights at Fredericksburg on 13 December 1862. At Chancellorsville on 3 and 4 May 1863, he led his regiment and distinguished himself by saving the Fifth Maine Battery's guns, abandoned to the enemy. For that, general orders complimented him, and Congress awarded him the Medal of Honor. In that campaign General Hancock gave him command of the picket line, and he covered the army's retreat.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-clement-of:
St. Clement of Ireland, also known as Clemens Scotus, was born in Ireland towards the middle of the eighth century. He died perhaps in France, probably after 818. This entry follows a man not to be confounded with Claudius Clemens. About 771 he left for France. An Irish monk of St. Gall wrote his Acts, dedicating them to Charles the Fat, and says Clement and his companion Albinus, or Ailbe, arrived in Gaul in 772, announcing himself as a vender of learning.

So great was their fame that Charlemagne sent for them to his court, where they stayed some months. Ailbe was then put in charge of a monastery near Pavia, but Clement was asked to stay in France as master of a higher school. These events may have taken place in winter 774, after Charlemagne had been in Italy. Clement was regent of the Paris school from 775 until his death.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-louis-bert:
Louis Bertrand, Dominican missionary of the New World, sailed for America in 1562 and reaped a harvest his canonization process celebrates. Born at Valencia on 1 January 1526 to Juan Bertrand and Juana Angela Exarch, he was related through his father to Vincent Ferrer, the Dominicans' great wonder-worker. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 9 October 1581.

His boyhood showed none of the prodigies that often forecast heroic sanctity. Early he conceived becoming a Friar Preacher, and despite his father's efforts to dissuade him, he took the Dominican habit at Valencia's St. Dominic convent on 26 August 1544. After probation, in which he outshone associates as an ideal religious, he professed himself bound to perfection's life. Grave, apparently humourless, yet gentle and sweet, he won all he met. Landing at Cartagena, he entered a missionary career of extraordinary fruit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-osmund:
Osmund, bishop of Salisbury under William the Conqueror, helped draw up Domesday Book before he built a cathedral and a liturgy. A Norman of exalted standing, said to be son of Henry, Count of Séez, he came to England with his uncle the king. He served as chancellor and sat among the chief commissioners for the great survey. Lanfranc consecrated him bishop of Sarum in 1078.

His diocese joined Dorset, Wiltshire, and Berkshire at Old Sarum, a fortress hill rather than a city. There he raised a cathedral and compiled the Sarum use, the order of worship that shaped English liturgy for centuries. Present at the great assembly of 1086 that accepted Domesday, he died in 1099. His feast is kept on 4 December.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stipend:
In canon law, a stipend is the fixed payment that supports a cleric. This entry explains how that support took shape across the centuries. It starts with the Latin roots of the word, a weighed-out gift or wage, then looks at early practice, when clergy often lived by a trade.

Paul the tentmaker set that pattern. Over time, tithes from the faithful became the main support. Bishops and councils pressed for them, and Charlemagne made them compulsory. Later sections sort out benefices, endowments, and the Mass offering, which gets full treatment here. Readers gain a compact history of how the Church paid its priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sts-wigand:
Three saints named Wigand appear in the Roman Martyrology, and this entry keeps them apart. The first, bishop and martyr kept on 1 April, succeeded Domnio at Salona before 312, and his body was brought from Dalmatia by John IV in 640. His relics lie in the Lateran baptistery, which shows him in mosaic.

The second, a youth of fifteen kept on 18 May, died with ten companions under Decius at Camerino in 254. He is patron of Camerino and Fabriano, pictured as a Roman knight with banner and sword. The third, an abbot kept on 13 October, came from Berri in the later fifth century, joined the monks of St Martin of Tours, and was soon elected abbot.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-switzerland:
Switzerland, the Confederatio Helvetica, is a confederation of twenty-two cantons in central Western Europe, three of them split into half-cantons. Covering 15,976 square miles and named for Schwyz, one of the founding cantons, it divides physically into Alps, central region, and Jura. The Alps run 170 miles in a straight line from Mont-Dolent to Piz Mondin, and Monte Rosa, at 15,217 feet, is the highest peak.

Four river basins drain the country. The Rhine runs to the North Sea, the Rhone to the western Mediterranean, and the Po to the eastern Mediterranean. The Inn runs through the Danube to the Black Sea, and the first three meet at the Gotthard watershed. Great lakes rim the Alps and Jura, from Geneva and Constance to Lucerne, Lugano, Maggiore, and Zürich. The long entry then treats history and church affairs, with a wide bibliography.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-heliand:
Old Saxon poetry retelling the Gospel takes centre stage here, in the oldest complete work of German literature. Its name means Saviour. A Latin preface published by Flacius Illyricus claims Louis the Pious ordered Old and New Testament renderings into Saxon, so his subjects might know Christianity better. A Cottonian fragment found by Junius before 1587 began modern study.

Hickes printed extracts in 1705, and Eckhart identified the poem in 1720. Schmeller's full edition of 1830, from a Munich manuscript, gave the work its title. Poetic craft, Gospel harmony, and Saxon warrior imagery make the Heliand a bridge between heroic song and Christian teaching.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-irish-in-:
Irish emigrants across the world, beyond Ireland itself, fill this vast survey, opening in the United States. Irish Catholics stood in Virginia before 1633, and Irish names thread the records of Jamestown and later colonies, though exact first landings stay conjectural. Jesuit Father Andrew White's voyage in the Ark and Dove brought a storied company to Maryland.

Later sections sweep through Canada, Australia, South America, and the Continent, tracking soldiers, priests, labourers, and merchants. Numbers, parishes, and public men mark each settlement's growth. For readers tracing the Irish diaspora, the entry gathers a scattered history into one long, rich narrative.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trebizond:
An Armenian Catholic diocese on the Black Sea, named for the trapezium shape of its site. A Greek colony from Sinope founded in the eighth century before Christ, it passed through the kingdoms of Armenia and Pontus to Rome. Pompey declared it a free city and Hadrian gave it an artificial harbour.

In 1204, when Latins took Constantinople, a Comnenus prince proclaimed himself Emperor of Trebizond. He founded a Greek empire that lasted some two and a half centuries. The entry also lists eighteen Greek bishops, from Domnus at Nicaea in 325 to Dorotheus, who signed the union decree at Florence in 1439.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-twiketal-of-c:
Twicetal, also called Thurcytel or Turketul, was a tenth-century English churchman of royal blood. He died in July 975. He is said to have served as chancellor to three kings: Athelstan, Edmund, and Edred. The entry warns that this claim rests on a doubtful source and must be taken with care. In 946 he left court life to become a monk at Croyland Abbey, a house wrecked by Danish raids and sunk in ruin and want.

Chosen abbot, he gave the abbey six of his own manors and raised it back to a flourishing state. He counted St Dunstan and St Ethelwold among his friends and shared their reforming spirit for English monastic life. The entry sorts honest evidence from invention, leaning on Ordericus Vitalis. It sets aside a long fanciful life printed under the name of Ingulf, a fourteenth-century forgery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-john-almo:
John Almond was an English priest and martyr born about 1577 who died at Tyburn on 5 December 1612. His childhood passed at Allerton near Liverpool, his birthplace, and at Much Woolton. His boyhood and early manhood were spent in Ireland, until at twenty he went to the English College at Rome. There he crowned his course brilliantly with the Grand Act, a public defence of theses covering all philosophy and theology.

Cardinals Baronius and Tarugi, who presided, warmly congratulated him. The account of his death calls him a reprover of sin and a good example. It praises his ingenious and acute understanding, his sharp conceits and answers, his modesty, and his courage and readiness to suffer for Christ. Arrested in 1608 and again later, he was tried for his priesthood and suffered at Tyburn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-thomas-ho:
Thomas Holland was a Lancashire Jesuit executed at Tyburn in December 1642. Born at Sutton in 1600, he studied at St-Omer and Valladolid, then entered the Jesuit novitiate at Watten in Flanders and was ordained at Liège. A skilled linguist, he spoke French, Spanish, and Flemish, and proved adept at disguise on the English mission.

Arrested on suspicion in a London street in October 1642, he was tried at the Old Bailey for being a priest. No firm proof was offered, but his refusal to swear that he was not a priest brought a guilty verdict. Crowds flocked to him in prison, where he heard confessions and said Mass. His brethren called him a library of piety, and he was allowed a long speech and prayers before he was hanged.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-william-i:
William Ireland, alias Ironmonger, was a Lincolnshire-born Jesuit executed at Tyburn in January 1679. Educated at St-Omer, he joined the Society at Watten in 1655, served for years as confessor to the Poor Clares at Gravelines. Was sent to the English mission in 1677 as procurator, or business manager, of the province.

Arrested in person by Titus Oates on the night of 28 September 1678, he was charged with plotting to kill the king at a Jesuit meeting the previous August. A journal he kept in Newgate gives a day-by-day account of where he was away from London from 3 August to 14 September. One woman's claim that she had seen him in Fetter Lane on 20 August outweighed that alibi. After two reprieves he was executed with layman John Grove, who protested their innocence at the gallows.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-widukind:
Widukind was a Saxon leader and head of the Westphalian nobility, the moving spirit of Saxon struggles for independence and heathen faith. Frankish accounts, coloured by national feeling, give only an outline of his character. After Charlemagne's victory in 777 he fled to Denmark, judging opposition useless for the moment. When Charlemagne went to Spain in 778, Widukind returned, trusting Saxon love of independence.

Organized a war of revenge: Saxon hordes plundered the middle Rhine region and threatened Fulda, so monks fled carrying St Boniface's remains, until a Frankish army defeated them at Laisa. Hatred turned against churches and priests and Willihad, first Bishop of Bremen, abandoned his mission for a time. Charlemagne's terrible punishment of four thousand Saxons at Verden on the Aller strengthened the national party. Widukind again fled to Denmark before persuading northern Elbe people and Frisians to join the revolt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zululand:
Zululand is the South African territory between 28 and 29 degrees south latitude, inhabited by the Zulus or Amazulus of the Bantu family. Early in the nineteenth century the Zulus were a small tribe of barely two or three thousand souls. Ten years later they could field 100,000 warriors and devastated much of South Africa, terrorizing Boers and British settlers alike.

This transformation came from the military genius Tchaka, the Zulu Napoleon. Succeeding his father in 1810, he joined Dinghwiswayo, King of the Umtewa, introduced military discipline, and incorporated conquered tribes' young men into his army. By 1818 his conquerors had exterminated or subjugated all neighbours except the Umdwandwe under Zuidi. Zuidi captured and killed Dinghwiswayo but was in turn overcome by Tchaka, whose power was then unchallenged. His empire in 1820 stretched from Delagoa Bay to the Saint John River, embracing Natal, Zululand, Swaziland, Tongaland, and part of the Transvaal.
children-of-the-whirlwind:
Leroy Scott wrote Children of the Whirlwind, a novel that opens on a shabby street near New York's East River. Maggie Carlisle grows up around the pawnshop kept by the Duchess, a shriveled old woman wrapped in rumor. Larry Brainard begins life on the same hard streets. Scott warns early that unpromising beginnings can hide strong souls.

Crime, prison, and the pull of old companions shape Larry's path. Maggie faces her own temptations in a world of easy money. Their stories cross as each tries to escape the whirlwind of the title. Scott mixes underworld detail with a belief in reform and second chances. Readers get a serious popular novel of New York poverty, punishment, and the slow work of starting over honestly.
chita-a-memory-of-last-island:
Lafcadio Hearn set Chita on Last Island, the Gulf resort off Louisiana destroyed by a hurricane in 1856. The book opens with the legend of L'Ile Derniere and a journey south from New Orleans by bayou steamer to the islands. A child survives the storm that drowns the pleasure-seekers, and fishermen raise her as Chita.

Hearn divides the tale into the legend, Out of the Sea's Strength, and The Shadow of the Tide. Creole speech, Catholic fishermen, and the recovered memory of her first family carry the plot toward recognition. Hearn's prose lingers on Gulf light, water, and wind. Written from his New Orleans years, Chita is his most loved American fiction.
comic-history-of-england:
Comic History of England, by Bill Nye, illustrated by W. W. Goodes and A. M. Richards, appeared in 1896. Its preface is the publishers', not the author's. Nye's final illness kept him from writing one, and the same illness stopped the history itself at the marriage of Henry VIII to Anne Boleyn.

The publishers promise real history under the jokes: events, successions, and dates are correct, only embellished. Chapters run from Caesar's invasion and the discovery of tin through the Roman yokes, the Angles, and the Danes. Richard III gets a biography chapter with a title like a charge sheet. The humor works by motive: a knight with the biggest chest measurement, we learn, generally got the heiress with the copper-colored hair.
contributions-to-all-the-year-round:
Charles Dickens's Contributions to All The Year Round, from the 1912 Gresham edition of his works, collects his uncollected journalism from the weekly he founded in 1859. The contents begin with the announcement in Household Words of the new journal, then The Poor Man and His Beer and Five New Points of Criminal Law, both from 1859. A remonstrance on Leigh Hunt follows at Christmas.

Later pieces include the Tattlesnivel Bleater satire, a martyr medium, and sketches of young men from the country. Dickens attacks the moral poison of most cheap publications while praising the few good ones, in the passage sampled here. The volume preserves the editor's voice that weekly readers across the empire knew as well as his novels.
danger-or-wounded-in-the-house-of-a-frie:
T. S. Arthur's Danger; Or, Wounded in the House of a Friend appeared in Philadelphia in 1875. Arthur, a veteran temperance novelist, states his case in the preface. Bars and saloons, he argues, are effects rather than causes of drunkenness. The true cause lies in social drinking inside respectable homes.

The novel opens at a fashionable party on a night of fierce snow. A boy of nineteen staggers out drunk into the storm. Panoramic scenes follow other guests down the road that began with a host's wine glass. Arthur attacks the temperate use of liquor itself, not only its excess. He aims the book at parents who pour for visitors of both sexes and all ages. It is a startling cry of danger from a master of the moral tale.
disturbed-ireland:
Letters from a troubled Ireland fill Bernard H. Becker's book, printed by Macmillan of London in 1881. Becker went as special commissioner of the Daily News in the winter of 1880 and 1881. His preface says the paper gave him no instructions and no introductions, leaving his mission unfettered. Route maps serve the letters.

In Clare, at Clare Castle, Kilrush, and Kilbaha, he finds small peasant cultivators who refuse work at the slob, a mud flat job. Smoking a pipe and watching a cow and calf graze suits them better, he reports, and the slob work is too hard entirely. Becker writes with a traveller's eye and a reporter's haste. The letters show the Land War winter from the road.
division-of-words-rules-for-the-division:
Where to break a word at a line's end fills Frederick W. Hamilton's manual of 1918. The United Typothetae of America published it at Chicago as part six, number thirty-five, of the Typographic Technical Series for Apprentices. Hamilton was the group's educational director.

Spelling, pronunciation, and accent come before the rules for division. Spacing and division in lines of display close the teaching. Study questions at the back ask what the early printers did when words would not fit the line, and what practice came in later. Two systems of division are set out for the apprentice to judge. The book is a printer's school text, plain and exact, from the days of hand-set type.
doe-osti-1686143-inkjet-printing-to-scal:
Maikel van Hest of the National Laboratory of the Rockies is the contact for cooperative final report CRD-17-00690, issued in February 2026. The project sought a way to inkjet print the active layer of perovskite solar cells. Printed cells could stand alone or sit on top of plain silicon cells in a stacked tandem design.

Early work reformulated the printing inks, since inkjet work needs a thicker fluid than spin coating uses. Adding methylammonium chloride raised the base ink, made from methylammonium iodide and lead iodide, into the needed range. The report closes by stating that the planned tasks were all carried out and most project goals were met.
doe-osti-1998088-eospac-user-s-manual-ve:
Los Alamos National Laboratory manual LA-UR-23-29913, written by David A. Pimentel and issued in August 2025, is the user's manual for EOSPAC version 6.5, second edition, revision 3. EOSPAC is a subroutine package that lets simulation codes pull equation-of-state data from the SESAME library, the laboratory's standard tables for how materials behave under heat and pressure. Codes call its routines instead of reading the tables directly.

Early chapters set out naming rules, data organization, and data types for the package. A theory chapter then explains the models behind the tables, covering entropy and ion models such as the ideal gas, Cowan, and number proportional forms. Further sections derive quantities like sound speed, compressibility, specific heats, and the Grüneisen coefficient. Appendices document table types and mnemonic conventions, and a revision history tracks changes since 2018.
doe-osti-2572517-turbulent-processes-tha:
Final technical report DE-SC0020398, by Vincent Larson of the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee and covering September 2019 to September 2024, tackles a quiet flaw in how atmospheric models get graded. Graders usually compare time-averaged profiles of temperature, moisture, and vertical velocity. Averaging can hide real errors, since a model that is too smooth or too jumpy can still land on the right mean.

Larson's fix is a jump detector built from the statistics of step-to-step changes in a profile. Kurtosis flags whether sharp jumps exist, and skewness shows which way they lean. Bootstrap sampling then tests whether observations fall inside the model's spread. Data came from a Doppler lidar at the ARM site in Oklahoma. A large-eddy simulation run under the LASSO project proved too smooth, as its coarse vertical grid and numerical diffusion would suggest. A single-column sampler model was checked the same way.
doe-osti-2574640-atomic-layer-deposition:
A 2023–2024 progress report for award DE-SC0001839, by Francisco Zaera of UC Riverside and dated August 4, 2025, continues a surface science study of atomic layer deposition running since 2009. ALD builds metal and metal oxide films one atomic layer at a time, and the chemistry on the surface can differ sharply from solution chemistry. Knowing those differences is the project's long-term goal.

Work this period characterized copper deposition on silicon oxide under ultrahigh vacuum, using iminopyrrolidinate precursors. Temperature-programmed desorption and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy tracked the reactions step by step. One finding: hydrogen gas is a poor reducing agent here and cannot do the job expected of it. The program sorts reactions into those that lay down clean film, those that assist, and those that seed impurities. A newer direction extends the same scrutiny to high-surface-area porous materials.
doe-osti-2583538-solar-and-battery-stora:
Report NREL/TP-6A20-95408, dated May 29, 2025, closes a permitting research CRADA that ended early for a business reason. Aaron Levine was NREL's contact; the partner was 1Climate, under CRADA CRD-24-30367 through Solar Prize Round 7. The project set out to map the rules that slow solar and storage development: local zoning ordinances, state permitting requirements, and federal bottlenecks, for commercial, community, and utility-scale projects alike.

A second thread tested whether large language models could reliably retrieve that permitting data for future versions of 1Climate's application, alongside a roadmap of federal statutes that shape timelines. Then the partner sold its intellectual property during the CRADA's execution. The report states plainly that the tasks were therefore only partially completed or not undertaken. It stands as an honest record of an interrupted project, preserving the plan and what was learned before the work stopped.
doe-osti-2584250-a-novel-generator-for-n:
Report NREL/TP-5F00-95622, dated April 25, 2025, closes a CRADA that ended early, and says so. David Ginley was NREL's contact; the participant was Edem Tsikata, developing a generator for downhole tools. The device would harvest vibration from a drill string and store it as electrical energy, powering instruments in high-temperature, high-pressure holes where batteries fail. Geothermal drilling in hard rock was the prize application.

NREL owed two things: modeling of the generator's likely downhole effectiveness, and packaging work for extreme environments based on laboratory intellectual property. The generator itself was never delivered, so the packaging experiments could not be run. The CRADA was terminated before its tasks were completed. Modeling delivered the verdict anyway: the technique, the benefit statement concludes, would not be transformative. The report stands as the full public record of a partnership that stopped, with the reasons and the partial results preserved.
doe-osti-2587019-in-situ-laser-diagnosti:
Mruthunjaya Uddi of Advanced Cooling Technologies leads this research performance progress report for Department of Energy award DE-SC0025398, dated August 30, 2025. Prawal Agrawal, Devon Jensen, and Phil Martin supported the work, with Princeton collaborators Arthur Dogariu and Anatoli Morozov. The Phase I project, running August 2024 to August 2025, built laser diagnostics for watching plasma-surface interaction during titanium thin film deposition.

Knowing what the plasma does to the growing film, atom by atom, is the key to better coatings. The team used laser methods to track species such as atomic hydrogen formed in the plasma. One thread studied methane dissociation under 275-nanometer light, a multiphoton process whose rate climbs when plasma vibrationally excites the molecules. Measurements like these let the team connect plasma settings to the chemistry that shapes the film as it deposits.
doe-osti-2589309-regime-characterization:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL-25/46, by Arka Mitra, sorts offshore wind conditions into patterns using machine learning methods that need no preset labels. Knowing which wind patterns are normal and which are rare matters for turbine design and daily operations. Earlier studies often defined extreme events with fixed cutoffs, which limits how general the results are.

The method combines three clustering tools and applies them to 23 years of hourly model data, from 2000 to 2022, for the Humboldt Wind Energy Area off California. Inputs included wind speed and direction near the surface, plus shear and veer measured across heights from 30 to 270 meters. Six normal regimes showed clear daily and seasonal cycles. Four unusual regimes were set apart as hard for weather models to predict.
doe-osti-2589597-solid-state-transformer:
Lee Rashkin, Timothy Donnelly, Ronald Matthews, and co-authors design a transformer that shrugs off magnetic storms and pulse attacks, in Sandia report SAND2025-11715R. A high-altitude electromagnetic pulse or a geomagnetic disturbance can push slow common-mode currents into the grid. Those currents strain the large magnetic transformers the grid depends on.

The design replaces the magnetic core with power electronics in three stages: rectify, convert, then invert back to alternating current. A battery store rides along to absorb the insult. Models of the full system were run against a simulated common-mode event. The solid-state unit recovered quickly, while a standard transformer suffers under the same push. A control focus is the output inverter's extra leg, which acts only when balance is broken.
doe-osti-2997308-replace-human-intellige:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2025-11995R covers a laboratory project by William Quadros, Nick Winovich, Corey Ernst, and Nya Hardy on teaching software to carve up engineering models. Before a part can be simulated, experts split its computer model into blocks that mesh cleanly with brick-shaped elements. That judgment step is slow, variable, and hard to scale for high-stakes simulations.

The pipeline shrinks a 3D model to a 2D skeleton, then to a graph of surface and curve nodes. Each node is labeled with the cutting action an expert would take in the Cubit tool. A graph neural network trained on those labels predicts five surface actions and three curve actions on new shapes it never saw. Training used an 80/20 split and 2,000 passes over the data. The aim is expert speed without losing expert judgment.
doe-osti-2997330-gadras-drf-validation-f:
Megan Smith and Steve Horne validate a radiation analysis tool used in nuclear safeguards, in Sandia report SAND2025-11964 dated September 2025. GADRAS-DRF builds a detector response function, a model of how a gamma-ray detector sees the world, so inspectors can identify isotopes from measured spectra. Trust in its peak shapes and isotope calls must be earned with reference materials.

Work paired validation runs with upgrades to custom peak fitting software. One test series used a uniform rotating drum measured on a high-purity germanium detector. Reference uranium samples from the national standards laboratory anchor the mass calculations dated August 2020, with uranium-235 certified from 2.95 up to 52.49 percent. Matching computed masses to those certified values shows where the tool stands for safeguards use.
doe-osti-2997648-pyarc-status-report-new:
Argonne National Laboratory status report ANL/NSE-25/62 covers PyARC, the Python front end that manages fast reactor analysis workflows for the ARC code family. Authors Kalin Kiesling, Shikhar Kumar, Hansol Park, and co-authors describe new integrations and upgrades. Analysts drive many linked codes from one input file written in a structured notation, with schema checks catching errors early.

The headline change is a rebuilt language server, version 3.0.0, the background service that powers editing help. Interface upgrades improve diagnostics, validation, and navigation while a case is being written. A refactor folded the PyGriffin tool into PyARC, bringing cross-section processing, Griffin runs, post-processing, and error handling under one roof. One check, matching the Griffin and MPI executables, did not port cleanly and is noted as a gap. The report is the release record for the workflow tool.
doe-osti-2999857-foil-bearing-supported-:
R&D Dynamics Corporation's final technical report for award DE-EE0009617, led by principal investigator Giri Agrawal, covers May 2022 to June 2025. The company built a compressor-expander for heavy-duty fuel cell trucks. Fuel cells need a steady stream of compressed air, and the machine that supplies it eats power. Foil gas bearings, which float the spinning shaft on a cushion of air, allow very high speeds in a small package with no oil.

The unit pairs a centrifugal compressor with a radial turbine that claws back exhaust energy. A compact motor drives the compressor, run by a sensorless high-speed drive using silicon carbide switches, which shrank the electronics. A variable-area turbine nozzle widened the turbine's useful range. The report walks through design, tests and team roles, and closes with the path toward production. The evidence record lists no creator; the report itself names Agrawal as lead.
doe-osti-2999894-ion-irradiation-testing:
Hyosim Kim, Matthew Schneider, Emma Gordon and co-workers at Los Alamos National Laboratory compare reactor steels under bombardment in LA-UR-25-30563, issued 23 October 2025. Two steels faced self-ion irradiation at 450 degrees Celsius, up to a peak damage dose of 500 displacements per atom. That punishing dose scouts ahead of a planned neutron test in Japan's JOYO reactor, checking which steel's inner structure survives.

The candidate was 14YWT, an oxide-dispersion-strengthened steel, in its older NFA-1 and newer NFA-2 versions. Both changed little: grain size held steady, with only minor element drift at grain boundaries, though larger titanium-rich particles in NFA-2 proved unstable. The benchmark steel, HT-9, fared far worse. It showed heavy segregation and fresh precipitates, including G-phase and chromium carbides. The contrast supports 14YWT's reputation for exceptional stability in hot, high-dose service.
doe-osti-3000085-enhanced-production-of-:
Stephen Mayfield of the University of California, San Diego, leads the final technical report for award DE-EE0009671, covering October 2021 to March 2025, on squeezing more from algae. Microalgae can make oils and starches, but yields have kept algae fuels and plastics uncompetitive. The project aimed to raise biomass productivity while harvesting two product streams: lipids for fuel, and carbohydrates that serve as polyurethane precursors, the building blocks of foams and coatings.

Partners at the University of California, Davis, and Algenesis Corporation joined the work. The team combined genetic engineering, traditional breeding and high-throughput screening, then scaled to pilot ponds. Algal strains yielded natural precursor chemicals in both a cyanobacterium and a green alga, which were measured as a baseline. Breeding and directed evolution lifted biomass productivity by over 20 percent under salty, industry-like conditions. The closing chapters weigh economics and lessons, including promoters that failed in a new host.
doe-osti-3000714-developing-stable-criti:
Kevin Huang of the University of South Carolina, with Olga Marina of Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, closes grant DE-FE0032111 in this final report, submitted 30 September 2025. Reversible solid oxide cells can run both ways: burning fuel to make power, or using power to split steam into hydrogen. Running hot and hard in both directions eats electrodes, so the project hunted stable materials and structures that raise hydrogen output without early failure.

The headline result is a barrier-layer-free oxygen electrode, a BYC-LSM recipe, tuned for mid-temperature zirconia-based cells. Removing the barrier layer simplifies the cell and its cost. Studies also mapped which charge carrier rules when: proton conduction dominates in wet gas at or below 500 degrees Celsius, while oxide-ion conduction rules in dry gas at or above 700. The technology readiness level rose from 3 to 4 across the project, from concept evidence to a validated bench component.
doe-osti-3001739-energy-efficiency-for-t:
Naushita Sharma and Paul Lemar of Oak Ridge write a practical guide, ORNL/TM-2025/4259, dated October 2025, for an industry that spends heavily on electricity to clean water. Wastewater treatment runs pumps, blowers and aeration basins around the clock; energy is among its largest operating costs, yet many plants, especially smaller utilities, lack staff who specialise in efficiency. The guide comes from the Sustainable Wastewater Infrastructure of the Future initiative under Better Buildings, Better Plants.

Contents survey where energy goes in treatment processes and which upgrades pay back: aeration control, blower and pump optimisation, process tweaks and operational discipline among them. The document is written as a working resource rather than a research report, with the industry's current state and the programme's support structures as background. Utilities get a structured starting point for cutting energy bills without compromising permit compliance. Sharma and Lemar updated the resource for the programme's second phase.
doe-osti-3002277-resource-recovery-for-t:
In Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4028, dated October 2025, Naushita Sharma and Paul Lemar turn from energy to everything else a wastewater plant can recover. Modern plants increasingly act as resource factories. Treated water itself, nutrients such as nitrogen and phosphorus, and biosolids for land application all have value beyond disposal.

The report walks through recovery routes and the tools that help a plant choose among them. Federal resources listed include biogas toolkits and a food waste diversion tool that gives facility-specific leads. Diverting material from landfills is a recurring theme. The audience is utility staff weighing upgrades: recovery can cut disposal costs and create products, but each route carries its own equipment and market demands. The authors organize the options so a plant can start with its own waste streams.
doe-osti-3007466-em-musikal-multiphysics:
MuSIKAL, a coastal digital twin platform built by a four-institution team, is described in the final report for DOE award DE-SC0022211. Clint Dawson at the University of Texas at Austin led the work, joined by Notre Dame, Louisiana State, and Pacific Northwest National Laboratory. A digital twin is a live computer copy of a real coast, fed with fresh data.

Physics models of wind, rain, storm surge, and river flow feed flood forecasts for the U.S. Gulf Coast, checked against hurricanes Ike, Harvey, Ida, and Ian. The twin was built to pull diverse data into one place and configure multi-scale simulations on demand. Machine learning patches model errors and speeds the forecasts: one learned model mapped flooding in about 21 seconds with average depth error near 0.7 centimeters. A neural-operator surrogate stayed accurate up to three hours ahead in Houston tests.
doe-osti-3012483-advanced-energy-storage:
Marcus Worsley's abbreviated final report LLNL-TR-2014722, issued by Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in January 2026, closes out AESTEC, a project on energy storage for extreme conditions. AESTEC built ways to design and make storage devices that keep working under heat, cold, and mechanical stress severe enough to degrade ordinary devices or make them fail.

The project combined Livermore's strengths in computer modeling, materials synthesis, and design optimization, working from the atom scale up to full devices. Its studies targeted three processes that wear devices out: ion transport, shape change inside materials, and solid mechanics. Tests confirmed that advanced materials and better designs improved device performance. The framework serves national security work and the wider energy storage field.
doe-osti-3012692-improving-high-resoluti:
Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution's final technical report, dated January 9, 2026, for award DE-EE0009424, with Anthony Kirincich as principal investigator, closes out the third Wind Forecast Improvement Project. The project gathered observations in the Massachusetts and Rhode Island offshore wind lease areas. Its aim was sharper high-resolution wind resource assessments and forecasts over the coastal ocean, where marine air behaves in ways land-based models miss.

Instruments on shore sites, buoys, and towers measured winds, turbulence, and ocean surface currents through the field campaign. A network of high-frequency radars produced surface current maps checked against in-water instruments, agreeing within about 7 centimeters per second. The data were used to test and improve both regional and operational weather prediction models for offshore wind energy.
doe-osti-3013880-regulatory-and-technica:
Melissa Louie and Rachid Darbali-Zamora wrote Sandia report SAND2026-15630, printed January 2026, on the regulatory and technical barriers facing distributed wind energy on farms. A farm turbine can supply power on site, add resilience, and sell surplus to the grid. In practice, interconnection procedures built for generic distributed energy resources can stall or kill such projects.

Wind brings its own complications: gusty output can cause backfeeding and unintentional islanding, both dangerous to line crews, and turbines face storm damage risks other generators do not. The report maps the roles of grid operators, developers, regulators, and standards bodies, then works through federal and state rules. A recurring finding is that overlapping requirements usually repeat each other rather than conflict, which patient developers can exploit.
doe-osti-3014377-examining-aerosol-verti:
Yang Wang of the University of Miami wrote this final technical report for award DE-SC0023668, dated January 26, 2026, on aerosol transport and removal during deep convective events. Aerosols shape Earth's energy budget directly and through clouds, and the free troposphere is a major source region. Thunderstorms both lift particles upward and wash them out, and models handle that double role poorly.

Measurements at the Amazon Tall Tower Observatory and the ZF2 site in Brazil linked storm strength to particle changes below. Deep convective events reduced boundary layer potential temperature and shrank the Aitken mode aerosol size, meaning particles under 100 nanometers. Stronger convection, marked by higher cloud tops, produced larger reductions. The project cost 126,798 dollars, all from DOE, and ends with conclusions and lessons for field campaigns.
doe-osti-3016098-aoi-5-improved-efficien:
Cummins Inc of Columbus, Indiana, submitted this final technical report for award DE-EE0009460, covering work from May 2021 through July 2025. Jay Shah served as principal investigator and technical project lead. The project sought better efficiency from medium- and heavy-duty engines that burn natural gas or propane. Those fuels are used widely in trucks and off-road machines.

Spark-ignited heavy-duty natural gas engines lose efficiency at part load, because throttling needed for clean combustion wastes energy. Trucks spend much of their time at low load. The team's answer was cylinder deactivation, shutting down selected cylinders so the rest work harder and waste less. The design had to keep torque output while meeting noise, vibration, and harshness targets. The report details the rocker arm hardware that switches cylinders off and on with oil pressure.
doe-osti-3016998-center-for-alternate-sy:
Amir Osman and colleagues at Oak Ridge National Laboratory prepared the CAST PTP Network Monitoring Report in November 2025 for the Energy Department's Office of Electricity. CAST is the Center for Alternate Synchronization and Timing. The report studies how network faults disturb Precision Time Protocol, the system that keeps power grid clocks in step.

Experiments on a dedicated testbed applied set faults: symmetric static delays, asymmetric static delays, jitter, and packet loss. Results were checked by correlation analysis against timing measures. One finding: symmetric static delays largely do not affect synchronization, because the added delay cancels out during offset calculation, even though the measured mean delay rises. A commercial monitoring tool was also assessed for spotting packet loss. Grid operators who depend on precise timing for protection and measurement get a fault-by-fault guide to what actually matters.
doe-osti-3017343-s-amp-tr-september-2025:
The September 2025 issue of Science and Technology Review, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory's magazine, is cataloged here as LLNL-TR-2010131. E Jaffe, H Auten, L Ackerman, and S Hyland are the names on the issue. Its cover story marks twenty years of the laboratory's Computing Grand Challenge program. That program allocates supercomputer time to bold, large-scale projects.

Also in the issue: simulating thermonuclear weapon detonation, what asteroids reveal about the history of the solar system, and the evolution of dark matter detection. A commentary piece and a laboratory-in-the-news section round out the magazine. A quantum algorithm article describes a model that captures direction-dependent particle scattering behavior more accurately. The issue is a public-facing snapshot of a national laboratory's year in computing and physics, written for general readers rather than specialists.
doe-osti-3017503-integrated-process-mode:
Justin Galbraith of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory and John Post of Longview Fusion Energy Systems led this cooperative research final report, CRADA TC02463, dated February 8, 2026. The work used and developed an integrated process model for inertial fusion energy plant design. The model descends from the earlier LIFE power plant effort, developed with Parsons Corporation.

Under the agreement, the participant mentored the laboratory team while the process model code moved from version 1.0 to version 2.0. Funding across the eighteen-month effort totaled 474,950 dollars in cash and in-kind support. The final report lists deliverables through the final abstract, and records that no subject inventions were reported. For fusion startups, the value is a plant-level model that links physics choices to plant systems, maintained with industry at the table.
doe-osti-3017516-integrated-process-mode: Inertial fusion got process-modeled again, and this DOE text develops integrated models. The pages detail the utilization findings. The fusion folks get their data. The development was model. The data were fusion. The model was development. The fusion was inertial.
doe-osti-3020165-atomic-layer-deposition:
Francisco Zaera's final report for DOE award DE-SC0023119, from the University of California, Riverside, covers a surface science project on better oxidation catalysts, running from September 2022 to August 2025. The hosted text carries the project title 'Selective Oxidation of Oxygenates with Well-Defined Gold-Based Surface Catalytic Sites.' The team combined gold nanoparticles with thin oxide films grown one atomic layer at a time, a method called atomic layer deposition.

The goal was control over exactly where reactions happen on a catalyst surface. Researchers built platinum and titania model systems, mapped where carbon monoxide binds, and measured reaction rates. Depositing titania over platinum partly covered the metal but created new interface sites where carbon monoxide binds more weakly. Those interface sites appear to be a key stop in the reaction path. The findings guide the design of catalysts that make only the desired product.
doe-osti-3020411-em-musikal-multiphysics: MuSIKAL got AI/ML-multiphysicsed, and this DOE text discovers knowledge through simulations. The pages detail the findings. The computing folks get their data. The technologies were AI/ML. The data were computing. The discovery was knowledge. The MuSIKAL was simulations.
doe-osti-3022411-mesoscale-modeling-for-:
INL report INL/RPT-25-88176 Revision 1, by Sudipta Biswas, Larry Aagesen, and Pierre-Clement Simon of the lab with Xiaoyu Guan of the University of Florida. It models what happens inside high burnup uranium dioxide fuel. Near the pellet rim, the so-called dark zone, the original grains restructure into much smaller ones and the fuel can fragment. That change matters when a transient suddenly heats the fuel and fission gas escapes.

Mesoscale simulations follow grain size evolution and the restructured volume fraction together, producing fitted correlations for use in larger fuel performance codes. Parameter tables give rate constants and exponents at temperatures from 900 to 1,150 kelvin, with the fitted temperature dependence written as closed-form expressions. The work feeds transient fission gas release simulations in the NEAMS program.
doe-osti-3023103-high-frequency-data-int:
Patty Oikawa of California State University East Bay led this final report for award DE-SC0022185, with Lisamarie Windham-Myers of USGS, Karina Schafer of Rutgers, Rodrigo Vargas, Chris Gough, and Sara Knox. Tidal marshes store large amounts of carbon, yet Earth system models represent them poorly. The project fed high-frequency field data into landscape models to cut that uncertainty.

Eddy covariance towers supplied greenhouse gas flux readings every 30 minutes at the study marshes. The team compared ways of splitting those fluxes, including a neural network method and nighttime and daytime methods, and charted daily patterns of ecosystem respiration for summer. An isotope campaign added detail, though the authors caution that more observations are needed to confirm the patterns.
doe-osti-3023955-discerning-influences-f:
Rachel Getman's final report, covering July 2020 through December 2025 under a Department of Energy Basic Energy Sciences grant, studies how water changes catalysis inside porous zeolites. Biomass conversion reactions run in liquid, at surfaces where enthalpy and entropy of solvation pull in different directions. Knowing which force wins, and where, helps explain how catalysts act in ways gas-phase models miss.

The team computed solvation thermodynamics for eleven small oxygenates, from one to three carbons, inside titanium FAU zeolite pores made in water-shunning and water-loving forms. A convolutional neural network with an attention mechanism was trained to predict those traits, and machine learning work extended to a platinum surface dataset. Published work includes an essay on modeling of catalysis across scales at liquid-solid surfaces, prepared for ACS Catalysis.
doe-osti-3025689-cyber-informed-engineer:
Charles MaGill and Maurice Martin presented these slides in July 2025 to introduce Cyber-Informed Engineering to standards bodies. The program is sponsored by the Energy Department's cybersecurity office, CESER, and performed by Idaho National Laboratory and the National Laboratory of the Rockies. Standards bodies write the rules industries build to, so building cyber thinking into standards themselves is the leverage point.

Cyber-Informed Engineering, in their telling, designs consequences down from the start: engineered controls such as fail-safes and redundancy that cut cyber-induced failures and speed recovery. The slides warn against complacency, like assuming that piling on more security tools equals security, and against blind trust in AI. Standards groups are urged toward consequence-focused design and toward secure protocols and rules written directly into their documents.
doe-osti-3027660-alabama-carbon-storage-:
Marcella R McIntyre-Redden, Tiffany T Olsen, Christopher H Hooks, and five Geological Survey of Alabama colleagues. They close award DE-FE0032373, covering December 2023 to December 2025, with a report on carbon storage data sharing and engagement in Alabama. Storing carbon dioxide underground starts with knowing the rock, and with telling landowners and officials what is known. The geological chapters therefore carry much of the weight.

The Tuscaloosa Group is described layer by layer from well logs. A pilot sand, under 180 feet thick, holds more than 90 feet of porous sandstone in the southwest. Porous sandstone in the unit below runs 150 to 400 feet thick in the same area before turning shaly to the southeast. Above sits a marine shale about 500 feet thick, the kind of seal a storage site needs.
doe-osti-3027725-irradiation-tailoring-o:
Janelle Wharry of Purdue University reports contract DE-SC0020150, covering September 2019 to August 2024, on how radiation changes the way face-centered cubic alloys deform. Strained cold, these metals can flip patches of crystal into new phases, hexagonal epsilon martensite or cubic alpha-prime martensite. Irradiation seems to encourage the flip, as it encourages twinning and dislocation channeling, but the mechanism was unknown, and most earlier work blamed the twins.

Microscopy on Alloy 625 indents shows the cast of features up close. Shear band complexes hold twins, epsilon martensite, and untouched parent phase side by side, with diffraction patterns indexing a distorted Shoji-Nishiyama orientation relationship between the phases. The deformation in the imaged bands is almost entirely dislocation-mediated. Earlier evidence that pores enhance the transformation is part of the puzzle the project assembled.
doe-osti-3218390-unifi-specifications-fo:
Andy Hoke, Ben Kroposki, and Deepak Ramasubramanian present this February 2026 slide set on version 3 of the UNIFI grid-forming inverter specifications. UNIFI is a consortium that writes vendor-neutral rules so inverters from many makers can steady the grid together. Version 2, from March 2024, drew 140 comments from 24 people at 15 organizations. Themes ran from clearer categories and fault current to ride-through duties and power sharing.

Version 3 sorts grid-forming skill into four tiers and sets duties for normal and disturbed conditions. Modeling rules point to a draft IEEE standard, and the team plans the move to a formal IEEE standard next. Fault test tables pair full and half output, charging and discharging, with three-phase and two-phase faults at set impedances. Industry tests carry no pass or fail marks yet.
doe-osti-3367468-grid-architecture-mappi:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report, dated February 2026, defines GAMUT, a method for mapping electric grid architecture so utilities can plan transformation. Artis Riepnieks, Eric Stephan, Priya Mana, Jaime Kolln, Paul Wetherbee, and Jeff Dagle wrote it. Grid architecture work describes the whole system's structure, components, and interactions; GAMUT makes that mapping repeatable instead of bespoke.

A documentation framework anchors the method: the life cycle of documents and knowledge artifacts is itself managed, since architecture decisions scatter across slide decks, models, and meeting notes that vanish. Sections catalog knowledge sources and management practices the team adopts during projects. For utilities facing electrification and new market structures at once, the method promises design work that survives staff turnover.
doe-osti-3367547-coupling-noah-multipara:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL/EVS-26/12, by Akash Dhruv, Aaron Lattanzi, Michael Buehlmann, and colleagues, describes coupling the Noah-MP land surface model into the Energy Research and Forecasting Model. The weather model then feels a more realistic ground: soil moisture, snow, vegetation, and surface fluxes that feed back on storms and heat. Land surface schemes are where weather models quietly gain or lose skill.

The coupling leaned on an AI-assisted code pipeline the team calls CodeScribe. Large language models generated boilerplate and structural code for the legacy Fortran interface, and one model configuration achieved the lowest combined developer time for review and testing. The authors present the pipeline as reusable for scientific software with complex type hierarchies and rigid language boundaries. Climate and weather groups get both a coupled model and a development case study.
doe-osti-3374714-refabriation-of-hera-hb:
Idaho National Laboratory report INL/RPT-25-87750, dated September 2025, documents the refabrication of three pre-irradiated fuel segments. Seven authors are listed, led by Jason Schulthess, Jordan Argyle, and Spencer Parker. The segments are named HERA-HBu-2, LOC-HBu-1, and LOC-HBu-2. They belong to the lab's Advanced Fuels Campaign, which studies high burnup fuel for light water reactors.

Commercial fuel rods run about four meters long. Research reactor cores stand about one meter tall. So burned fuel must be cut down before follow-on tests can run. Gamma scans guided the cutting plans for a rod called 9EU. One sample showed a burnup of 67.2 megawatt-days per kilogram of uranium. A grid spacer shadow forced extra fuel removal near the ends. The cutting used a precision mill inside a hot cell, with vacuum capture for the removed material.
doe-osti-3375175-grid-architecture-mappi:
Pacific Northwest National Laboratory report on the GAMUT concept, by Jaime T. Kolln and Artis Riepnieks and dated July 2025, defines a mapping effort for the changing power grid. GAMUT stands for Grid Architecture Mapping to Understand Transformation. The grid is being rebuilt by new tech, new rules, and new users all at once.
